knowledge_statements.title: Intersections of Convex Quadratic Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite intersections of convex quadratic sublevel sets represented by rotated second-order cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,n\in\mathbb N\). For each \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(Q_i\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(q_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(r_i\in\mathbb R\), and choose \(k_i\in\mathbb N\) and \(L_i\in\mathbb R^{k_i\times n}\) such that \(Q_i=L_i^{\mathsf T}L_i\). Define \(\mathcal Q_r^{k_i+2}=\{(u,v,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{k_i}:u\ge0,\ v\ge0,\ 2uv\ge\lVert z\rVert_2^2\}\). Then
\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^m\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x^{\mathsf T}Q_ix+2q_i^{\mathsf T}x+r_i\le0\right\}
=
\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\left(\frac{t_i}{2},1,L_ix\right)\in\mathcal Q_r^{k_i+2},\ t_i=-2q_i^{\mathsf T}x-r_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\right\}.
\]
Thus each quadratic inequality contributes one cone block sharing the variable \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection of positive-semidefinite quadratic sublevel sets is represented by one rotated second-order cone constraint per quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) belongs to the intersection exactly when all displayed rotated-cone constraints hold.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperbolic Quadratic Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOC representation of the convex branch of a hyperbolic quadratic inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(p\in\mathbb N\), \(x,y\in\mathbb R\), and \(z\in\mathbb R^p\), the convex hyperbolic region
\[
\mathcal H=\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^p:x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ xy\ge\lVert z\rVert_2^2\right\}
\]
has the second-order-cone representation
\[
\mathcal H=\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^p:\lVert(2z,x-y)\rVert_2\le x+y\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative branch of the hyperbolic inequality xy at least the squared norm of z is exactly one standard second-order cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ xy\ge\lVert z\rVert_2^2\iff\lVert(2z,x-y)\rVert_2\le x+y\).

knowledge_statements.title: SOC-Representable Projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted definition of sets obtained by projecting affine slices of products of SOC blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is second-order-cone representable if there exist \(p,m\in\mathbb N\), dimensions \(d_j\in\mathbb N\), a lift variable \(y\in\mathbb R^p\), matrices \(F_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j\times n}\) and \(G_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j\times p}\), vectors \(h_j\in\mathbb R^{d_j}\), and standard or rotated second-order cones \(K_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_j}\) such that
\[
S=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p\ \text{such that}\ F_jx+G_jy+h_j\in K_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(S\) is the coordinate projection onto the \(x\)-space of an affine inverse image of \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOC-representable set is the projection of a finite-dimensional lifted affine system constrained by finitely many standard or rotated second-order cones.
assumptions_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
The number of cone blocks and lift variables is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is the projection of the displayed lifted conic feasible set.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary lift variable eliminated by projection.
A standard or rotated second-order cone in R^{d_j}.

children.title: Portfolio Risk Models
children.top_down_role: SOC interfaces for portfolio risk limits, penalties, and risk-adjusted objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Portfolio Risk Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOCP epigraph for standard deviation under a positive-semidefinite covariance model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) be portfolio weights, let \(\Sigma\in\mathbb S_+^n\), and choose \(L\) with \(L^{\mathsf T}L=\Sigma\). The standard-deviation risk bound
\[
\sqrt{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}\le t
\]
is equivalent to the second-order-cone constraint
\[
\lVert Lx\rVert_2\le t.
\]
Consequently, minimizing \(t\), imposing \(t\le\rho\), or combining this risk epigraph with affine budget, return, and position constraints produces an SOCP whenever the remaining objective and constraints are linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Portfolio standard deviation is the norm of a covariance factor applied to portfolio weights, so its epigraph and upper bounds are SOC constraints.
assumptions_latex: All additional portfolio constraints are affine when claiming an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}\le t\iff\lVert Lx\rVert_2\le t\).

notation.meaning: Covariance factor satisfying L-transpose L equals Sigma.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous conic reformulation of a single-period Sharpe-optimal portfolio problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(SR(x)=(\widehat r^\top x-r_f)/\sqrt{x^\top\Sigma x}\), where \(r_f\geq0\), \(\mathbf1^\top x(0)=1\), the risk-free asset is excluded from the portfolio, \(\widehat r^\top x>r_f\), and \(\Sigma\succ0\). With \(x=x(0)+u\), define \(\widetilde u=\gamma u\) and \(\widetilde x=\gamma x(0)+\widetilde u\), where \(\gamma>0\). For \(\mathrm{ns}\in\{0,1\}\), Sharpe-ratio maximization is equivalent to minimizing \(t\) subject to \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}\widetilde x\|_2\leq t\), \(\widehat r^\top\widetilde x-\gamma r_f=1\), \(\mathbf1^\top\widetilde u=0\), \(\widetilde x=\gamma x(0)+\widetilde u\), and \(\mathrm{ns}\,\widetilde x\geq0\). The original transaction vector is recovered by \(u=\gamma^{-1}\widetilde u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When excess expected return is positive and covariance is positive definite, Sharpe-ratio maximization can be homogenized and normalized to an SOCP. Dividing the scaled transaction vector by the positive scaling variable recovers the original portfolio update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max SR(x)\text{ over the stated portfolio constraints is equivalent to the stated SOCP, and }u=\gamma^{-1}\widetilde u.

children.title: Factor Risk Models
children.top_down_role: Portfolio models organized through common-factor exposure and idiosyncratic components.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Risk Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOC risk epigraph for covariance decomposed into systematic factors and diagonal specific risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the covariance model be \(\Sigma=FF^{\mathsf T}+D\), where \(F\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\succeq0\). For portfolio weights \(x\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x=\lVert F^{\mathsf T}x\rVert_2^2+\lVert D^{1/2}x\rVert_2^2.
\]
Hence the total-risk epigraph is represented by
\[
\left\lVert\begin{pmatrix}F^{\mathsf T}x\\D^{1/2}x\end{pmatrix}\right\rVert_2\le t.
\]
The factor exposure \(F^{\mathsf T}x\) and asset-specific exposure \(D^{1/2}x\) may therefore be assembled without forming the dense covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systematic factor exposure and diagonal specific risk stack into one norm whose SOC epigraph equals total portfolio standard deviation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}\le t\iff\left\lVert(F^{\mathsf T}x,D^{1/2}x)\right\rVert_2\le t\).

children.title: Factorized Covariance Interfaces
children.top_down_role: SOC representations using covariance factors or low-rank-plus-diagonal structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorized Covariance Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-factor interface avoiding explicit construction of a dense covariance matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a covariance matrix is supplied through factors \(A_j\in\mathbb R^{p_j\times n}\) satisfying
\[
\Sigma=\sum_{j=1}^m A_j^{\mathsf T}A_j.
\]
Define the stacked operator \(A x=(A_1x,\ldots,A_mx)\). Then
\[
x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x=\sum_{j=1}^m\lVert A_jx\rVert_2^2=\lVert Ax\rVert_2^2,
\qquad
\sqrt{x^{\mathsf T}\Sigma x}\le t\iff\lVert Ax\rVert_2\le t.
\]
Thus an SOCP canonicalizer may consume the factor operators directly and need not assemble or factorize \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A covariance expressed as a sum of Gram factors gives a stacked linear operator whose norm is the portfolio risk.
assumptions_latex: All matrices and variables are real and finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The covariance-risk epigraph is the SOC constraint \(\lVert Ax\rVert_2\le t\).

notation.meaning: Vertical stacking of all factor operators.

children.title: Risk-Budget Couplings
children.top_down_role: Conic organization of multiple portfolio risk limits across groups, periods, or scenarios.

knowledge_statements.title: Risk-Budget Couplings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex allocation of an aggregate risk limit across SOC-representable risk components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_gx+b_g\) denote the exposure assigned to risk group \(g=1,\ldots,G\), and let \(w_g\ge0\). A conic risk-budget coupling is
\[
\lVert A_gx+b_g\rVert_2\le t_g\quad(g=1,\ldots,G),
\qquad t_g\ge0,
\qquad \sum_{g=1}^G w_gt_g\le R.
\]
Its projection onto \(x\) is precisely
\[
\left\{x:\sum_{g=1}^G w_g\lVert A_gx+b_g\rVert_2\le R\right\}.
\]
This formulation allocates an aggregate convex risk budget; it does not assert equivalence to nonlinear Euler risk-contribution equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Groupwise SOC risk epigraphs can share an aggregate linear budget, yielding a convex weighted sum-of-norms risk limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection eliminates \(t_g\) and yields \(\sum_g w_g\lVert A_gx+b_g\rVert_2\le R\).

notation.meaning: Epigraph variable allocated to risk group g.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weighted sum-of-norms projection is mathematically plausible, but no source supports this particular meaning of risk-budget coupling. A source must distinguish it from Euler risk-contribution or risk-parity formulations.

children.title: Filter-Design Models
children.top_down_role: SOC interfaces for filter response fitting, ripple control, and magnitude bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Filter-Design Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frequency-sampled minimax filter design expressed through SOC magnitude constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\in\mathbb R^n\) be filter coefficients. At sampled frequencies \(\omega_k\), let the complex response be \(H_k(h)=a_k^{\mathsf T}h\), with \(a_k\in\mathbb C^n\), and let \(d_k\in\mathbb C\) be the desired response. The minimax constraints
\[
|H_k(h)-d_k|\le t,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,m,
\]
are equivalent to
\[
\left\lVert\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}(a_k^{\mathsf T}h-d_k)\\
\operatorname{Im}(a_k^{\mathsf T}h-d_k)
\end{pmatrix}\right\rVert_2\le t,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,m.
\]
Minimizing \(t\) subject to these constraints and affine coefficient restrictions is an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At sampled frequencies, complex filter-response errors become two-dimensional real norms, making minimax magnitude-error design an SOCP.
assumptions_latex: The filter coefficient vector \(h\) is real.
Additional coefficient restrictions are affine when claiming an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each bound \(|a_k^{\mathsf T}h-d_k|\le t\) is one SOC constraint.

notation.meaning: Complex filter response at sampled frequency k.
Desired complex response at sampled frequency k.

children.title: Array-Design Models

knowledge_statements.title: Array-Design Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sampled complex array-pattern fitting represented by two-dimensional SOC constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(w\in\mathbb C^n\) be array weights, let \(a_k\in\mathbb C^n\) be the steering vector at sample \(k\), and let \(d_k\in\mathbb C\) be a desired response. Writing \(w=w_R+\mathrm i w_I\), the sampled minimax constraint
\[
|a_k^{\mathsf H}w-d_k|\le t
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\left\lVert\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{Re}(a_k^{\mathsf H}w-d_k)\\
\operatorname{Im}(a_k^{\mathsf H}w-d_k)
\end{pmatrix}\right\rVert_2\le t.
\]
Both components are real affine functions of \((w_R,w_I)\); hence minimizing \(t\) over finitely many samples and affine weight constraints is an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complex array-pattern error at each steering sample is a two-dimensional real norm, giving an SOC minimax design model.
assumptions_latex: The steering set is replaced by finitely many samples.
Additional restrictions on real and imaginary weight components are affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each sampled magnitude-error bound is representable by one second-order cone.

notation.meaning: Complex steering vector at sample k.
Real embedding of the complex weights.

children.title: Frequency-Sampled Design Interfaces

knowledge_statements.title: Frequency-Sampled Design Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-grid interface converting complex affine response bounds into independent SOC blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and suppose the response at sample \(k\) is the complex affine function \(r_k(x)=c_k^{\mathsf T}x+d_k\). For prescribed centers \(s_k\in\mathbb C\) and radii \(u_k\ge0\),
\[
|r_k(x)-s_k|\le u_k
\]
is equivalent to
\[
\left\lVert\begin{pmatrix}
\operatorname{Re}(c_k^{\mathsf T}x+d_k-s_k)\\
\operatorname{Im}(c_k^{\mathsf T}x+d_k-s_k)
\end{pmatrix}\right\rVert_2\le u_k.
\]
Applying this conversion independently for \(k=1,\ldots,m\) yields a finite product of SOC blocks. The formulation certifies only the sampled frequencies unless an additional interpolation bound is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite frequency grid maps complex affine disk constraints to independent SOC blocks; unsampled frequencies remain uncertified without an interpolation argument.
assumptions_latex: The frequency sample set is finite.
Each response is affine in the real design vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sampled response constraints form a finite product of second-order cones.

notation.meaning: Complex affine response at frequency sample k.
Allowed response-disk radius at sample k.

children.title: Complex-Response Embeddings

knowledge_statements.title: Complex-Response Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real SOC embedding of the modulus of a complex affine scalar response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(z=u+\mathrm iv\in\mathbb C^n\), define the real embedding \(\mathcal R(z)=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{2n}\). If \(r(x)\in\mathbb C\) is affine in real variables \(x\), then
\[
|r(x)|=\left\lVert\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}r(x)\\\operatorname{Im}r(x)\end{pmatrix}\right\rVert_2.
\]
Therefore, for \(t\in\mathbb R\),
\[
|r(x)|\le t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left(t,\operatorname{Re}r(x),\operatorname{Im}r(x)\right)\in\mathcal Q^3,
\]
where \(\mathcal Q^3=\{(t,y):\lVert y\rVert_2\le t\}\). This embedding preserves affine dependence on the real decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The modulus of a complex affine scalar equals the Euclidean norm of its real and imaginary parts, producing a three-dimensional SOC constraint.
assumptions_latex: The optimization variables are represented by real coordinates.
The complex response is affine in those coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|r(x)|\le t\iff(t,\operatorname{Re}r(x),\operatorname{Im}r(x))\in\mathcal Q^3\).

notation.meaning: Real embedding that stacks real and imaginary parts.

children.title: Truss-Design Models
children.top_down_role: SOC interfaces for sizing, compliance, stress, and load-bearing truss formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Truss-Design Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground-structure truss sizing with compliance bounded through rotated SOC member constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For members \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(a_i\ge0\) be cross-sectional area, \(q_i\) axial force, \(\ell_i>0\) length, and \(E_i>0\) elastic modulus. Given equilibrium matrix \(B\), load \(f\), and compliance limit \(C\), introduce \(s_i\ge0\) and impose
\[
Bq=f,
\qquad
(a_i,s_i/2,q_i)\in\mathcal Q_r^3,
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{\ell_i}{E_i}s_i\le C.
\]
The cone constraint is equivalent to \(q_i^2\le a_is_i\). Thus minimizing the linear volume \(\sum_i\ell_i a_i\) subject to these constraints is an SOCP relaxation that is exact for the stated separable compliance epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Axial-force equilibrium plus rotated-cone force-area epigraphs gives an SOCP formulation of minimum-volume truss sizing under a compliance limit.
assumptions_latex: Compliance is modeled by \(\sum_i\ell_i q_i^2/(E_i a_i)\), with the closed perspective convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The compliance-bounded minimum-volume ground-structure model has the displayed SOCP representation.

notation.meaning: Cross-sectional area of truss member i.
Axial force in truss member i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rotated-cone perspective model is plausible, but the application-specific compliance interpretation, closed perspective convention, and exactness claim have no cited support. A truss-design source with a precise model locator is required.

children.title: Structural-Design Models
children.top_down_role: SOC interfaces for broader structural sizing and response-constrained design.

knowledge_statements.title: Structural-Design Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOCP compliance formulation for a linearly elastic truss under one static load.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each member \(i=1,\ldots,m\), introduce \(s_i\ge 0\) and impose
\[
\left\|(2q_i,a_i-s_i)\right\|_2\le a_i+s_i,
\]
which is equivalent to \(q_i^2\le a_i s_i\) with \(a_i,s_i\ge0\). Hence the compliance-limited minimum-material model
\[
\min_{a,q,s}\ c^\top a\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bq=f,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i s_i\le\Gamma,
\]
together with the displayed second-order-cone constraints and any linear bounds on \(a\), is an SOCP. For \(a_i>0\), \(s_i\) upper-bounds \(q_i^2/a_i\); when \(a_i=0\), the cone forces \(q_i=0\). If an optimum exists, an optimal representative can be selected with \(s_i=q_i^2/a_i\) when \(a_i>0\) and \(s_i=0\) when \(a_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truss material is minimized subject to equilibrium and a compliance limit, with every force-squared-over-area term represented by a rotated second-order cone. The epigraph variables can be selected tight at an attained optimum.
assumptions_latex: Member areas satisfy \(a_i\ge 0\), and axial forces satisfy equilibrium \(Bq=f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The structural-design problem is an SOCP in \((a,q,s)\).

children.title: Load-Case Couplings
children.top_down_role: Conic organization of shared design variables across multiple structural load cases.

assumptions_latex: There are load cases \(\ell=1,\ldots,L\) with forces \(f^\ell\) and weights \(w_\ell\ge0\).
All load cases share the same area vector \(a\ge0\).
Each load case has forces \(q^\ell\) satisfying \(Bq^\ell=f^\ell\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shared design variables and a common epigraph couple otherwise separable load-case SOCP blocks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite deterministic load cases with shared truss areas and aggregate or worst-case compliance.

source_refs.locator: 10 Second-order cone and robust models p. 347

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every member \(i\) and load case \(\ell\), impose
\[
\left\|(2q_i^\ell,a_i-s_i^\ell)\right\|_2\le a_i+s_i^\ell,
\qquad Bq^\ell=f^\ell.
\]
The same \(a_i\) appears in all cases. Weighted aggregate compliance is modeled by
\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^L w_\ell\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i s_i^\ell\le\Gamma,
\]
whereas worst-case compliance is modeled by \(\sum_i\alpha_i s_i^\ell\le t\) for every \(\ell\), followed by minimizing or bounding \(t\). Thus each case supplies a separate conic block, while \(a\) and possibly \(t\) create the load-case coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiple equilibrium systems have separate force variables but share member areas; aggregate or worst-case compliance constraints couple the resulting conic blocks.

children.title: Structural Degeneracy Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation issues involving vanishing members, singular stiffness, or inactive load paths.

assumptions_latex: The closed conic formulation imposes \(q_i^{\ell 2}\le a_i s_i^\ell\) with \(a_i,s_i^\ell\ge0\).

notation.meaning: force in member \(i\) under load case \(\ell\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary behavior caused by zero-area members and absence of a strictly feasible truss design.

source_refs.locator: 10 Second-order cone and robust models p. 347

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(a_i=0\), the closed rotated-cone inequality \(q_i^{\ell 2}\le a_i s_i^\ell\) implies \(q_i^\ell=0\) for every load case \(\ell\). Consequently, a prescribed zero-area pattern \(Z\) is feasible only if each load admits an equilibrium force vector satisfying
\[
Bq^\ell=f^\ell,\qquad q_i^\ell=0\quad(i\in Z).
\]
If no such vector exists, that boundary face is infeasible. Moreover, if every feasible design necessarily has some \(a_i=0\), some active compliance bound, or some conic equality, the SOCP has no strictly feasible point; standard Slater-based dual attainment and numerical regularity guarantees then need not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-area member must carry zero force. Boundary designs can therefore be infeasible, and forced boundary activity may eliminate Slater strict feasibility.

children.title: Robust-Estimation Models
children.top_down_role: SOC interfaces for bounded-influence fitting, outlier-resistant residuals, and uncertainty-aware estimation.

knowledge_statements.title: Robust-Estimation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional robust regression using the scalar Huber loss and an exact SOCP epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Huber loss by
\[
h_\kappa(r)=\begin{cases}\tfrac12r^2,&|r|\le\kappa,\\ \kappa|r|-\tfrac12\kappa^2,&|r|>\kappa.\end{cases}
\]
It has the infimal representation \(h_\kappa(r)=\min_{u+v=r}\{\tfrac12u^2+\kappa|v|\}\). Therefore \(t_i\ge h_\kappa(r_i(x))\) is represented by variables \(u_i,v_i,s_i,w_i\) satisfying
\[
u_i+v_i=r_i(x),\quad \|(2u_i,s_i-1)\|_2\le s_i+1,\quad -w_i\le v_i\le w_i,\quad t_i\ge s_i/2+\kappa w_i.
\]
Thus minimizing \(\sum_i t_i\) over any SOCP-representable feasible set gives an SOCP robust-estimation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Huber regression is an SOCP after splitting each residual into quadratic and absolute-value components and epigraphing both components with the correct quadratic scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimizing a sum of Huber losses with convex SOCP-representable constraints is representable as an SOCP.

children.title: Friction Models
children.top_down_role: SOC interfaces for friction cones, contact-force limits, and related mechanical constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Friction Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact isotropic Coulomb cone for a unilateral point contact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The admissible isotropic Coulomb contact forces form the closed convex cone
\[
\mathcal{F}_\mu=\{(f_t,f_n)\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}:\|f_t\|_2\le\mu f_n,\ f_n\ge0\}.
\]
For \(\mu>0\), membership is equivalently \((\mu f_n,f_t)\in\mathcal{Q}^{p+1}\), where \(\mathcal{Q}^{p+1}=\{(s,z):\|z\|_2\le s\}\); the cone inequality then already implies \(f_n\ge0\). When \(\mu=0\), the model reduces to the linear conditions \(f_t=0\) and \(f_n\ge0\). Linear force-balance equations and multiple contact cones may therefore be combined directly in a conic optimization model, and in an SOCP when \(\mu>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unilateral isotropic Coulomb contact has nonnegative normal force and bounds the tangential-force norm by the friction coefficient times that normal force; for positive friction this is one second-order-cone constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\mu>0\), the isotropic unilateral Coulomb friction law is a second-order-cone constraint; for \(\mu=0\), it reduces to linear constraints.

children.title: Residual-Loss Conic Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Conic representations of robust residual penalties used in estimation.

assumptions_latex: For each loss \(\rho_i\), its epigraph has a finite conic representation using a closed convex cone \(K_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The separable residual-loss objective admits a product-cone formulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical product-cone interface for separable convex losses of affine residuals.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that, for each \(i\), there are matrices and vectors such that
\[
t_i\ge\rho_i(r_i)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists z_i:\ F_i r_i+g_i t_i+G_i z_i+h_i\in K_i.
\]
Then the problem
\[
\min_{x}\ \sum_{i=1}^N\rho_i(A_i x-b_i)
\]
subject to any conic-representable constraints is equivalent to minimizing \(\sum_i t_i\) subject to \(r_i=A_i x-b_i\) and the displayed cone-membership constraints. Stacking the independent blocks gives membership in the product cone \(K_1\times\cdots\times K_N\). This interface covers norm, absolute-value, quadratic, and Huber residual atoms whenever their stated epigraph representations are used.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each convex residual loss is replaced by an epigraph cone block; stacking the blocks yields one product-cone optimization model.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Loss Conic Interfaces

children.title: Friction-Cone Approximation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between exact SOC friction models and polyhedral or simplified approximations.

assumptions_latex: The tangential cross-section is two-dimensional and \(\mu f_n>0\).
The approximation uses \(m\ge3\) equally spaced facet directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regular polyhedral friction cones have explicit radial errors that vanish quadratically in \(m\).

notation.meaning: exact tangential disk at fixed normal force

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular polygonal inner and outer approximations of a three-dimensional Coulomb friction cone.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At fixed \(f_n>0\), let \(D=\{f_t:\|f_t\|_2\le\mu f_n\}\). For regular polygons with \(m\) equally spaced directions,
\[
P_m^{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq D\subseteq P_m^{\mathrm{out}}.
\]
The largest radial shortfall of the inscribed polygon, relative to the disk radius, is \(1-\cos(\pi/m)\); the largest radial excess of the circumscribed polygon is \(\sec(\pi/m)-1\). Both are \(O(m^{-2})\). An inner approximation is conservative for force feasibility, while an outer approximation may admit forces violating the exact Coulomb law. Thus a fixed finite number of facets cannot represent the circular friction cone exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular polygonal friction cones converge quadratically in facet count; inner models are conservative, while outer models can accept physically inadmissible forces.
knowledge_statements.title: Friction-Cone Approximation Boundaries

children.top_down_role: Reusable representation transformations, their correspondence properties, and their exactness boundaries.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Graph implementations and canonical-form transformations
Conic quadratic, exponential-cone, power-cone, and semidefinite modeling chapters

assumptions_latex: The extended-real objective \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) attains its infimum when an optimizer is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective epigraphization preserves the optimal value and optimizer set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact epigraph reformulation of a minimization objective.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The minimization problem
\[
p^\star=\inf_{x\in X} f(x)
\]
is equivalent in value to
\[
p^\star=\inf_{x,t}\{t:x\in X,\ f(x)\le t\}.
\]
For every feasible \((x,t)\), replacing \(t\) by \(f(x)\) cannot worsen the objective. Consequently, whenever the infimum is attained, \(x^\star\) solves the original problem if and only if \((x^\star,f(x^\star))\) solves the epigraph problem. If \(X\) and \(\operatorname{epi}f\) possess conic representations, their intersection with the affine variable-identification constraints yields a conic formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a function equals minimizing an upper-bound variable constrained to its epigraph, preserving both value and minimizing decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Epigraphization

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

assumptions_latex: The epigraph of \(f\) and hypograph of \(g\) use compatible scalar variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Introducing an intermediate scalar gives an exact constraint reformulation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifting of a convex-versus-concave scalar inequality.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scalar-valued functions \(f\) and \(g\) on a common domain,
\[
f(x)\le g(x)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists t:\ f(x)\le t\ \text{ and }\ t\le g(x).
\]
Thus a constraint with convex \(f\) and concave \(g\) can be canonicalized by placing \((x,t)\) in \(\operatorname{epi}f\) and \((x,t)\) in \(\operatorname{hypo}g\). In the special case \(f(x)\le\beta\), only the epigraph constraint \(f(x)\le t\) and the linear bound \(t\le\beta\) are required. The reformulation is conic whenever the relevant epigraph and hypograph admit conic representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional inequality is lifted through a scalar lying above the left side and below the right side, enabling separate conic representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Epigraphization

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact intermediate-variable splitting and convex canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equivalence \[f(x)\le g(x)\iff\exists t:\ f(x)\le t\le g(x)\] requires no convexity. Convexity of \(f\) and concavity of \(g\) guarantee convexity of the standard lifted set but are not necessary for convexity of its projection. For example, \(f(x)=-x^2\) and \(g(x)=0\) give the projected feasible set \(\mathbb R\), while \(\{(x,t):-x^2\le t\le0\}\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intermediate-variable splitting is always algebraically exact, but the convex-versus-concave discipline guarantees a convex lift.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are scalar-valued on a common domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Algebraic exactness does not by itself imply convexity of the lifted formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Exactness Versus Convex Lifting

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite componentwise inequalities split through one intermediate coordinate per component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f,g:X\to\mathbb R^m\), with inequalities interpreted componentwise, \[f(x)\le g(x)\iff\exists t\in\mathbb R^m:\ f(x)\le t\le g(x).\] If every \(f_i\) is convex and every \(g_i\) is concave, the lift is convex; it is conic representable when the component epigraphs and hypographs are conic representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite componentwise functional inequality is split exactly using one intermediate coordinate per component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\le g(x)\iff\exists t\in\mathbb R^m:\ f(x)\le t\le g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Constraint Epigraphization

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hypograph of \(g\) is convex and supports conic modeling when it is conic representable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional hypograph convention for concave atoms in conic canonicalization.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The hypograph of \(g\) is
\[
\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb{R}:t\le g(x)\}.
\]
Concavity of \(g\) is equivalent to convexity of \(\operatorname{hypo}g\). A constraint \(t\le g(x)\) is therefore a convex constraint in the lifted variables. It is conic representable when there exist an auxiliary variable \(z\), a closed convex cone \(K\), and affine data \(F,G,h,k\) such that
\[
t\le g(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists z:\ Fx+Gz+ht+k\in K.
\]
Maximizing \(g(x)\) may then be written as maximizing \(t\) over this representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave function's hypograph consists of points below its graph; it is convex and can serve as a lifted conic constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Concave Hypograph Models

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness relative to a closed finite-dimensional domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(g:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be concave. Then \(\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t):x\in C,\ t\le g(x)\}\) is closed if and only if \(g\) is upper semicontinuous relative to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave hypograph over a closed domain is closed exactly when the function is upper semicontinuous on that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{hypo}g\text{ is closed}\iff g\text{ is upper semicontinuous relative to }C\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness of Concave Hypographs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hypograph canonicalization under affine substitution, affine offsets, and positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) is conic representable, then \(a^{\mathsf T}x+\beta\le g(Ax+b)\) is represented by substituting \((Ax+b,a^{\mathsf T}x+\beta)\) for its hypograph coordinates. More generally, for \(\lambda>0\), \[t\le\lambda g(Ax+b)+a^{\mathsf T}x+\beta\iff \frac{t-a^{\mathsf T}x-\beta}{\lambda}\le g(Ax+b),\] so the transformed inequality inherits the same conic lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition, affine offsets, and positive scaling preserve a conic hypograph representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities are conic representable by affine coordinate substitution.

notation.meaning: affine transformation data and positive scale

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Pullbacks of Hypograph Models
Quasiconvex Level-Set Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bisection interface for quasiconvex minimization with conic-representable sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \((L,U)=(L_0,U_0)\) and store \(\bar x\), where \(\bar x\in C\) and \(f(\bar x)\le U_0\). While \(U-L>\varepsilon\), set \(\tau=(L+U)/2\) and call the conic feasibility oracle for
\[
x\in C,
\qquad f(x)\le\tau.
\]
If feasible, store a returned feasible point \(x_\tau\) as \(\bar x\) and set \(U=\tau\); otherwise set \(L=\tau\). Upon termination, output \([L,U]\) and \(\bar x\). Because feasibility is monotone in \(\tau\), the invariant \(L<p^\star\le f(\bar x)\le U\) is maintained. The algorithm uses at most
\[
\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\log_2\left(\frac{U_0-L_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\right\rceil\right\}
\]
oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bisection tests conic-representable sublevel sets while retaining a feasible upper-bound point, and terminates with an objective bracket of the requested width.
assumptions_latex: The function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex on a convex set \(C\).
For each level \(\tau\), feasibility of \(x\in C\) and \(f(x)\le\tau\) can be decided by a conic oracle.
The tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\), and the initial data satisfy \(L_0<p^\star\le f(\bar x)\le U_0\) for a supplied point \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bisection returns a bracket \([L,U]\) with \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) and a feasible point \(\bar x\) satisfying \(f(\bar x)\le U\).

notation.meaning: current lower and upper objective bounds

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-strict lower-bound invariant for possibly unattained quasiconvex infima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^\star=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\) be finite. With exact feasibility decisions and a retained feasible upper-bound point, level-set bisection maintains \[L\le p^\star\le f(\bar x)\le U.\] The lower inequality need not remain strict: if the infimum is unattained and a trial level equals \(p^\star\), its sublevel set is empty and the update can set \(L=p^\star\). At termination, \(f(\bar x)-p^\star\le U-L\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unattained infimum the correct lower bracket is non-strict, while the retained feasible point is still epsilon-suboptimal.
assumptions_latex: Trial sublevel feasibility is decided exactly.
A feasible upper-bound point is retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le p^\star\le f(\bar x)\le U\), and termination with \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) gives \(f(\bar x)-p^\star\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.title: Correct Bisection Invariant Without Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent characterization underlying the level-set interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) on a convex set \(C\), the following are equivalent: \[f((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\quad(0\le\theta\le1),\] and \[S_\tau=\{x\in C:f(x)\le\tau\}\text{ is convex for every }\tau\in\mathbb R.\] Moreover, \(\tau_1\le\tau_2\) implies \(S_{\tau_1}\subseteq S_{\tau_2}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is quasiconvex exactly when all its sublevel sets are convex, and those sets are nested by level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff S_\tau\text{ is convex for every }\tau\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity by Convex Sublevel Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Correctness Boundary for Level Bisection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinction between sound feasibility decisions and heuristic solver statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bisection updates preserve an exact bracket only when every empty-set declaration is a sound infeasibility conclusion and every nonempty-set declaration supplies or certifies a point in \(S_\tau\). Unknown, inaccurate, or tolerance-only responses cannot safely update an endpoint without additional error margins. Quasiconvexity alone supplies neither these certificates nor a conic representation of \(S_\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level bisection needs sound oracle outcomes; quasiconvexity alone provides neither certificates nor conic representability.
assumptions_latex: Bisection updates its bracket using an oracle for \(S_\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncertified oracle outcomes do not preserve the exact objective bracket.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Correctness Boundary for Level Bisection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic structure of the perspective on positive scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p_f(x,t)=t f(x/t)\) with \(t>0\), \[p_f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda p_f(x,t)\qquad(\lambda>0),\qquad p_f(x,1)=f(x).\] Moreover, \((x,t,s)\in\operatorname{epi}p_f\) if and only if \((x,t,s)=t(u,1,r)\), where \(u=x/t\), \(r=s/t\), and \((u,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive-scale perspective is positively homogeneous, recovers the base function at scale one, and positively homogenizes its epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_f(\lambda x,\lambda t)=\lambda p_f(x,t)\) and \(p_f(x,1)=f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Homogeneity and Unit-Slice Recovery

assumptions_latex: The function \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The continuous perspective \(p_f\) is convex on its positive-scale domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-scale perspective only; the closed extension at \(t=0\) belongs to the boundary model.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The continuous perspective of \(f\) is the extended-real function
\[
p_f(x,t)=t f(x/t),
\qquad t>0,
\]
with domain \(\{(x,t):t>0,\ x/t\in C\}\). Its epigraph satisfies
\[
\operatorname{epi}p_f=\{(x,t,s):t>0,\ (x/t,s/t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.
\]
Equivalently, \((x,t,s)\in\operatorname{epi}p_f\) exactly when \(t>0\) and \(s\ge t f(x/t)\). The function \(p_f\) is convex because its epigraph is the positive homogenization of the convex set \(\operatorname{epi}f\). This definition makes no assignment at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For positive scale, the perspective multiplies a convex function by the scale after dividing its argument by that scale; the result remains convex.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Perspective Models

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-perspective boundary specialization for supercoercive functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, convex, and supercoercive, then \[f^\infty(0)=0,\qquad f^\infty(x)=+\infty\quad(x\ne0).\] Consequently, the finite zero-scale portion of the closed-perspective epigraph is \(\{(0,0,r):r\ge0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a supercoercive convex function, the closed perspective is finite at zero scale only when the numerator variable is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, and supercoercive.
knowledge_statements.title: Supercoercive Zero-Scale Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Naive Infinite Boundary Extension Is Not Closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of assigning positive infinity at every zero-scale point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(u)=u^2\), the positive-scale perspective is \(p(x,t)=x^2/t\). Assigning \(+\infty\) at every point with \(t=0\) is not lower semicontinuous because \((0,t,0)\in\operatorname{epi}p\) for \(t>0\) and \((0,t,0)\to(0,0,0)\), which that assignment excludes. The closed perspective instead has \(f^\pi(0,0)=0\) and \(f^\pi(x,0)=+\infty\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning infinity everywhere at zero scale can destroy closedness; the quadratic perspective must include its origin boundary ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The positive-scale perspective extended by \(+\infty\) on all of \(t=0\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Naive Infinite Boundary Extension Is Not Closed
Closed-Perspective Boundary Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed extension of a convex perspective at zero scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(f^{\infty}\) be its recession function. The closed perspective of \(f\) is \[f^{\pi}(x,t)=\begin{cases}t f(x/t),&t>0,\\ f^{\infty}(x),&t=0,\\ +\infty,&t<0.\end{cases}\] Its epigraph is the closure of the ordinary perspective epigraph: \[\operatorname{epi}f^{\pi}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,t,r):t>0,\ t f(x/t)\le r\}.\] Thus zero-scale feasible points encode recession directions rather than an arbitrary value assigned at the boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective extends the usual positive-scale perspective to zero scale using the recession function, producing a closed convex epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f^{\pi}=\operatorname{cl}\{(x,t,r):t>0,\ t f(x/t)\le r\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and boundary interpretation are mathematically standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the recession-function boundary formula or epigraph-closure identity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Is Essential in Perspective Cone Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the unclosed conic hull to include zero-scale recession points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(u)=0\) on \(\mathbb R\). For every \(x\in\mathbb R\) and \(t>0\), \((x,t,0)=t(x/t,1,0)\) belongs to \(\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1,r):r\ge0\}\), and \((x,t,0)\to(x,0,0)\) as \(t\downarrow0\). For \(x\ne0\), the limit is absent from the unclosed conic hull but belongs to its closure. Thus omitting closure loses genuine zero-scale recession points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for the constant-zero function, the raw conic hull omits nonzero zero-scale limits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1,r):r\ge0\}\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Is Essential in Perspective Cone Generation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit-Slice Recovery of the Base Epigraph
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery and normalization properties of the perspective epigraph cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the perspective epigraph cone \(K_f\), \[(u,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f\iff(u,1,r)\in K_f.\] Every point with \(t>0\) normalizes uniquely as \[(x,t,s)=t(x/t,1,s/t).\] Thus the base epigraph is the unit-scale slice, while the face \(t=0\) contains recession data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The original epigraph is the scale-one slice of its perspective cone, and every positive-scale cone point uniquely normalizes to that slice.
assumptions_latex: \(K_f\) is the closed perspective epigraph cone of a proper closed convex function \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(u,r):(u,1,r)\in K_f\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Slice Recovery of the Base Epigraph
Perspective Cone Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph embedding of a closed perspective as a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \[K_f=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{cone}\{(u,1,r):f(u)\le r\}.\] Then \[K_f=\{(x,t,r):f^{\pi}(x,t)\le r\}=\operatorname{epi}f^{\pi}.\] Consequently, for \(t>0\), the nonlinear inequality \(t f(x/t)\le r\) is equivalent to conic membership \((x,t,r)\in K_f\); at \(t=0\), the same membership enforces \(f^{\infty}(x)\le r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a closed perspective is the closed conic hull of the original epigraph embedded at unit scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_f=\operatorname{epi}f^{\pi}\).

notation.meaning: perspective epigraph cone generated by f

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits Perspective Cone Embeddings and is consistent with the closed perspective, but the conic-hull identity and its zero-scale interpretation have no cited source.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional-Problem Homogenization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Charnes–Cooper homogenization of an affine-fractional program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,p\in\mathbb{N}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(c,d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\). Consider \[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}\left\{\frac{c^{\mathsf T}x+\alpha}{d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta}:Ax\le b,\ d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta>0\right\}.\] With \(t=(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta)^{-1}\) and \(y=tx\), every feasible \(x\) corresponds to exactly one feasible pair \((y,t)\) for \[\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n,\,t\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{c^{\mathsf T}y+\alpha t:Ay\le bt,\ d^{\mathsf T}y+\beta t=1,\ t>0\right\}.\] Conversely, every feasible \((y,t)\) corresponds to \(x=y/t\). Corresponding points have identical objective values, so the problems have equal infima and their attained optimizers correspond bijectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-denominator affine-fractional problem is transformed into a homogeneous linear model by scaling with the reciprocal denominator; the transformation is a value-preserving bijection between feasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta>0\) at every feasible point of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\leftrightarrow(y,t)=\left(x/(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta),1/(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta)\right)\) is a feasibility- and objective-preserving bijection.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why replacing the positive Charnes–Cooper scale by a nonnegative scale need not preserve exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The inverse Charnes–Cooper map \(x=y/t\) requires \(t>0\). Replacing it by \(t\ge0\) may admit zero-scale points satisfying the homogenized constraints but corresponding to no finite original decision. A closed formulation using \(t\ge0\) is exact only when all feasible zero-scale points are excluded or are separately proved harmless for the asserted value and attainment conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse transformation requires positive scale; closing the model at zero can introduce recession points with no original counterpart.
assumptions_latex: The homogenized model comes from a positive-denominator fractional problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible zero-scale homogenized points invalidate feasible-point bijection unless separately excluded or analyzed.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity and Zero-Scale Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenization of affine cone-membership constraints under a positive affine denominator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\{x:Ax+b\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a convex cone, and suppose \(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta>0\) on \(X\). With \[t=(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta)^{-1},\qquad y=tx,\] the constraints become \[Ay+bt\in K,\qquad d^{\mathsf T}y+\beta t=1,\qquad t>0.\] The inverse is \(x=y/t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Charnes–Cooper homogenization converts affine cone membership into homogeneous cone membership plus a scale normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(d^{\mathsf T}x+\beta>0\) on the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated substitution, \(Ax+b\in K\iff Ay+bt\in K\).
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Charnes–Cooper Constraints
Auxiliary-Variable Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulations whose projection recovers the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). An auxiliary-variable lift of \(S\) is a set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\), described using variables \((x,z)\), such that \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists z\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ (x,z)\in Q\}=\operatorname{proj}_x Q.\] If an objective depends only on \(x\), then optimizing it over \(S\) is equivalent in value to optimizing it over \(Q\). The variable \(z\) is auxiliary and may encode epigraphs, graph relations, cone memberships, or intermediate affine expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An auxiliary-variable lift represents a feasible set as the projection of a higher-dimensional set while preserving objectives depending only on original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x Q\).

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of exact lifts under successive introduction of auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) for \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\), and \(Q=\operatorname{proj}_{x,z}R\) for \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m+\ell}\). Then \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xR\). Thus successive exact lifts compose to an exact lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact auxiliary-variable lifts compose; all auxiliary blocks may be existentially eliminated together.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\operatorname{proj}_xR.

notation.meaning: successive auxiliary-coordinate blocks in Q and R

knowledge_statements.title: Composition of Auxiliary-Variable Lifts

children.title: Variable-Splitting Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Reformulations that partition variable roles, expressions, or constraint participation.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Splitting Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable-term splitting by explicit image variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(A_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\) be linear, and let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The problem \[\inf_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(A_i x)\] has the exact split formulation \[\inf_{x,z_1,\ldots,z_q}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(z_i):x\in X,\ z_i=A_i x\ \text{for all }i\right\}.\] Projection onto \(x\) preserves feasibility, each feasible \(x\) has a unique compatible tuple \((z_i)_{i=1}^q\), and corresponding objective values agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introduce one image variable per separable term and equality constraints linking those variables to the original decision variable.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_i\) is linear and each \(f_i\) is extended-real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in X}\sum_i f_i(A_i x)=\inf\{\sum_i f_i(z_i):x\in X,\ z_i=A_i x\}\).

notation.meaning: split image variable corresponding to term i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact image-variable splitting representation is mathematically sound and fits the leaf, but it has no source citation or locator.

children.title: Variable-Copying Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Reformulations introducing replicated variables for separate model components.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Copying Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus lifting of constraints or objective terms sharing one variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The shared-variable problem \[\inf_x\left\{\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(x):x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^q C_i\right\}\] is equivalent to \[\inf_{x_1,\ldots,x_q,z}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^q f_i(x_i):x_i\in C_i,\ x_i=z\ \text{for all }i\right\}.\] The consensus equations give a bijection between original feasible points and feasible copied tuples, namely \(x\mapsto(x_1,\ldots,x_q,z)=(x,\ldots,x,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicate a shared variable into local copies and impose consensus equalities, allowing each term or constraint to use its own copy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shared-variable and consensus-copy formulations have identical feasible images and objective values.

notation.meaning: local copy used by component i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consensus-copy representation and bijection are correct and locally appropriate, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Copy-Consistency Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Equality-link structures and metadata connecting replicated variable instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Copy-Consistency Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-incidence condition enforcing equality of distributed variable copies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph with \(|V|=q\), choose an orientation, and let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times |E|}\) be its incidence matrix. For copies \(x_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), stack \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_q)\). The edge-consistency interface is \[(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)\mathbf{x}=0.\] If \(G\) is connected, this condition holds exactly when \(x_1=\cdots=x_q\). If \(G\) is disconnected, it enforces equality only within each connected component and therefore does not implement global consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incidence-matrix equalities enforce agreement of all copies exactly when the communication graph is connected.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an undirected graph with an arbitrarily oriented incidence matrix \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For connected \(G\), \((B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)\mathbf{x}=0\iff x_1=\cdots=x_q\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The incidence-matrix condition correctly characterizes global consensus for a connected graph and componentwise consensus otherwise, but the claim lacks a source locator.

children.title: Splitting Overhead Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Representation growth, redundancy, and sparsity effects caused by splitting or copying.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact row rank and redundancy of graph-based full-copy consistency constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) have \(|V|=q\), \(c\) connected components, and oriented incidence matrix \(B\). For copies in \(\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{rank}(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)=(q-c)n.\] The matrix has \(|E|n\) scalar rows, so its row redundancy is \((|E|-q+c)n\). A forest has no redundant consistency rows, while each additional cycle edge adds \(n\) redundant scalar rows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph consensus has rank (q−c)n; cycle edges add equality rows without shrinking its nullspace.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is an undirected graph with \(c\) connected components.
Every vertex carries a full copy in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}(B^{\mathsf T}\otimes I_n)=(q-c)n.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Redundancy in Consensus Equalities
Splitting Overhead Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal scalar dimension and equality rank required by full-copy consensus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,q\in\mathbb{N}\). Suppose one variable in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is replaced by \(q\) full copies \(x_1,\ldots,x_q\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The lifted copy space has \(qn\) scalar coordinates, an increase of \((q-1)n\). Its consensus subspace \[\mathcal{C}=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_q):x_1=\cdots=x_q\}\] has dimension \(n\) and codimension \((q-1)n\). Therefore every linear equality interface whose nullspace is exactly \(\mathcal{C}\) has rank \((q-1)n\); a spanning-tree interface attains this rank using \(q-1\) vector equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Creating q full copies adds (q−1)n coordinates, and exact linear consensus necessarily has rank (q−1)n; tree equalities attain the bound.
assumptions_latex: \(n,q\in\mathbb{N}\), and each of the \(q\) copies belongs to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
Consistency is imposed solely by linear homogeneous equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{codim}\mathcal{C}=(q-1)n\), so an exact linear interface has rank \((q-1)n\).

children.title: Projection Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Reformulations obtained by removing auxiliary coordinates from lifted feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential extended formulation of a feasible set by coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\) and define \(S=\operatorname{proj}_x Q\). Explicitly, \[x\in S\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m\ \text{such that }(x,y)\in Q.\] Hence, for any objective \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \[\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}f(x).\] If either side has an optimizer, projection or selection of a witnessing lift transfers optimal solutions between the formulations. Convexity of \(Q\) implies convexity of \(S\), although closedness need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection reformulation replaces membership in a set by existence of auxiliary coordinates in a higher-dimensional feasible set.
assumptions_latex: The lifted objective depends only on the projected coordinate \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) and \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{(x,y)\in Q}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebra of successively eliminating auxiliary coordinate blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m+\ell}\), coordinate projection is associative: \[\operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{proj}_x\bigl(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}Q\bigr).\] Thus auxiliary coordinate blocks may be eliminated simultaneously or successively while retaining the same final coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive coordinate projections equal direct projection onto the final retained coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_xQ=\operatorname{proj}_x(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}Q).
knowledge_statements.title: Associativity of Coordinate Projection

children.title: Partial-Minimization Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Representations obtained by optimizing out selected auxiliary variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugate identity associated with elimination of an auxiliary coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\). Then, as an extended-real identity, \(g^*(u)=F^*(u,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a partial minimum is the joint conjugate evaluated at zero dual coordinate for the eliminated variable.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of F in both coordinate blocks
Fenchel conjugate of the partial-minimum value function

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate of a Partial Minimum

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of a value function obtained by optimizing out auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be jointly convex and define \(g(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\). If \(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\), then \(g\) is an extended-real-valued convex function. Fiberwise attainment is not required for convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimizing auxiliary variables out of a jointly convex function preserves convexity when no fiber value is minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity under Partial Minimization
Partial-Minimization Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-function representation obtained by minimizing over auxiliary coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), define \[g(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m}F(x,y),\] and assume \(g(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \[\{(x,r):\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ F(x,y)\le r\}\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g.\] Equality holds if the infimum defining \(g(x)\) is attained whenever \(g(x)<+\infty\). Under this attainment condition, for every set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), minimizing \(g\) over \(X\) is equivalent in value to minimizing \(F(x,y)\) over \(x\in X\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and attained solutions transfer through an attaining auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial minimization removes an auxiliary variable. If negative-infinite fiber values are excluded and every finite fiber infimum is attained, the value function's epigraph is exactly the projection of the lifted epigraph.
assumptions_latex: For epigraph equality, the fiber infimum is attained whenever \(g(x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}g=\operatorname{proj}_{x,r}\operatorname{epi}F\) under the stated fiberwise attainment and no-negative-infinity assumptions.

children.title: Projected-Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Mappings between retained variables and compatible lifted solutions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic recovery procedure when only retained coordinates are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\) and \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), recover discarded coordinates by solving \(\text{find }y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in Q\). This feasibility problem succeeds exactly when \(x\in S\). Any returned \(y\) is a valid lifted witness, and recovery is unique exactly when the fiber \(Q_x=\{y:(x,y)\in Q\}\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover discarded coordinates by solving the fiber-feasibility problem; it succeeds exactly for projected-feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in S\iff Q_x\ne\varnothing,\qquad |Q_x|=1\iff\text{the compatible lift is unique}.

notation.meaning: fiber of compatible auxiliary coordinates over x

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Witness Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact correspondence between projected and lifted optimizers for objectives using only retained coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), let the lifted objective be \(f(x)\), and write \(Q_x=\{y:(x,y)\in Q\}\). Then \[\operatorname{argmin}_{(x,y)\in Q}f(x)=\{(x,y):x\in\operatorname{argmin}_{u\in S}f(u),\ y\in Q_x\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lifted optimizers are exactly the feasible auxiliary witnesses lying over projected optimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{argmin}_{(x,y)\in Q}f(x)=\bigcup_{x\in\operatorname{argmin}_{u\in S}f(u)}\{x\}\times Q_x.

notation.meaning: fiber of feasible lifted witnesses over x

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer Fiber Correspondence
Projected-Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery and certification of an original optimizer from a lifted solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), and suppose the lifted problem minimizes \(f(x)\) over \((x,y)\in Q\). If \((x^\star,y^\star)\in Q\) and a valid lower bound \(L\) satisfies \[f(x^\star)=L\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in S,\] then \(x^\star\) is an optimizer of the projected problem. The pair \((x^\star,y^\star)\) supplies a directly checkable feasibility witness, while the matching lower bound certifies optimality. Without a retained witness \(y^\star\), projected feasibility may require solving a separate completion problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Project the lifted optimizer; its auxiliary coordinates witness feasibility, and a matching valid lower bound certifies optimality in the original problem.
assumptions_latex: The lifted objective is \(f(x)\), independent of \(y\).
\(L\) is a valid lower bound on \(f\) over \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^\star,y^\star)\in Q\) and \(f(x^\star)=L\) certify \(x^\star\in\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in S}f(x)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility witness plus matching lower bound is a valid optimality certificate and the content kind fits the recovery leaf, but no source is cited.

children.title: Projection Closure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Closedness, attainment, and representability issues arising after coordinate removal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential mechanism by which a closed lift can have a missing projected limit point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\) be closed. If \(x_k\in\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), \(x_k\to\bar x\), and \(\bar x\notin\operatorname{proj}_xQ\), then every selection \(y_k\) with \((x_k,y_k)\in Q\) satisfies \(\lVert y_k\rVert\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A missing projected limit point forces every compatible sequence of auxiliary witnesses to escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall y_k\in Q_{x_k}:\ \lVert y_k\rVert\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Escaping-Witness Mechanism

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient condition preventing loss of closedness under coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times K\) be closed, where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is compact. Then \(\operatorname{proj}_xQ\) is closed. More generally, the conclusion holds when every sequence \((x_k,y_k)\in Q\) with convergent \(x_k\) has a subsequence whose \(y\)-coordinates converge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed lift has a closed projection when auxiliary witnesses cannot escape, in particular when they lie in a compact set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_xQ\text{ is closed}.

notation.meaning: compact set containing all auxiliary coordinates

knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Fiber Closed-Projection Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Important representation class in which finite-dimensional projection preserves closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\) is a polyhedron, then \(\operatorname{proj}_xP\) is a polyhedron and therefore closed. Thus the nonclosed-projection pathology cannot arise from a finite system of non-strict linear equalities and inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate projections of polyhedra remain polyhedra and hence remain closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_xP\text{ is a closed polyhedron}.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Projection Closedness
Projection Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex sets can have nonclosed linear projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the closed convex set \[C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ xy\ge1\}.\] Equivalently, \(C\) is the epigraph of the closed extended-real convex function equal to \(1/x\) for \(x>0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Its projection onto the first coordinate is \[\operatorname{proj}_x C=(0,+\infty),\] which is not closed. Thus finite-dimensional linear projection preserves convexity but not closedness; closure or an attainment condition is required when identifying a projected epigraph with a closed value-function epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection preserves convexity but can destroy closedness, as the closed convex set xy≥1 in the nonnegative quadrant demonstrates.
assumptions_latex: Projection is onto the first coordinate of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex, but \(\operatorname{proj}_xC=(0,+\infty)\) is not closed.

children.title: Variable-Elimination Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Exact removal of variables through affine substitution or recoverable structural relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Elimination Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination of an unrestricted variable block through a nonsingular equality subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,m\ge 1\), \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a closed convex cone, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c_x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(c_y\in\mathbb R^m\). For unrestricted \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), consider
\[\inf_{x\in K,\,y\in\mathbb R^m}\{c_x^{\mathsf T}x+c_y^{\mathsf T}y:Ax+By=b\}.\]
Its exact variable-elimination reformulation is
\[\inf_{x\in K}\left\{c_x^{\mathsf T}x+c_y^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}(b-Ax)\right\}.\]
The feasible points correspond bijectively under \(y=B^{-1}(b-Ax)\), so the two problems have the same feasible objective values and the same extended-real optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A free variable block determined by a nonsingular equality subsystem can be substituted out exactly without changing feasible objective values or the extended-real optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=B^{-1}(b-Ax)\) gives an objective-preserving bijection between the original and reduced feasible sets.

notation.meaning: Retained and eliminated variable blocks in \(\mathbb R^n\) and \(\mathbb R^m\), respectively.

source_refs.locator: 9.5 Modeling with LP and QP p. 320

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Modeling with LP and QP p. 320

children.title: Model-Condensation Reformulations
children.top_down_role: Reduced representations formed by aggregating or compressing model components.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Condensation Reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block substitution that constructs a smaller equivalent conic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,m,\ell\ge1\), \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^\ell\) be closed convex cones, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), \(F\in\mathbb R^{\ell\times n}\), \(G\in\mathbb R^{\ell\times m}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(h\in\mathbb R^\ell\), \(c_x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(c_y\in\mathbb R^m\). Given
\[\inf_{x\in K,\,y\in\mathbb R^m}\{c_x^{\mathsf T}x+c_y^{\mathsf T}y:Ax+By=b,\ Fx+Gy-h\in C\},\]
compute \(y(x)=B^{-1}(b-Ax)\) and replace every occurrence of \(y\) by \(y(x)\), obtaining
\[\inf_{x\in K}\{c_x^{\mathsf T}x+c_y^{\mathsf T}y(x):Fx+Gy(x)-h\in C\}.\]
Solve the condensed problem and retain \(y(x)\) as the recovery map for the removed variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Condensation solves a nonsingular equality subsystem, substitutes its solution throughout the model, and retains the substitution map for recovering the removed variables.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^\ell\) are closed convex cones.
\(y\in\mathbb R^m\) is unrestricted apart from the displayed constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure constructs a model in \(x\) exactly equivalent to the original model under \(y=y(x)\).

notation.meaning: Affine recovery map for eliminated variables.
Cones in the retained-variable and conic constraints.

source_refs.locator: 9.5 Modeling with LP and QP p. 320

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Modeling with LP and QP p. 320

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-level form of nonsingular block substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed model, substituting \(y=B^{-1}(b-Ax)\) gives objective \[\bigl(c_x-A^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_y\bigr)^{\mathsf T}x+c_y^{\mathsf T}B^{-1}b\] and cone expression \[\bigl(F-GB^{-1}A\bigr)x+GB^{-1}b-h\in C.\] The objective constant may be dropped only when optimal decisions, rather than the optimal value, are being retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block substitution explicitly transforms the objective and cone coefficients and produces a recoverable objective constant.
assumptions_latex: The eliminated block is substituted in every constraint and the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c=c_x-A^{\mathsf T}B^{-\mathsf T}c_y,\qquad \bar F=F-GB^{-1}A.
knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Condensed Data

children.title: Eliminated-Variable Recovery
children.top_down_role: Metadata and mappings used to reconstruct removed variables from reduced solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Eliminated-Variable Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of removed primal variables from a condensed solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,m\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). Suppose an original model in \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\) contains \(Ax+By=b\), and its condensed model is obtained by substituting
\[R(x)=B^{-1}(b-Ax)\]
for \(y\) in every other constraint and in the objective. For every condensed-feasible \(x\), \((x,R(x))\) is original-feasible; conversely, every original-feasible \((x,y)\) satisfies \(y=R(x)\). Consequently, if \(x^\star\) is optimal for the condensed model, then \((x^\star,R(x^\star))\) is optimal for the original model with the same objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stored affine substitution uniquely reconstructs eliminated variables and lifts every condensed optimum to an original optimum with the same objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
The condensed model is obtained by exact substitution in every constraint and the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x^\star\) is condensed-optimal, then \((x^\star,R(x^\star))\) is original-optimal with the same objective value.

notation.meaning: Data of the equality subsystem used for recovery.

source_refs.locator: 9.5 Modeling with LP and QP p. 320

source_witnesses.locator: 9.5 Modeling with LP and QP p. 320

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning boundary for numerical back-substitution of eliminated variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x)=B^{-1}(b-Ax)\) with nonsingular \(B\). For any \(\widehat x\) and computed \(\widetilde y\), define \(r=b-A\widehat x-B\widetilde y\). Then \[\widetilde y-R(\widehat x)=-B^{-1}r,\qquad \|\widetilde y-R(\widehat x)\|\le\|B^{-1}\|\,\|r\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Back-substitution error is the inverse pivot applied to the equality residual, so ill-conditioning can amplify a small residual.
assumptions_latex: The vector norm and induced operator norm are compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\widetilde y-R(\widehat x)\|\le\|B^{-1}\|\,\|b-A\widehat x-B\widetilde y\|.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Residual Amplification

children.title: Condensation Sparsity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Fill-in, coupling growth, and structural losses caused by model condensation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-level criterion for preserving a prescribed sparsity pattern under exact block condensation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the condensed affine operator be \(\bar F=F-GB^{-1}A\), where \(B\) is nonsingular, and let \(\mathcal P\) be a prescribed set of permitted matrix positions containing \(\operatorname{supp}(F)\). Condensation preserves \(\mathcal P\) exactly if and only if \((GB^{-1}A)_{ij}=0\) for every \((i,j)\notin\mathcal P\). Absent exact cancellation, every nonzero product path from retained coordinate \(j\) through \(A\), \(B^{-1}\), and \(G\) can create a fill entry at \((i,j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prescribed sparsity pattern survives condensation exactly when the substitution product has no entries outside that pattern; inverse-block coupling can otherwise create fill.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{supp}(F-GB^{-1}A)\subseteq\mathcal P\iff (GB^{-1}A)_{ij}=0\ \forall(i,j)\notin\mathcal P.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Condensation No-Fill Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Arrow Condensation Can Be Dense
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp fill-in example for exact scalar-pivot condensation of a sparse symmetric system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\in\mathbb R^{p	imes p}\) be diagonal, \(\alpha
e0\), and \(a_i
