children.title: Sign Inference
children.top_down_role: Propagation and refinement of expression sign information for disciplined model analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound bottom-up propagation of sign attributes through an expression DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an expression DAG whose leaves have declared sign sets contained in \(\{-,0,+\}\), process nodes in topological order. Assign constants their exact sign and variables their declared sign. For a sum, return all signs attainable by adding operands with the recorded signs; for a product, use the usual sign table. For each atomic function, apply its registered range-sign and monotonicity rules on the inferred argument signs. Intersect all sound conclusions, stopping after the root is processed. The output is a sound sign set containing the sign of every domain-feasible evaluation; if no strict refinement is justified, return \(\{-,0,+\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sign inference propagates declared leaf signs through algebraic and registered atomic rules, returning the smallest sound sign set justified by those rules.
assumptions_latex: Every atomic function has sound registered sign rules.
Leaf sign declarations contain every feasible leaf value's sign.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{sign}(e(x))\in\Sigma_e\) for every domain-feasible evaluation \(x\).

notation.meaning: Inferred sign set for expression e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits, but the atom rules, use of monotonicity in sign propagation, and claimed precision depend on the disciplined-analysis framework. No source identifies or validates that framework.

children.title: Domain Inference
children.top_down_role: Propagation of atom domains and implicit domain restrictions through expression trees.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive construction of the effective domain of a composite expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression \(e=a(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\), recursively infer each child domain \(D_i\) and use the registered domain \(D_a\) of atom \(a\). Return \[D_e=\{x:x\in D_i\ \text{for every }i,\ (e_1(x),\ldots,e_k(x))\in D_a\}.\] Constants have the ambient domain, and variables use their declared domains. Processing a finite expression DAG in topological order terminates at the root and outputs the conjunction of generated constraints. Examples include \(u>0\) for \(\log u\), \(u\ge0\) for \(\sqrt u\), and \(u\ne0\) for \(u^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain inference recursively combines child domains with each atom's registered input domain, yielding the exact domain relative to the atom library.
assumptions_latex: Every atom \(a\) has a specified domain \(D_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in D_e\Longleftrightarrow x\in\bigcap_iD_i\) and \((e_1(x),\ldots,e_k(x))\in D_a\).

notation.meaning: Inferred effective domain of expression e
Registered input domain of atom a

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive domain construction is coherent, but its claimed exactness depends on the atom library and representation of generated constraints. No supporting disciplined-analysis source is supplied.

children.title: Sign–Domain Interaction
children.top_down_role: Mutual refinement between inferred signs and admissible expression domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign–Domain Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint propagation between domain constraints and sign attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sign and domain inference are coupled by sound constraint propagation. If domain inference establishes \(e(x)\ge0\), then the sign set for \(e\) may be intersected with \(\{0,+\}\); if it establishes \(e(x)>0\), the set may be intersected with \(\{+\}\). Conversely, an inferred positive sign certifies domain conditions such as the argument requirement of \(\log e\), while a nonnegative sign certifies that of \(\sqrt e\). Alternating these refinements to a fixed point preserves every feasible evaluation, although incomplete rules may leave an attribute unknown.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Domain constraints refine signs, and inferred signs can certify atom domains; sound alternating propagation preserves all feasible evaluations but may remain incomplete.
assumptions_latex: All sign and domain propagation rules are sound.
Each update only intersects with a constraint valid for every feasible evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_e^{\star}\) contains every feasible evaluation and \(\Sigma_e^{\star}\) contains every feasible sign.

notation.meaning: Domain information at the propagation fixed point
Sign information at the propagation fixed point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated propagation directions are sound under the assumptions, but the fixed-point objects and implementation behavior are framework-dependent and lack a supporting citation.

children.title: Unknown-Attribute Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where available metadata cannot establish a required sign or domain classification.

assumptions_latex: The attribute analyzer is sound: every inferred sign set and domain contains all values attainable under the accumulated constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unknown attribute supplies no premise to a rule requiring a definite sign or domain relation; failure to infer an attribute is not a certificate that the expression is mathematically invalid.

notation.meaning: Inferred value set for the expression
Domain required by an atom argument

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conservative abstract interpretation boundary for sign and domain metadata
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative boundary for static sign-domain inference in a disciplined convex analysis parser.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an expression \(e\), sign is unknown when the sound enclosure \(V(e)\) is not contained in any strict sign class required by a rule. Domain compatibility with a required set \(D\) is unknown when the analyzer cannot establish \(V(e)\subseteq D\). In either case, a composition rule whose hypotheses require that missing fact is inapplicable. The analyzer must not replace the unknown attribute by nonnegative, nonpositive, or domain-compatible. It may reject the composition as unverified, but it cannot conclude solely from unknownness that \(e\) has no feasible value or that the represented function is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unknown sign or domain metadata cannot satisfy a rule requiring definite metadata, although unknownness alone does not prove infeasibility or nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Unknown-Attribute Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the distinction between unknown metadata and mathematical invalidity is plausible. However, no cited source establishes the proposed sound-enclosure semantics, strict sign classes, or the validator behavior, so the exact formulation cannot be independently confirmed.

assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and each atom carries declared curvature, argument monotonicity, and domain metadata.
Leaves are classified as constant, affine, or invalid.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a sound curvature label; an unknown or invalid label is returned whenever no applicable certified rule exists.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive scalar curvature inference for a finite disciplined-expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process expression nodes in topological order. Assign constants the label constant and affine combinations of affine children the label affine. For a node \(e=h(e_1,\ldots,e_m)\), first verify the declared domain of \(h\). Then test the certified composition rules using the inferred curvature and sign-domain metadata of every child. Assign convex or concave only when all hypotheses of a corresponding rule hold; assign affine when both labels are certified. If the domain is contradicted, return invalid. If the domain or a required attribute is unproved, or no rule applies, return unknown. Output the label of the root node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature is propagated bottom-up from leaves through atom metadata; unsupported compositions become unknown and contradicted domains become invalid.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Inference

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: An algorithm is an appropriate role for bottom-up curvature inference, but the record gives an implementation-specific label system without evidence. In particular, the phrase assigning affine when both labels are certified requires a sourced definition of the two labels, and the distinction among unknown, invalid, and contradicted domain states needs authoritative support.

assumptions_latex: Each inner function is defined on a convex set containing the modeled domain.
The outer function has known curvature and coordinatewise monotonicity on the attained inner-value set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated coordinatewise curvature and monotonicity tests certify the curvature of the composition.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard convex-composition rule with coordinatewise monotonicity
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise composition rule used by disciplined convex analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\) is convex, then \(f\) is convex when, for every coordinate \(i\), one of the following holds on the relevant domain: \(h\) is nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is convex; \(h\) is nonincreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is concave; or \(g_i\) is affine. Dually, if \(h\) is concave, then \(f\) is concave when nondecreasing coordinates receive concave arguments, nonincreasing coordinates receive convex arguments, and unrestricted coordinates receive affine arguments. Constant arguments satisfy either curvature requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer monotonicity determines which curvature each inner expression must have for the composition to retain convexity or concavity.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity-Aware Composition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind and local placement are appropriate, and the coordinatewise convex and concave composition conditions are standard in substance. No source or inspectable locator is supplied, however, so the precise hypotheses, including the relevant attained-value domain and treatment of constant arguments, remain unsupported.

children.title: Objective Validation
children.top_down_role: Classification and acceptance checks for minimization or maximization objectives.

assumptions_latex: The objective expression is scalar-valued and real on every feasible point accepted by the analyzer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimization objective is valid exactly when certified convex, and a maximization objective is valid exactly when certified concave.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard DCP objective admissibility condition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic objective admissibility for convex minimization and concave maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective pair \((s,f_0)\) passes disciplined convex validation precisely when its shape is scalar, its domain obligations are established on the modeled feasible set, and either \(s=\min\) with \(f_0\) certified convex or \(s=\max\) with \(f_0\) certified concave. An affine objective is admissible in either direction. Unknown curvature, a vector-valued objective, or an unverified domain obligation causes validation failure, even if the underlying optimization problem might admit an equivalent valid reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid scalar objective is convex for minimization or concave for maximization, with all domain obligations established.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition fits Objective Validation, and scalar convex-minimization or concave-maximization admissibility is standard. The stronger implementation claim that every domain obligation must be established on the modeled feasible set, and that an unverified obligation necessarily causes validation failure, depends on the particular DCP system and needs a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Constraint Validation
children.top_down_role: Classification and acceptance checks for equality, inequality, set-membership, or cone constraints.

assumptions_latex: Every constraint expression has compatible finite-dimensional shape.
All atom-domain obligations are included in, or implied by, the modeled constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The model is constraint-valid exactly when every constraint matches one of the certified convex forms.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard DCP inequality, equality, and affine-cone membership forms
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible constraint forms for disciplined convex and conic canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar inequality \(f(x)\leq g(x)\) is valid when \(f\) is certified convex and \(g\) is certified concave. An equality \(f(x)=g(x)\) is valid when both sides are affine. A cone-membership constraint \(A(x)\in K\) is valid when \(A\) is affine and \(K\) is a supported closed convex cone. Vector inequalities are interpreted componentwise and must satisfy the scalar rule in every component. Any unknown curvature, incompatible shape, unsupported cone, or unproved domain requirement makes the corresponding constraint invalid for canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraints must be convex-below-concave inequalities, affine equalities, or affine memberships in supported closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind matches the leaf, and the scalar inequality and affine-equality rules are standard. The accepted cone-membership form, componentwise vector interpretation, supported-cone restriction, and treatment of atom domains are system-specific and have no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Validation Diagnostic Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Structural locations, classifications, and messages associated with rejected model components.

assumptions_latex: Validation traverses a finite expression graph and uses deterministic atom metadata and composition rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned diagnostic identifies a reproducible failing node and the unmet rule premise without asserting mathematical nonconvexity beyond the recognizer.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: verifiable diagnostic contract for rule-based model validation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal machine-checkable interface for disciplined-validation diagnostics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A validation interface returns \(q=\mathrm{pass}\) only when every objective, constraint, and expression node is certified. Otherwise it returns \(q=\mathrm{fail}\) and a record \(d=(v,r,a,o)\), where \(v\in V\) is a failing node, \(r\) names the attempted validation rule, \(a\) is the inferred attribute tuple at \(v\), and \(o\) lists unmet domain, shape, sign, curvature, or monotonicity obligations. Verification consists of recomputing \(a\) from the children of \(v\) and checking that at least one obligation in \(o\) required by \(r\) is not certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A failure diagnostic names the expression node, attempted rule, inferred attributes, and unmet obligations so the failure can be reproduced.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation Diagnostic Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record is locally relevant, but it specifies a particular diagnostic tuple and verification procedure not implied by standard DCP mathematics. Treating that interface as a certificate is reasonable only if an authoritative software or formal-system source documents the tuple, deterministic failing-node policy, and recomputation semantics.

children.title: Validation Recognition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Convex model structures that remain unrecognized under the active disciplined ruleset.

assumptions_latex: The validator recognizes only expressions derivable from its finite atom library and certified composition rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Recognizer rejection is not equivalent to mathematical nonconvexity; it certifies only absence of a derivation in the implemented rule system.

notation.meaning: Mathematically convex functions on the modeled domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: incompleteness boundary of syntax-directed DCP recognition
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes sound syntactic recognition from complete mathematical convexity detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sound disciplined validation guarantees \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal V\), but generally \(\mathcal R\neq\mathcal V\). For example, \(e(x)=\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\), yet a syntax-directed rule may reject the displayed composition because the square root is concave and increasing while its argument \(x^2\) is convex. Rewriting \(e\) as a supported absolute-value atom can make the same function recognizable. Thus failure means that the current expression lacks a certified derivation; it does not establish that no convex reformulation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disciplined validation is sound but incomplete: a convex function may be rejected until expressed using recognizable atoms and compositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Validation Recognition Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind precisely fits this leaf, and the sound-but-incomplete recognition distinction is standard. The displayed square-root composition is rejected by common syntax-directed DCP rule sets, but actual recognition behavior depends on the atom library and simplification system; a specific authoritative source is required.

children.title: Scalar Atoms
children.top_down_role: Single-output atom interfaces, metadata, and graph-representation coverage.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar primitive semantics with curvature and graph-interface metadata.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar atom is a primitive function of finitely many scalar arguments. A convex atom is represented as \(\phi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), while a concave atom is represented as \(\psi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\). Its interface declares its effective domain, curvature, sign and coordinatewise monotonicity information, argument signature, and any registered exact epigraph or hypograph implementation. These declarations support composition validation but do not replace the function's mathematical semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar atom is a scalar primitive with one-sided extended-value semantics and declared domain, curvature, monotonicity, sign, shape, and optional exact graph implementation.
assumptions_latex: Convex and concave atoms use their respective one-sided extended-value conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\phi=\{x:\phi(x)<+\infty\},\qquad \operatorname{dom}\psi=\{x:\psi(x)>-\infty\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Atom Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic convex graph interfaces independent of a particular cone implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex scalar atom \(\phi\), \(\operatorname{epi}\phi=\{(x,t):\phi(x)\le t\}\) is convex and \(\phi(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}\phi\}\). For a proper concave scalar atom \(\psi\), \(\operatorname{hypo}\psi=\{(x,t):t\le\psi(x)\}\) is convex and \(\psi(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}\psi\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex scalar atom is recovered from its epigraph and a proper concave atom from its hypograph.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is proper convex or \(\psi\) is proper concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(x)=\inf\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}\phi\},\quad \psi(x)=\sup\{t:(x,t)\in\operatorname{hypo}\psi\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Epigraph and Hypograph Interfaces

assumptions_latex: Each atom is interpreted as an extended-real-valued function on a specified finite-dimensional domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The atom metadata defines both its mathematical semantics and the local obligations used for validation and graph canonicalization.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: extended-value scalar atom with DCP and graph metadata
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar atoms as metadata-bearing primitives of a canonicalization library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar atom is a primitive extended-real function \(\phi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty,-\infty\}\) together with metadata \(M_\phi\) specifying its effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}\phi\), curvature, sign, coordinatewise monotonicity, argument shapes, and a supported conic graph or epigraph implementation. An occurrence \(\phi(e_1,\ldots,e_m)\) is well formed only when argument shapes agree with the signature and the inferred joint range lies in \(\operatorname{dom}\phi\). Its curvature is certified only through the declared metadata and applicable composition rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar atom is a primitive extended-real function equipped with domain, curvature, monotonicity, shape, sign, and conic implementation metadata.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Atoms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for Scalar Atoms, but the proposed metadata bundle and mandatory conic implementation are library-architecture choices. The simultaneous codomain containing both positive and negative infinity also requires a stated convention, since convex and concave extended-value treatments commonly use different one-sided extensions.

children.title: Elementwise Atoms
children.top_down_role: Entrywise atom interfaces over vector, matrix, or tensor-shaped expressions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Product-Cone Lift of an Elementwise Atom
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise replication of an exact scalar conic graph implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the scalar epigraph of \(\phi:\mathbb R^m\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has an exact affine-conic representation over a cone \(K\). For arrays indexed by a finite set \(I\), the inequalities \(T_i\ge\phi(X_i^1,\ldots,X_i^m)\) for all \(i\in I\) are represented exactly by independent auxiliary variables and one product-cone constraint in \(K^{|I|}\). The construction uses one scalar graph copy per output index and introduces no cross-index coupling. The analogous statement holds for hypographs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementwise atom's conic graph is the Cartesian product of independent scalar graph copies, one for each output entry.
assumptions_latex: The scalar graph implementation is exact.
All arguments have a common finite output index set after broadcasting.
The same scalar implementation cone is used at every index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{graph}_{I}(\Phi)=\prod_{i\in I}\operatorname{graph}(\phi),\qquad K_{\mathrm{elementwise}}=K^{|I|}.

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of one implementation cone per index
elementwise lift of the scalar atom

knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Lift of an Elementwise Atom

assumptions_latex: A scalar atom has a common scalar domain and is applied independently at each selected output index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Elementwise lifting preserves separability of values and domain checks, while output shape is determined by the common index set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: coordinatewise lifting of scalar atoms
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise lifting of scalar atoms to array-valued expressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given arrays \(X^1,\ldots,X^m\) indexed by the same finite set \(I\), the elementwise lift of \(\phi\) is the array-valued map \(\Phi\) defined by \(\Phi(X^1,\ldots,X^m)_i=\phi(X^1_i,\ldots,X^m_i)\) for every \(i\in I\). Its domain is the set of input arrays for which \((X^1_i,\ldots,X^m_i)\in\operatorname{dom}\phi\) at every index. Sign and monotonicity metadata lift coordinatewise. Scalar curvature metadata applies to each output component; any later scalar reduction must be validated as a separate composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementwise atom applies one scalar atom independently at every output index, with domain and metadata checked coordinate by coordinate.
knowledge_statements.title: Elementwise Atoms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the coordinatewise lifting described here, and the formula is internally coherent. No source supports this exact definition, its metadata-lifting claims, or the rule that every scalar reduction must be validated separately.

children.title: Broadcasting Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Shape propagation and scalar-to-array expansion within elementwise atom expressions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-operator form, adjoint accumulation, and intrinsic size of a fixed broadcasting map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite index map \(b:I\to I_0\), define \(B\in\{0,1\}^{|I|\times|I_0|}\) by \(B_{i,j}=1\) exactly when \(j=b(i)\). Every row contains exactly one unit entry, \(\operatorname{nnz}(B)=|I|\), and broadcasting is \(\widetilde x=Bx\), where \(\widetilde x_i=x_{b(i)}\). Its adjoint is \[(B^Tz)_j=\sum_{i:b(i)=j}z_i.\] Thus forward replication and reverse accumulation both require linear work in the output size when the index map is explicitly available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed broadcast is a sparse zero-one replication operator; its transpose sums contributions from all positions sharing an input entry.
assumptions_latex: \(b:I\to I_0\) is a total deterministic map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde x=Bx,\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(B)=|I|,\qquad (B^Tz)_j=\sum_{i:b(i)=j}z_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Broadcast Replication Operators

assumptions_latex: For each argument, a deterministic index map from output indices to valid input indices is specified.
Broadcasting duplicates values but performs no aggregation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Broadcasting is the pullback of each input array along its index map before elementwise atom evaluation.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: index-map semantics for array broadcasting
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shape-safe index-map semantics for broadcasting elementwise atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let argument \(k\) be indexed by \(I_k\), and let \(I\) be the declared output index set. A broadcasting interface is a family of maps \(b_k:I\to I_k\). For a scalar atom \(\phi\), it defines \(Y_i=\phi(X^1_{b_1(i)},\ldots,X^m_{b_m(i)})\) for every \(i\in I\). The interface is valid only if every \(b_k\) is total and conforms to the declared shape rule. Broadcast replication preserves the sign and curvature metadata of each selected scalar entry; incompatible dimensions or ambiguous index maps are shape errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Broadcasting uses explicit index maps to replicate compatible input entries before coordinatewise atom evaluation; incompatible shapes are rejected.
knowledge_statements.title: Broadcasting Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The index-map representation is mathematically coherent and well matched to Broadcasting Interfaces. Broadcasting conventions and conforming shape rules vary across modeling systems, however, and the declared shape rule is not defined or cited; authoritative interface documentation with a precise locator is needed.

children.title: Elementwise Domain Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Entrywise domain restrictions and shape-related recognition limits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain condition for a finite broadcast elementwise application.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}\phi\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), let \(I\) be the output index set, and let \(b_k:I\to I_k\) be total broadcast maps. Then \((X^1,\ldots,X^m)\) is in the effective domain of the lifted atom exactly when \((X^1_{b_1(i)},\ldots,X^m_{b_m(i)})\in D\) for every \(i\in I\). One violating index places the whole lifted expression outside its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A broadcast elementwise atom is defined exactly when every indexed scalar argument tuple lies in the scalar atom's domain.
assumptions_latex: The output index set is finite and every broadcast map is valid and total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\Phi=\{(X^1,\ldots,X^m):(X^1_{b_1(i)},\ldots,X^m_{b_m(i)})\in D\ \forall i\in I\}.

notation.meaning: broadcast index map for argument k

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Effective-Domain Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary of an Independent Finite Elementwise Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary geometry when the lifted scalar tuples are independent rather than identified by broadcasting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(I\) is finite and nonempty and \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty and closed, then \(\operatorname{int}(D^I)=(\operatorname{int}D)^I\) and \(\partial(D^I)=\{x\in D^I:\exists i\in I,\ x_i\in\partial D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An independent finite elementwise domain is interior exactly when every tuple is interior and is on the boundary exactly when some tuple is on the scalar boundary.
assumptions_latex: The lifted domain is the Cartesian product \(D^I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{int}(D^I)=(\operatorname{int}D)^I,\quad \partial(D^I)=\{x\in D^I:\exists i,\ x_i\in\partial D\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary of an Independent Finite Elementwise Domain

assumptions_latex: The elementwise operation is induced by a scalar atom with effective domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^m\).
All broadcast index maps are valid and total.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The elementwise expression is domain-valid exactly when every broadcast argument tuple lies in the scalar domain.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: coordinatewise domain boundary under elementwise lifting and broadcasting
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain predicate for broadcast elementwise atom applications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For input arrays \(X^k\), the broadcast elementwise application is defined precisely on \(\{(X^1,\ldots,X^m):(X^1_{b_1(i)},\ldots,X^m_{b_m(i)})\in D\ \text{for every}\ i\in I\}\). A violation at one output index places the entire array expression outside its effective domain. Static validation succeeds only when every indexed membership follows from known attributes and constraints. An unproved membership yields an unknown domain obligation, whereas a provably excluded tuple yields a domain contradiction; these outcomes must remain distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A broadcast elementwise expression is defined only when every indexed argument tuple belongs to the scalar atom's domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Elementwise Domain Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition fits this terminal container, and the pointwise effective-domain formula is coherent under the stated total index maps. The static distinction among certified membership, unknown obligation, and domain contradiction is analyzer-specific and unsupported by any cited source.

children.title: Vector Atoms
children.top_down_role: Atom interfaces whose arguments or outputs carry vector structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature semantics when an atom has a genuinely vector-valued output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K\subseteq\mathbb R^p be a convex cone inducing u\preceq_K v when v-u\in K. A map F:D\to\mathbb R^p is K-convex when F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preceq_K\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y) for all x,y\in D and \theta\in[0,1]. Thus vector-valued curvature requires a declared output order; componentwise convexity is the case K=\mathbb R_+^p. Scalar-valued atoms with vector inputs instead use ordinary scalar curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector-valued curvature requires an output order cone; vector input alone does not.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a convex cone defining the output preorder}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=\mathbb R_+^p\text{ yields componentwise curvature}.

notation.meaning: preorder induced by the output cone K

knowledge_statements.title: Ordered Curvature for Vector-Valued Atoms

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vector Shape Does Not Imply Coordinate Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between vector interfaces and nonseparable primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar atom \phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R, define F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n by F(x)_i=\phi(x_i). This map has vector input and output but is separable across coordinates. Therefore vector shape alone does not imply nonseparability, and its graph can be represented by the product of the corresponding scalar-atom graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elementwise scalar lift is vector-shaped but separable, so coordinate coupling cannot be required by a shape-only definition.
assumptions_latex: \phi\text{ is defined at every coordinate under consideration}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\not\Rightarrow F\text{ couples coordinates}.

notation.meaning: ith component of the lifted map

knowledge_statements.title: Vector Shape Does Not Imply Coordinate Coupling

assumptions_latex: Inputs and outputs lie in specified finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
Each primitive has declared domain, curvature, monotonicity, shape, and conic graph metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vector atom is validated and canonicalized as one nonseparable primitive rather than as independent scalar-coordinate evaluations.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonseparable vector primitive with conic graph metadata
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonseparable vector-valued or vector-input primitives in an atomic canonicalization library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A vector atom is a primitive map \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) with effective domain \(D_F\), whose semantics or graph couple multiple input coordinates and therefore are not merely an elementwise lift of one scalar atom. Its library record specifies input-output shapes, domain, applicable scalar or componentwise curvature ordering, sign and monotonicity information, and a conic graph representation \(\mathcal G_F\). An occurrence \(F(x)\) is admissible only when \(x\in D_F\) is certified and the surrounding scalar objective or constraint consumes its vector output through a valid composition or cone relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector atom is a coordinate-coupling primitive with explicit domain, shape, curvature, monotonicity, and conic graph metadata.
knowledge_statements.title: Vector Atoms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition fits Vector Atoms, but this formulation makes coordinate coupling and nonseparability definitional, although some libraries may classify vector primitives differently. Curvature for a vector-valued map also requires an explicitly defined ordering or componentwise convention. The proposed metadata and graph requirements therefore need a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Matrix Atoms
children.top_down_role: Atom interfaces using matrix shape, linear-algebraic structure, or matrix-valued expressions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonspectral atom primitives with matrix-shaped arguments or outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix atom is a primitive whose declared signature contains a matrix-shaped argument or output and whose semantics depend on matrix structure rather than entrywise lifting. A scalar-valued convex matrix atom uses the extended-value convention \(f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and may expose an exact epigraph lift. A symmetric-matrix-valued atom \(F:\mathcal D\to\mathbb S^p\) may instead expose a Loewner-order graph interface. Shape, symmetry, domain, curvature, and implementation metadata are part of the interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix atom is a non-entrywise primitive with matrix-shaped arguments or outputs and ordinary or Loewner-order graph metadata.
assumptions_latex: All matrix dimensions and structural declarations are fixed by the signature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Scalar-valued atoms use ordinary epigraphs; symmetric-matrix-valued atoms may use Loewner epigraphs.}

notation.meaning: real symmetric matrices of order p

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Atom Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact graph interfaces for scalar- and symmetric-matrix-valued matrix atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scalar-valued convex matrix atom has an exact conic epigraph lift when \((X,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\iff\exists y,\ A\operatorname{vec}(X)+By+ct+d\in K\). For \(F:\mathcal D\to\mathbb S^p\), the Loewner epigraph is \(\operatorname{epi}_{\succeq}F=\{(X,T):T-F(X)\succeq0\}\); on a convex domain, \(F\) is matrix convex exactly when this set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar-valued matrix atoms use ordinary epigraph lifts; symmetric-matrix-valued atoms use Loewner epigraphs, whose convexity characterizes matrix convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone for the scalar epigraph lift.
\(\mathcal D\) is convex for the matrix-convexity equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is matrix convex}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{epi}_{\succeq}F\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar and Loewner Epigraph Interfaces
Matrix Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-valued primitives equipped with exact conic graph implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix atom is a function \(f:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) together with declared curvature, monotonicity, and domain data, and a finite-dimensional conic graph implementation. For a convex atom this implementation consists of affine maps \(A,B\), a vector \(c\), and a closed convex cone \(K\) such that \[f(X)=\inf_{y,t}\{t: A\operatorname{vec}(X)+By+ct\in K\}.\] The implementation is exact when the displayed value equals \(f(X)\) throughout \(\mathcal D\), including the convention \(f(X)=+\infty\) outside the represented domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix atom couples a matrix function and curvature metadata with an exact finite conic representation of its epigraph value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)=\inf\{t:\exists y,\ A\operatorname{vec}(X)+By+ct\in K\}\).

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Matrix Atoms leaf, but the cited convex-matrix-functions section does not directly support the asserted atom metadata contract or exact finite-dimensional conic graph interface. A direct modeling-system or graph-implementation source is required.

children.title: Spectral Atoms
children.top_down_role: Atom interfaces governed by eigenvalue, singular-value, or spectral-function structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orthogonally invariant matrix atoms induced by symmetric eigenvalue or singular-value functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric matrices, a spectral atom has the form \(F(X)=\phi(\lambda(X))\), where \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), \(\lambda(X)\in\mathbb R^n\) lists the eigenvalues, and \(\phi\) is invariant under coordinate permutations. For rectangular matrices, it has the form \(F(X)=\psi(\sigma(X))\), where \(\sigma(X)\) lists singular values and \(\psi\) is absolutely symmetric. The atom is convex whenever its inducing function is convex with the stated symmetry; its canonicalizer may therefore use a conic graph of the inducing spectral function rather than individual eigenvectors or singular vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral atom applies a symmetric scalar function to eigenvalues or singular values, preserving convexity under the appropriate symmetry.
assumptions_latex: \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) for eigenvalue atoms, or \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) for singular-value atoms.
\(\phi\) is permutation invariant, or \(\psi\) is absolutely symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(X)=\phi(\lambda(X))\) or \(F(X)=\psi(\sigma(X))\), with convexity inherited from the inducing function.

notation.meaning: eigenvalue vector of a symmetric matrix
real symmetric matrices of order n

source_refs.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.7 Convex matrix functions p. 26

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy of Closed Convex Spectral Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel conjugacy for eigenvalue- and singular-value-induced atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\phi:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, convex, and permutation invariant, and set \(F(X)=\phi(\lambda(X))\) on \(\mathbb S^n\). Then \(F^*(Y)=\phi^*(\lambda(Y))\) under the trace pairing. Likewise, if \(\psi:\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, convex, and absolutely symmetric and \(G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X))\), then \(G^*(Y)=\psi^*(\sigma(Y))\) under the Frobenius pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel conjugation commutes with forming closed convex eigenvalue and singular-value spectral functions.
assumptions_latex: The inducing function is proper, closed, convex, and has the required symmetry.
Matrix duality uses the trace or Frobenius pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^*(Y)=\phi^*(\lambda(Y)),\qquad G^*(Y)=\psi^*(\sigma(Y)).
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy of Closed Convex Spectral Functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous spectral-basis descriptions, including repeated eigenvalues and singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(X)=\phi(\lambda(X))\), \(H\in\partial F(X)\) exactly when there is an orthogonal eigenbasis \(U\) with \(X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^T\) and \(H=U\operatorname{Diag}(g)U^T\) for some \(g\in\partial\phi(\lambda(X))\). For \(G(X)=\psi(\sigma(X))\), \(H\in\partial G(X)\) exactly when \(X\) and \(H\) admit a compatible simultaneous singular-vector representation with singular-value coefficient vector in \(\partial\psi(\sigma(X))\). Bases may vary inside repeated spectral subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex spectral subgradients are obtained from subgradients of the inducing function in a compatible eigenbasis or singular-vector basis.
assumptions_latex: The inducing function is proper, closed, convex, and has the required symmetry.
Compatible bases may vary within repeated spectral subspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial(\phi\circ\lambda)(X)=\{U\operatorname{Diag}(g)U^T:X=U\operatorname{Diag}(\lambda(X))U^T,\ g\in\partial\phi(\lambda(X))\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Subdifferentials of Convex Spectral Atoms

children.title: Spectral Structure Recognition
children.top_down_role: Recognition limits involving symmetry, definiteness, dimensions, and spectral metadata.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Orthogonal Invariance Is Insufficient for Spectral Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition boundary separating invariance from valid spectral-atom classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orthogonal invariance alone does not certify a supported convex or concave spectral graph. For example, E(X)=\det X satisfies E(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=E(X) for every Q\in O(n), but on \mathbb S^n with n\ge 2 it is neither convex nor concave. A sound recognizer must also verify the domain, inducing function, curvature, dimensions, and availability of a graph implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determinant shows that orthogonal invariance alone establishes neither usable curvature nor a supported spectral graph.
assumptions_latex: Recognition must preserve the atom's declared curvature and domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: E(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=E(X)\ \forall Q\in O(n)\not\Rightarrow E\text{ is a supported convex or concave spectral atom}.
knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Invariance Is Insufficient for Spectral Routing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarantee obtainable from verified metadata matching without semantic-equivalence solving.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal R be a registry whose entries have verified domains, symmetry classes, curvature, dimensions, and graph implementations. Routing an expression only after a metadata-compatible match is sound relative to \mathcal R. It need not be complete, because an equivalent spectral expression can fail the implemented syntactic or certified-pattern match.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verified registry matching can be sound while rejecting valid spectral expressions written in unrecognized forms.
assumptions_latex: Every registry entry has verified metadata and a valid graph implementation.
Matching preserves dimensions and domain restrictions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{route}(E)\Rightarrow E\text{ has a verified registered implementation},\qquad E\text{ spectral}\not\Rightarrow\operatorname{route}(E).
knowledge_statements.title: Sound but Incomplete Registry Recognition
Spectral Structure Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition rule for routing invariant matrix expressions to spectral canonicalizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matrix expression \(E(X)\), first determine whether its domain requires \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) or permits \(X\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Test the expression metadata for invariance: \(E(QXQ^{\mathsf T})=E(X)\) for every orthogonal \(Q\) in the symmetric case, or \(E(UXV^{\mathsf T})=E(X)\) for every compatible orthogonal \(U,V\) in the rectangular case. If the expression matches a registered eigenvalue or singular-value inducing function with compatible curvature, select its spectral graph implementation; otherwise retain the generic matrix representation or report the atom as unsupported.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recognizer checks orthogonal invariance, domain, and registered curvature before selecting a spectral graph implementation.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) has declared domain and curvature metadata.
The implementation registry identifies supported inducing functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\) is routed to a spectral implementation exactly when its domain, invariance, inducing function, and curvature checks succeed.

children.title: Set Atoms
children.top_down_role: Symbolic set constructors and membership interfaces used by canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic parameterized set membership before support and graph-rule resolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set atom is a symbolic constraint \(e(u)\in S(\theta)\), where \(S(\theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a parameterized set constructor, \(\theta\) is fixed data, and \(e(u)\) has the declared shape. The interface records the parameter domain, ambient dimension, and available structural metadata such as convexity. A conic representation may be registered separately; its absence does not change the set atom's mathematical membership semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set atom is parameterized symbolic set membership with shape, parameter-domain, and structural metadata; conic support is a separate property.
assumptions_latex: \(e(u)\) has the constructor's declared ambient shape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Feas}(e\in S(\theta))=\{u:e(u)\in S(\theta)\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Set Atom Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact semantics of basic symbolic constructors without prescribing their cone expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finite intersections, Cartesian products, and affine preimages define set atoms by \(x\in\bigcap_iS_i\iff x\in S_i\ \forall i\), \((x_i)_i\in\prod_iS_i\iff x_i\in S_i\ \forall i\), and \(u\in E^{-1}(S)\iff Eu+e\in S\). If the component sets are convex, these constructors preserve convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersection, product, and affine-preimage set atoms use their ordinary membership semantics and preserve convexity when their components are convex.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many component sets are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_i\text{ convex for all }i\Longrightarrow \bigcap_iS_i,\ \prod_iS_i,\ E^{-1}(S_i)\text{ are convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Set-Constructor Membership Semantics
Set Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive convex-set membership constraints exposed to canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set atom is a parameterized family \(S(\theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) supplied with a membership predicate and conic representation metadata. It is admissible for convex canonicalization when every instantiated set is convex and membership has an exact representation \[x\in S(\theta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\; A(\theta)x+B(\theta)y+b(\theta)\in K,\] where \(K\) is a supported closed convex cone and the displayed maps are affine in the optimization variables. Parameters must satisfy the atom's declared parameter domain before canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set atom is a convex membership primitive whose feasible points are exactly the projection of an affine conic system.
assumptions_latex: \(S(\theta)\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex for every admissible parameter \(\theta\).
\(K\) is a supported closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in S(\theta)\Longleftrightarrow\exists y,\ A(\theta)x+B(\theta)y+b(\theta)\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits Set Atoms and is internally precise, but no evidence is supplied for treating a set atom as this particular parameterized membership interface with exact supported-cone metadata.

children.title: Cone Atoms
children.top_down_role: Cone-specific constructors, memberships, and graph representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive affine membership in a supported closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone atom is a constraint \(z(u)\in K\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is a declared closed convex cone and \(z\) is affine in the optimization variables. Its interface records the cone family, dimension, admissible parameters, coordinate convention, and, when relevant, the associated dual-cone convention. A native solver block preserves this membership without changing its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone atom is affine membership in a declared closed convex cone with dimension, parameter, coordinate, and dual-convention metadata.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a declared closed convex cone.
\(z\) is affine and dimensionally compatible with \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{u:z(u)\in K\}=z^{-1}(K)\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone Atom Interface

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stacking finitely many affine cone memberships.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed convex cones \(K_j\) and affine maps \(z_j\), requiring \(z_j(u)\in K_j\) for every \(j\) is equivalent to \((z_1(u),\ldots,z_r(u))\in\prod_jK_j\). The product cone is closed and convex, and under the blockwise Euclidean pairing \((\prod_jK_j)^*=\prod_jK_j^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite cone atoms stack into one product-cone atom, whose dual is the product of the block dual cones.
assumptions_latex: Every \(K_j\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_jz_j^{-1}(K_j)=z^{-1}(\prod_jK_j),\quad (\prod_jK_j)^*=\prod_jK_j^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Product Structure of Cone Atoms
Cone Atoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive memberships in supported convex cones and their affine images.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cone atom is a membership constraint \(z\in K\), where \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is a registered closed convex cone and \(z\) is an affine expression in the optimization variables. The atom records the cone dimension, parameter restrictions, primal membership convention, and, when needed, a dual-cone convention. Canonicalization preserves \(z\in K\) as a native cone block or replaces it by an equivalent affine lift into supported cone blocks; equivalence requires equality of the projected feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone atom represents affine membership in a registered closed convex cone, either natively or through an exact supported lift.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^q\) is a registered closed convex cone.
\(z\) is affine in the optimization variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in K\) is retained natively or replaced by an equivalent lifted conic membership system.

children.title: Set-to-Cone Canonicalization
children.top_down_role: Mappings from recognized set memberships to solver-facing cone blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compositional expansion of finitely many independent supported memberships.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each constraint \(e_i(u)\in S_i\), select an applicable exact registered representation, introduce its required fresh lift variables, substitute \(e_i(u)\), and emit the resulting cone blocks. Independent blocks may be emitted separately or stacked in a product cone. Expansion order does not alter the projected feasible set, provided lift variables are not accidentally shared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expand each supported membership with fresh lifts and emit separate or product-stacked cone blocks without changing the model-variable feasible set.
assumptions_latex: Every selected representation is exact and applicable.
Lift variables are fresh unless sharing is part of the registered representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_u\{(u,y_i):A_ie_i(u)+B_iy_i+b_i\in K_i\ \forall i\}=\{u:e_i(u)\in S_i\ \forall i\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Set-to-Cone Expansion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted conversion of one supported set membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By+b\in K\}\) and \(e(u)\) is affine, then canonicalization may replace \(e(u)\in S\) by a fresh variable \(y\) and \(Ae(u)+By+b\in K\). The replacement is exact precisely because projecting its feasible set onto \(u\) gives \(\{u:e(u)\in S\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Substitute an affine membership argument into its exact lifted cone representation and introduce the lift variables existentially.
assumptions_latex: The displayed representation of \(S\) is exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e(u)\in S\Longleftrightarrow\exists y,\ Ae(u)+By+b\in K.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Set-to-Cone Substitution
Set-to-Cone Canonicalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted conversion of supported convex-set membership into cone constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a supported convex set with lifted conic description \[S=\{x:\exists y,\ Ax+By+b\in K\}.\] Canonicalization replaces the constraint \(e(u)\in S\), where \(e\) is affine in the model variables \(u\), by a fresh variable \(y\) and the cone constraint \(Ae(u)+By+b\in K\). The conversion is feasible-set exact because projection onto \(u\) yields precisely \(\{u:e(u)\in S\}\); auxiliary variables may enlarge the formulation but not its projected feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supported set membership is replaced by its lifted cone system, with exactly the same feasible model variables after projection.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a supported closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(u)\in S\Longleftrightarrow\exists y,\ Ae(u)+By+b\in K\).

children.title: Unsupported-Set Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Set descriptions lacking an available cone representation or registered graph implementation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Does Not Imply LP-Lift Representability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Library-relative separation between convexity and support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the selected cone library contains only nonnegative orthants and permits finite affine lifts, every represented set is polyhedral. For \(n\ge2\), the Euclidean unit ball \(B_2^n=\{x:\|x\|_2\le1\}\) is convex and nonpolyhedral, so it has no such LP lift. It becomes directly supported when the Lorentz cone is admitted because \(B_2^n=\{x:(1,x)\in\mathcal Q^{n+1}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean ball is unsupported by finite LP lifts but supported once a Lorentz cone is available.
assumptions_latex: Only finite affine lifts over nonnegative orthants are allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B_2^n\text{ is not LP-lift representable, while }B_2^n=\{x:(1,x)\in\mathcal Q^{n+1}\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Does Not Imply LP-Lift Representability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Library-relative conditions preventing exact set-to-cone expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set membership is unsupported by an exact registered canonicalizer when no applicable rule represents the instantiated set over the selected cone library, when declared parameter or shape conditions fail, or when the argument violates the rule's required affine structure. Convexity alone does not imply support. Replacing the set by a strict inner or outer approximation is not an exact canonicalization and must be represented as a distinct modeling operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set can be convex yet unsupported because no applicable exact rule exists or its parameter, shape, or argument conditions fail; approximation is a different operation.
assumptions_latex: Support is evaluated relative to a fixed registered rule set and cone library.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \neg\operatorname{ApplicableExactRule}(S,e)\Longrightarrow\text{exact set-to-cone canonicalization is unavailable}.

notation.meaning: an exact registered rule applicable to the instantiated membership

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Support Boundary for Set Atoms
Unsupported-Set Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a set constraint cannot enter the supported conic pipeline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constraint \(e(u)\in S\) lies outside the set-to-cone canonicalizer when no registered rule supplies a finite-dimensional supported-cone representation of \(S\), when the rule's parameter domain is violated, or when \(e\) has composition curvature incompatible with the rule. In particular, convexity of \(S\) alone does not guarantee representability by the solver's cone library. The canonicalizer must reject or defer such a constraint rather than substitute an outer or inner approximation unless approximation has been explicitly requested and its direction recorded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity alone does not ensure supported conic representability; missing rules, invalid parameters, or incompatible composition require rejection or explicit approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(e(u)\in S\) is presented to a finite registered canonicalization system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\neg\operatorname{Supported}(S,e)\) implies rejection or explicit deferral, not silent approximation.

notation.meaning: existence of an applicable exact registered representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf, and the distinction between convexity and supported conic representability is sound. No source supports the registered-rule failure conditions or the mandatory reject/defer and no-silent-approximation policy.

children.title: Epigraph Graph Implementations
children.top_down_role: Graph representations supporting convex atom outputs through epigraph-oriented canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Graph Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted conic representation used to canonicalize convex atom upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex. An exact epigraph graph implementation consists of a closed convex cone \(K\) and affine maps such that \[t\ge f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y,\ Ax+By+ct+d\in K.\] Replacing an occurrence constrained above by \(t\) with this lifted system preserves the feasible projection onto \((x,t)\). If the infimum over auxiliary variables is not attained, the implementation must encode the closed epigraph directly or state the closure convention; mere equality of optimal values is insufficient for graph exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex atom's epigraph implementation exactly equates its upper-bound relation with a lifted affine conic system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge f(x)\Longleftrightarrow\exists y,\ Ax+By+ct+d\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and projected-epigraph exactness criterion fit the leaf, but no source is supplied for the conic graph interface or the stated attainment and closure requirements.

children.title: Hypograph Graph Implementations
children.top_down_role: Graph representations supporting concave atom outputs through hypograph-oriented canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Graph Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted conic representation used to canonicalize concave atom lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\) be concave. An exact hypograph graph implementation consists of a closed convex cone \(K\) and affine maps such that \[t\le g(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y,\ Ax+By+ct+d\in K.\] Equivalently, it may be obtained from an exact epigraph implementation of the convex function \(-g\) by sign reversal. The lifted system must preserve the feasible projection onto \((x,t)\), including domain restrictions and any closure convention required for unattained auxiliary limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave atom's hypograph implementation exactly equates its lower-bound relation with a lifted affine conic system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\le g(x)\Longleftrightarrow\exists y,\ Ax+By+ct+d\in K\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role and hypograph formulation fit the leaf, including the sign-reversal relation to an epigraph of the convex function \(-g\). No source is supplied for the graph interface or its domain and closure conditions.

children.title: Graph Orientation Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection of graph orientation from expression context, curvature, and constraint placement.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Orientation Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature-directed choice between epigraph and hypograph graph forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an atom occurrence \(z=f(e(u))\), select an epigraph implementation when \(f\) is convex and the surrounding model requires an upper bound \(z\ge f(e(u))\); select a hypograph implementation when \(f\) is concave and the model requires a lower bound \(z\le f(e(u))\). Equality \(z=f(e(u))\) is directly convex-representable through one orientation only when contextual monotonicity or the objective forces the corresponding inequality tight. Otherwise both inequalities are required, and their conjunction is generally nonconvex unless \(f\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex upper bounds use epigraphs and concave lower bounds use hypographs; nonlinear equality needs contextual tightness or becomes generally nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: The atom's curvature and contextual inequality direction are known.
The argument composition satisfies the modeling system's curvature rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ convex}\Rightarrow z\ge f(e(u))\) uses an epigraph; \(f\text{ concave}\Rightarrow z\le f(e(u))\) uses a hypograph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle content kind fits Graph Orientation Selection, and the epigraph/hypograph directions are mathematically appropriate. A source is required for the contextual-tightness rule and the canonicalizer's orientation-selection policy.

children.title: Graph Exactness Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries between exact graph representations, closures, and relaxation-based implementations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rotated-cone-representable lift whose projection omits a boundary point although its closure is the target epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=\delta_{[0,\infty)}\), so \(\operatorname{epi}f=[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\). Consider \[G=\{(x,t,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ 2xy\ge1,\ t\ge0\},\] where \(2xy\ge1\) is rotated-second-order-cone representable. Then \[\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G=(0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)\subsetneq\operatorname{epi}f,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G)=\operatorname{epi}f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed conic lift can project to an open half-strip whose closure is the desired epigraph, so closure equality is weaker than graph equality.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta_{[0,\infty)}\) is zero on the nonnegative ray and \(+\infty\) elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G\ne\operatorname{epi}f\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G)=\operatorname{epi}f.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Equality Without Graph Exactness
Graph Exactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact graph projection from relaxations and value-only equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proposed lifted epigraph system \(G=\{(x,t,y):L(x,t,y)\in K\}\) is graph-exact precisely when \[\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G=\operatorname{epi}f.\] If the projection strictly contains \(\operatorname{epi}f\), the system is an outer relaxation; if it is strictly contained, it is an inner restriction. Equality only after closure, \(\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G)=\operatorname{epi}f\), does not certify pointwise graph exactness without an explicit closure convention. Likewise, agreement of optimal values for one objective does not establish equality of graphs. The analogous statements hold for hypographs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph exactness requires equality of projected lifted and original graphs, not merely closure equality, containment, or agreement for one objective.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a lifted conic feasible set.
\(f\) is an extended-real-valued function with a specified epigraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,t}G=\operatorname{epi}f\) is necessary and sufficient for epigraph graph exactness.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, and equality of the projected lift with the epigraph is the appropriate exactness criterion. No source is supplied for the distinctions among exactness, closure equality, relaxations, restrictions, and value-only equivalence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semantic Preservation by a Validated Atom Extension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic consequence of satisfying the abstract custom-atom extension contract; concrete API callbacks remain system-specific.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a custom atom declares metadata that is sound on its declared domain, every accepted occurrence satisfies the composition rules, and the selected supported conic implementation projects exactly to the required epigraph or hypograph relation. Replacing each accepted occurrence by that lifted system preserves the feasible projection and objective values on the original variables. Therefore the original and canonicalized problems have the same infimum, and whenever optimal solutions exist their projections onto the original variables coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound metadata and an exact supported graph implementation make accepted custom-atom canonicalization semantics-preserving.
assumptions_latex: The declared domain, shape, sign, curvature, and required monotonicity metadata are sound.
The occurrence passes the modeling system's composition rules.
The selected graph implementation is projection-exact and uses supported cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{proj}_{x}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{lift}}=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{original}},\qquad \inf p_{\mathrm{lift}}=\inf p_{\mathrm{original}}.

notation.meaning: feasible set under the declared atom semantics

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Preservation by a Validated Atom Extension
Custom-Atom Extension Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness obligations for adding an atom without changing the canonicalization core.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A custom atom \(f\) is admissible only if its extension declares an ambient domain, output shape, curvature, sign, and argument-wise monotonicity sufficient for composition checking, and supplies an epigraph or hypograph conic implementation with supported cones. For every admissible argument \(x\), the supplied lifted system must project exactly to the declared graph orientation; its parameter validation must exclude instances for which the declaration or representation fails. Canonicalization may accept the atom only after shape, domain, curvature-composition, cone-support, and graph-exactness checks all succeed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A custom atom must declare complete semantic metadata and provide a supported, parameter-valid, exact conic graph implementation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proposed as a custom modeling atom.
The canonicalizer has finite registries of semantic rules and supported cones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Accept}(f)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{MetadataValid}(f)\land\operatorname{CompositionValid}(f)\land\operatorname{GraphExact}(f)\land\operatorname{ConesSupported}(f)\).

notation.meaning: the supplied lifted graph projects to the declared graph
