knowledge_statements.title: Robust Least-Squares Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact SOCP epigraph for spectral-norm-bounded perturbations of a least-squares matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\rho\ge0\). Under matrix uncertainty \(A+\Delta\) with \(\|\Delta\|_2\leho\), one has \(\sup_{\|\Delta\|_2\leho}\|(A+\Delta)x-b\|_2=\|Ax-b\|_2+ho\|x\|_2\). Hence the robust epigraph constraint is equivalent to the existence of \(s,r\ge0\) satisfying \(\|Ax-b\|_2\le s\), \(\|x\|_2\le r\), and \(s+ho r\le t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Spectral-norm matrix uncertainty adds the uncertainty radius times the decision norm to the nominal least-squares residual, producing an SOCP epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(\|\cdot\|_2\text{ denotes the Euclidean vector norm and induced spectral matrix norm.}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\|\Delta\|_2\leho}\|(A+\Delta)x-b\|_2\le t\iff\exists s,r\ge0:\ \|Ax-b\|_2\le s,\ \|x\|_2\le r,\ s+ho r\le t.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Quadratic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOCP representation of a robust squared residual under spectral-norm matrix uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\rho\ge0\), and \(t\ge0\). For perturbations \(\Delta\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfying \(\|\Delta\|_2\le\rho\), the robust quadratic constraint \(\|(A+\Delta)x-b\|_2^2\le t\) for every admissible \(\Delta\) is equivalent to the existence of \(s,r,w\ge0\) such that \(\|Ax-b\|_2\le s\), \(\|x\|_2\le r\), \(s+ho r\le w\), and \(w^2\le t\). The last inequality has a rotated-second-order-cone representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared residual under spectral-norm-bounded matrix uncertainty is represented by SOC bounds for the nominal residual and decision norm, followed by a rotated-cone square epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\ b\in\mathbb R^m,\ x\in\mathbb R^n.\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|(A+\Delta)x-b\|_2^2\le t\ \forall\Delta\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\text{ with }\|\Delta\|_2\le\rho\iff\exists s,r,w\ge0:\ \|Ax-b\|_2\le s,\ \|x\|_2\le r,\ s+ho r\le w,\ w^2\le t.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Portfolio SOC Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOCP template combining ellipsoidal mean-return uncertainty with a covariance risk bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let portfolio weights satisfy \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let uncertain mean return be \(\mu=\hat\mu+Pz\) with \(\|z\|_2\leho\), and let \(\Sigma\succeq0\). The requirements \(\mu^	op x\ge R\) for every admissible \(\mu\) and \(x^	op\Sigma x\le s^2\), with \(s\ge0\), are equivalent to \(\hat\mu^	op x-ho\|P^	op x\|_2\ge R\) and \(\|\Sigma^{1/2}x\|_2\le s\). If \(X\) is SOC-representable, the resulting portfolio model is an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoidal mean uncertainty subtracts a dual-norm return penalty, while covariance risk is a Euclidean-norm constraint; together they form an SOCP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu^	op x\ge R\ \forall\mu\iff\hat\mu^	op x-ho\|P^	op x\|_2\ge R,\qquad x^	op\Sigma x\le s^2\iff\|\Sigma^{1/2}x\|_2\le s.\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lossless scalar-multiplier characterizations of global implications between real quadratic inequalities, under strict feasibility of the antecedent inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let A,B\in\mathbb S^n. (i) If \(\exists\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\bar x^TA\bar x>0\), then
\[
(\forall x\in\mathbb R^n)\;[x^TAx\ge 0\Rightarrow x^TBx\ge 0]
\iff
\exists\lambda\ge 0:\ B-\lambda A\succeq 0.
\]
(ii) Let \(a,b\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\). If \(\exists\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(\bar x^TA\bar x+2a^T\bar x+\alpha>0\), then
\[
(\forall x\in\mathbb R^n)\;[x^TAx+2a^Tx+\alpha\ge 0\Rightarrow x^TBx+2b^Tx+\beta\ge 0]
\]
if and only if
\[
\exists\lambda\ge 0:\
\begin{bmatrix}
B-\lambda A & b-\lambda a\\
(b-\lambda a)^T & \beta-\lambda\alpha
\end{bmatrix}\succeq 0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility of the antecedent quadratic inequality, its global implication of another quadratic inequality is equivalent to a nonnegative scalar-multiplier certificate. For affine-quadratic functions, the certificate is positive semidefiniteness of the corresponding augmented matrix.
assumptions_latex: \exists\bar x\in\mathbb R^n:\ \bar x^TA\bar x+2a^T\bar x+\alpha>0\quad\text{for part (ii)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated global quadratic implication holds}\iff\exists\lambda\ge0\text{ such that the corresponding residual quadratic form has a positive-semidefinite matrix representation.}

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Quadratic-Uncertainty Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic implication with one scalar quadratic describing the uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_i(z)=z^{\mathsf T}Q_i z+2a_i^{\mathsf T}z+b_i\), where \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), for \(i=0,1\). The single-quadratic-uncertainty regime is the robust implication
\[q_1(z)\le 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_0(z)\le 0\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^n.\]
Thus the uncertainty set is determined by exactly one quadratic inequality, although the uncertain consequence may itself be quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single quadratic inequality defines the uncertainty set, and another quadratic inequality must hold for every point in that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_1(z)\le0\Rightarrow q_0(z)\le0\) for all \(z\in\mathbb R^n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Lossless Quadratic Counterparts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous-matrix counterpart of the strict-feasibility S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) and let \(q_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(q_i(z)=z^{\mathsf T}Q_i z+2a_i^{\mathsf T}z+b_i\), where \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), for \(i=0,1\). Suppose there exists \(\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(q_1(\bar z)<0\). Then
\[q_1(z)\le0\Longrightarrow q_0(z)\le0\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\]
holds if and only if there exists \(\lambda\ge0\) such that
\[\begin{bmatrix}Q_0-\lambda Q_1&a_0-\lambda a_1\\(a_0-\lambda a_1)^{\mathsf T}&b_0-\lambda b_1\end{bmatrix}\preceq0.\]
Consequently, the semi-infinite quadratic implication has a lossless semidefinite counterpart involving one nonnegative scalar multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict feasibility of the uncertainty inequality, the robust quadratic implication is equivalent to one negative-semidefinite matrix constraint with a nonnegative multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(q_i(z)=z^{\mathsf T}Q_i z+2a_i^{\mathsf T}z+b_i\), where \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), for \(i=0,1\).
There exists \(\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\) such that \(q_1(\bar z)<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication \(q_1(z)\le0\Rightarrow q_0(z)\le0\) holds for all \(z\in\mathbb R^n\) if and only if the displayed matrix is negative semidefinite for some \(\lambda\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Quadratic-Uncertainty Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-multiplier sufficient relaxation for intersections of quadratic uncertainty sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\ge2\), and let \(q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_m:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be quadratic functions. If there exist multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\) such that
\[q_0(z)-\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_iq_i(z)\le0\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^n,\]
then
\[q_i(z)\le0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_0(z)\le0.\]
The global quadratic inequality is representable by a negative-semidefinite coefficient matrix. For \(m>1\), existence of such scalar multipliers is generally sufficient but not necessary for the robust implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative scalar multipliers give an SDP-representable sufficient relaxation for multiple quadratic constraints, but the relaxation is generally not exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier inequality certifies the robust implication but need not characterize it exactly.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative scalar multiplier for the i-th constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: S-Lemma Regularity Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-feasibility condition for the inequality form of the S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the implication generated by one quadratic constraint \(q_1(z)\le0\), the standard S-lemma regularity condition is
\[\exists\,\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\quad q_1(\bar z)<0.\]
Equivalently, the quadratic uncertainty set has a point satisfying its defining inequality strictly. This condition excludes an empty strict sublevel set and supplies the constraint qualification under which the scalar-multiplier characterization of the quadratic implication is lossless.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The defining quadratic constraint must possess a strictly feasible point; this is the usual constraint qualification for the lossless inequality S-lemma.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(q_1(\bar z)<0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Reformulation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact semidefinite representation of one regular quadratic implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb N\) and let \(q_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(q_i(z)=z^{\mathsf T}Q_i z+2a_i^{\mathsf T}z+b_i\), where \(Q_i\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\), for \(i=0,1\). Assume \(q_1(\bar z)<0\) for some \(\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\). Then
\[q_0(z)\le0\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R^n\text{ satisfying }q_1(z)\le0\]
is equivalent to the existence of \(\lambda\ge0\) such that
\[\begin{bmatrix}Q_0&a_0\\a_0^{\mathsf T}&b_0\end{bmatrix}-\lambda\begin{bmatrix}Q_1&a_1\\a_1^{\mathsf T}&b_1\end{bmatrix}\preceq0.\]
Thus the multiplier LMI is an exact representation of the robust quadratic implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one strictly feasible quadratic uncertainty constraint, the multiplier LMI is equivalent to the original robust quadratic implication.
assumptions_latex: There exists \(\bar z\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(q_1(\bar z)<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The robust quadratic implication and the displayed multiplier LMI are equivalent.

knowledge_statements.title: S-Lemma Inexactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of scalar-multiplier necessity when strict feasibility is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), set \(q_1(z)=z^2\) and \(q_0(z)=z\). The uncertainty condition \(q_1(z)\le0\) forces \(z=0\), so the implication \(q_1(z)\le0\Rightarrow q_0(z)\le0\) is valid. However, no \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfies
\[q_0(z)-\lambda q_1(z)=z-\lambda z^2\le0\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R.\]
Indeed, for \(\lambda=0\) positive \(z\) violates the inequality, while for \(\lambda>0\) the value at \(z=1/(2\lambda)\) is positive. Thus losslessness can fail without strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the quadratic uncertainty set has no strictly feasible point, a valid implication may admit no nonnegative scalar-multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The implication is valid, but no scalar S-lemma multiplier exists.

notation.meaning: Degenerate uncertainty constraint whose feasible set is the singleton zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Matrix Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine dependence of a symmetric matrix pencil on uncertain parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,p\in\mathbb N\) and \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\). An affine uncertain symmetric matrix is
\[F(x,u)=F_0(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m u_iF_i(x),\]
where \(F_i(x)\in\mathbb S^p\) for \(i=0,\ldots,m\). Its robust positive-semidefinite constraint is
\[F(x,u)\succeq0\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U.\]
This is a semi-infinite matrix inequality unless the geometry of \(\mathcal U\) permits an exact conic reformulation or a finite sufficient relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine uncertain symmetric matrix pencil must be positive semidefinite for every parameter in a specified uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x,u)\succeq0\) for every \(u\in\mathcal U\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Fractional Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-denominator linear-fractional matrix model and its affine reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\in\mathcal U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), and suppose \(d(u)=d_0+d^{\mathsf T}u>0\) throughout \(\mathcal U\). A linear-fractional uncertain symmetric matrix has the form
\[F(u)=\frac{F_0+\sum_{i=1}^m u_iF_i}{d(u)}.\]
Because the denominator is positive,
\[F(u)\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_0+\sum_{i=1}^m u_iF_i\succeq0\]
for each \(u\in\mathcal U\). Thus a robust semidefinite condition with a common positive scalar denominator reduces pointwise to an affine-matrix uncertainty condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-fractional matrix inequality with a positive scalar denominator is equivalent to the affine matrix inequality obtained by clearing that denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robust positivity of the fractional pencil is equivalent to robust positivity of its affine numerator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust SDP with Linear-Fractional Matrix Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a robust semidefinite program with an affine-in-decision symmetric matrix constraint having well-posed linear-fractional dependence on uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=F(x)^T\) and \(L(x)\) be affine matrix-valued functions of \(x\), let \(R,D\) be fixed matrices, and let \(\Delta\in\mathbf{\Delta}\). Define
\[
\mathbf F(x,\Delta)=F(x)+L(x)\Delta(I-D\Delta)^{-1}R+\left(L(x)\Delta(I-D\Delta)^{-1}R\right)^T.
\]
Assume this linear-fractional representation is well posed over \(\mathbf{\Delta}\) and that \(\mathbf{\Delta}\) satisfies the stipulated uncertainty-set assumption. Then
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_x\ c^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbf F(x,\Delta)\succeq0\quad\text{for every }\Delta\in\mathbf{\Delta}
\]
is called a robust semidefinite program. The objective vector \(c\) may be assumed independent of \(\Delta\) without loss of generality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust SDP minimizes a linear objective subject to a positive-semidefinite matrix inequality for every admissible uncertainty matrix. Here the symmetric constraint matrix is affine in the decision variable and has the stated well-posed linear-fractional dependence on uncertainty. The objective vector may be taken to be uncertainty-independent without loss of generality.
assumptions_latex: F(x)=F(x)^T\text{, and }F\text{ and }L\text{ are affine matrix-valued functions of }x.
R\text{ and }D\text{ are fixed matrices, and }\Delta\in\mathbf{\Delta}.
\mathbf F(x,\Delta)\text{ has the displayed linear-fractional representation, well posed over }\mathbf{\Delta}.
\mathbf{\Delta}\text{ satisfies the uncertainty-set assumption stipulated in the source context}.
c\text{ is taken independent of }\Delta\text{ without loss of generality}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{minimize}_x\ c^Tx\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbf F(x,\Delta)\succeq0\quad\forall\Delta\in\mathbf{\Delta}\quad\text{is a robust SDP.}

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative scalar-multiplier certificates for robust matrix inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,p\in\mathbb N\), let
\[\mathcal U=\{u:g_j(u)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\},\]
and let \(H(x,u)\in\mathbb S^p\). A scalar-multiplier model selects \(\lambda_j\ge0\) and imposes
\[H(x,u)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j g_j(u)I_p\preceq0\qquad\text{for every }u.\]
This global matrix inequality is a sufficient certificate for
\[H(x,u)\preceq0\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal U.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative scalar multipliers combine uncertainty-set inequalities with a target matrix inequality to give a globally imposed sufficient certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiplier inequality implies \(H(x,u)\preceq0\) for every \(u\in\mathcal U\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative multiplier for the j-th uncertainty constraint.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrange-Relaxation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual upper representation for a constraint-defined worst-case problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(x\), define
\[\phi(x)=\sup\{f(x,u):g_j(u)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}.\]
For every multiplier vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\), the Lagrangian bound is
\[\phi(x)\le \sup_{u}\left(f(x,u)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_jg_j(u)\right).\]
Minimizing the right-hand side gives the relaxation
\[\phi(x)\le d(x):=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}\sup_u\left(f(x,u)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_jg_j(u)\right).\]
Requiring \(d(x)\le0\) is therefore sufficient for the robust constraint \(f(x,u)\le0\) on the uncertainty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lagrangian multipliers replace a constrained worst-case maximization by an unconstrained supremum and yield a conservative robust-feasibility test.
assumptions_latex: The displayed suprema and infimum are well-defined in the extended real sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi(x)\le d(x)\), so \(d(x)\le0\) certifies robust feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Tightness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-duality-gap criterion for exact Lagrangian robust reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Using the worst-case value \(\phi(x)\) and Lagrangian bound \(d(x)\), the relaxation is tight at \(x\) precisely when
\[d(x)=\phi(x).\]
It is feasibility-exact at threshold zero when
\[\phi(x)\le0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(x)\le0.\]
A sufficient regime for value tightness is strong Lagrangian duality for the inner worst-case problem, including attainment when an actual multiplier certificate is required. Outside such a regime weak duality only gives \(\phi(x)\le d(x)\), and the relaxed robust feasible set may be a strict subset of the original one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lagrangian robust relaxation is tight when its dual bound equals the true worst-case value; strong duality is a sufficient regime.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi(x)\) and \(d(x)\) are the primal worst-case and Lagrangian dual values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Value exactness is equivalent to \(d(x)=\phi(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Robust-SDP Approximation-Quality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective and feasibility ordering induced by sufficient robust-SDP relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider minimization of \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over the exact robust feasible set \(X_{\mathrm R}\), and let \(X_{\mathrm S}\) be the feasible set produced by a sufficient semidefinite certificate. Then
\[X_{\mathrm S}\subseteq X_{\mathrm R}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_{\mathrm R}\le v_{\mathrm S},\]
where \(v_{\mathrm R}=\inf_{x\in X_{\mathrm R}}c^{\mathsf T}x\) and \(v_{\mathrm S}=\inf_{x\in X_{\mathrm S}}c^{\mathsf T}x\). Exactness is the regime \(X_{\mathrm S}=X_{\mathrm R}\). Otherwise quality may be reported by an additive gap \(v_{\mathrm S}-v_{\mathrm R}\), or by the ratio \(v_{\mathrm S}/v_{\mathrm R}\) when both values are finite and \(v_{\mathrm R}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficient robust-SDP relaxation gives an inner feasible approximation and an upper objective bound for minimization; exactness means equality of feasible sets.
assumptions_latex: The optimization problem is a minimization problem.
The relevant optimal values are finite when a numerical gap is reported.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm R}\le v_{\mathrm S}\), with zero additive gap under exactness.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Gaussian SOC Counterparts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar Gaussian reformulation for affine uncertainty with risk at most one half.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\) in \(\mathbb R^m\), where \(\Sigma\succeq0\), and let \(a(x)\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b(x)\in\mathbb R\). For \(0<\varepsilon\leq 1/2\), the scalar chance constraint \[\mathbb P\!\left(a(x)^{\mathsf T}\xi\leq b(x)\right)\geq1-\varepsilon\] is equivalent to \[a(x)^{\mathsf T}\mu+\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\left\|\Sigma^{1/2}a(x)\right\|_2\leq b(x).\] If \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) are affine in \(x\), this inequality is second-order-cone representable because \(\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\geq0\). The formula also covers zero variance by continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar affine Gaussian chance constraint equals a deterministic mean-plus-quantile-standard-deviation inequality, which is SOC representable when the permitted violation probability is at most one half.
assumptions_latex: \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) are affine for the SOC modeling conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(a(x)^{\mathsf T}\xi\leq b(x))\geq1-\varepsilon\iff a(x)^{\mathsf T}\mu+\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\|\Sigma^{1/2}a(x)\|_2\leq b(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard one-dimensional Gaussian quantile reformulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact Gaussian quantile reformulation, zero-variance case, and SOC qualification are mathematically coherent and fit the representation container, but no inspectable citation with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Elliptical-Distribution Counterparts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar counterpart for a location-scale elliptical random vector with a fixed radial law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi=\mu+RAu\), where \(u\) is uniform on the unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^k\), \(R\geq0\) is independent of \(u\), and \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}\). Let \(Z=Ru_1\) have continuous distribution function \(F_Z\). For any \(a(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), \(b(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \[\mathbb P\!\left(a(x)^{\mathsf T}\xi\leq b(x)\right)\geq1-\varepsilon\] is equivalent to \[a(x)^{\mathsf T}\mu+F_Z^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\|A^{\mathsf T}a(x)\|_2\leq b(x).\] This is an SOC constraint when the quantile is nonnegative and the displayed mappings are affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed elliptical radial law, every scalar projection has a common standardized quantile, yielding a mean-plus-scaled-norm counterpart and, for a nonnegative quantile, an SOC model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(a(x)^{\mathsf T}\xi\leq b(x))\geq1-\varepsilon\iff a(x)^{\mathsf T}\mu+F_Z^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)\|A^{\mathsf T}a(x)\|_2\leq b(x)\).

notation.meaning: uniform random direction on the unit sphere
quantile function of the standardized scalar projection

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard location-scale projection property of elliptical distributions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection formula is plausible and appropriately classified as a representation, but its exact equivalence depends on the elliptical-law and generalized-quantile conventions. No inspectable source is supplied to establish those details.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Chance-Constraint Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bonferroni inner approximation using allocated marginal violation probabilities; no independence is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For measurable events \(E_i(x)=\{g_i(x,\xi)\leq0\}\), choose allocations \(\varepsilon_i\geq0\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^p\varepsilon_i\leq\varepsilon\). If every marginal constraint satisfies \[\mathbb P(E_i(x))\geq1-\varepsilon_i,\qquad i=1,\ldots,p,\] then Boole's inequality gives \[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^pE_i(x)\right)\geq1-\sum_{i=1}^p\varepsilon_i\geq1-\varepsilon.\] Thus conic counterparts for the marginal constraints form a safe inner approximation of the joint chance constraint. The approximation may be conservative because overlaps among violation events are ignored.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocating a total risk budget among marginal chance constraints guarantees the joint chance constraint by the union bound, without requiring independence, but can be conservative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl[\mathbb P(E_i(x))\geq1-\varepsilon_i\ \forall i\bigr]\Longrightarrow\mathbb P(\bigcap_iE_i(x))\geq1-\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: event that the ith uncertain constraint is satisfied

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Bonferroni construction is mathematically precise, requires no independence, and fits the joint-approximation container as a principle. An inspectable citation for the stated chance-constraint application is nevertheless absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Based Conic Safe Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust scalar chance constraint under known mean and covariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P(\mu,\Sigma)\) be the class of probability distributions on \(\mathbb R^m\) having mean \(\mu\) and covariance \(\Sigma\succeq0\). For \(0<\varepsilon<1\), the distributionally robust constraint \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P(\mu,\Sigma)}P\!\left(a(x)^{\mathsf T}\xi\leq b(x)\right)\geq1-\varepsilon\] is represented by the one-sided moment bound \[a(x)^{\mathsf T}\mu+\sqrt{\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}}\left\|\Sigma^{1/2}a(x)\right\|_2\leq b(x).\] Consequently, when \(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) are affine, the moment-based safe counterpart is second-order-cone representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With only mean and covariance known, a one-sided moment inequality yields a distributionally robust mean-plus-scaled-standard-deviation SOC counterpart.
assumptions_latex: Every distribution in \(\mathcal P(\mu,\Sigma)\) has finite second moments.
\(a(x)\) and \(b(x)\) are affine for the SOC conclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(x)^{\mathsf T}\mu+\sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon}\|\Sigma^{1/2}a(x)\|_2\leq b(x)\) safely enforces the robust chance constraint.

notation.meaning: ambiguity set of distributions with specified mean and covariance
a probability distribution in the ambiguity set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: scalar one-sided Chebyshev-Cantelli moment counterpart

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cantelli coefficient and SOC form are standard, but the wording that the full mean-covariance distributionally robust constraint is represented by this condition carries an exactness claim whose ambiguity-set hypotheses must be supported by a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical mixed-binary conic feasible-set interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A binary conic model is an optimization model whose feasible set can be written as \[\mathcal F=\left\{(x,z)\in\mathbb R^n\times\{0,1\}^q:Ax+Bz+c\in K\right\},\] possibly after introducing auxiliary continuous variables and taking a projection. Here \(K\) is a specified closed convex cone, or a Cartesian product of such cones. The binary vector \(z\) selects discrete alternatives, while all continuous constraints are encoded by affine membership in \(K\). An affine objective preserves the mixed-integer conic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary conic model combines binary variables with affine membership in a closed convex cone, allowing auxiliary continuous variables and projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{(x,z):Ax+Bz+c\in K,\ z\in\{0,1\}^q\}\) is a mixed-binary conic feasible set.

notation.meaning: closed convex cone or product cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical definition of a mixed-binary conic model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the binary-conic modeling container and is internally consistent, but no source with an inspectable definition, section, or page locator is cited.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Integer Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical conic interface with bounded or unbounded general-integer variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A general-integer conic model has a feasible set of the form \[\mathcal F=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^q:Ax+By+c\in K,\ \ell\leq y\leq u\right\},\] where integer bounds may have infinite components and \(K\) is a closed convex cone or a Cartesian product of closed convex cones. Auxiliary continuous or integer variables may be included, and projection onto the original variables is allowed. Unlike a binary conic model, components of \(y\) may assume more than two integer values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general-integer conic model imposes affine conic constraints on continuous and integer variables, optionally with finite or infinite integer bounds and auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F=\{(x,y):Ax+By+c\in K,\ y\in\mathbb Z^q,\ \ell\leq y\leq u\}\) is a general-integer conic feasible set.

notation.meaning: componentwise lower and upper integer bounds

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical definition of a mixed-integer conic model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes general-integer from binary conic models and fits the terminal container, but it lacks an inspectable supporting citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Semicontinuous Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary extended formulation of variables that are either zero or lie in a prescribed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constants \(0<\ell_i\leq u_i<\infty\), a scalar variable \(x_i\) is semicontinuous on \(\{0\}\cup[\ell_i,u_i]\) exactly when an auxiliary variable \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) satisfies \[\ell_i z_i\leq x_i\leq u_i z_i.\] Hence a semicontinuous conic model combines these inequalities with affine conic constraints such as \(Ax+Bz+c\in K\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone. The value \(z_i=0\) forces \(x_i=0\), whereas \(z_i=1\) forces \(x_i\in[\ell_i,u_i]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semicontinuous variable is either zero or within a positive interval; a binary variable and scaled bounds give an exact mixed-integer conic formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i\in\{0\}\cup[\ell_i,u_i]\iff\exists z_i\in\{0,1\}:\ell_i z_i\leq x_i\leq u_i z_i\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard binary formulation of a semicontinuous domain

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the explicitly positive finite bounds, the binary formulation is exact and fits the semicontinuous-model container. No inspectable source is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Conic Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical activation of an affine conic constraint by a binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, and define \(C=\{x:Fx+g\in K\}\). The indicator conic constraint \[z=1\ \Longrightarrow\ Fx+g\in K\] represents the disjunctive feasible set \[\bigl(\{0\}\times\mathbb R^n\bigr)\cup\bigl(\{1\}\times C\bigr).\] Thus the conic restriction is enforced when the indicator is active and imposes no restriction when it is inactive. Reversing the active value is obtained by replacing \(z\) with \(1-z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator conic constraint activates affine cone membership at one binary value and otherwise leaves the continuous variables unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=1\Rightarrow Fx+g\in K\) represents \((\{0\}\times\mathbb R^n)\cup(\{1\}\times C)\).

notation.meaning: continuous set defined by affine membership in the cone

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: logical disjunction represented by a binary indicator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logical disjunction and active-value convention are consistent and appropriately classified as a representation, but the record supplies no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.title: Big-M Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact big-M encoding when a valid cone-direction relaxation constant is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a closed convex cone, choose \(e\in K\), and suppose \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the inactive-state domain. If \(M\geq0\) satisfies \[Fx+g+Me\in K\qquad\text{for every }x\in X,\] then, for \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the constraint \[Fx+g+M(1-z)e\in K\] enforces \(Fx+g\in K\) when \(z=1\) and is redundant over \(X\) when \(z=0\). Therefore it is an exact big-M formulation of the indicator constraint relative to \(X\). An invalid or excessively large \(M\) respectively destroys validity or weakens the continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a valid cone-direction big-M term deactivates cone membership at one binary value; exactness depends on the chosen constant covering the entire inactive domain.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and \(e\in K\).
\(M\geq0\) makes \(Fx+g+Me\in K\) valid for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Fx+g+M(1-z)e\in K\) exactly models \(z=1\Rightarrow Fx+g\in K\) over \(X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cone-direction construction is coherent when exactness is understood relative to an enforced domain X. A specific source is required to support this generalized conic big-M formulation and its domain qualification.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Hull Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenized extended formulation for the closed convex hull of finitely many conic disjuncts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(j=1,\ldots,p\), let \(C_j=\{x:A_jx+b_j\in K_j\}\), where each \(K_j\) is a closed convex cone. The homogenized system \[x=\sum_{j=1}^p v_j,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^p\lambda_j=1,\qquad \lambda_j\geq0,\qquad A_jv_j+\lambda_jb_j\in K_j\] projects onto the closed convex hull of \(\bigcup_j C_j\), provided the homogenized cones introduce no extraneous zero-weight recession directions; this condition holds, in particular, for nonempty compact \(C_j\). Binary restrictions \(\lambda_j\in\{0,1\}\) recover the original disjunction, while continuous weights give its hull relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disaggregated variables, simplex weights, and homogenized conic constraints represent a disjunction; relaxing binary weights yields its closed convex hull under standard recession conditions.
assumptions_latex: Each \(K_j\) is a closed convex cone and each \(C_j\) is nonempty.
The homogenized formulation has no extraneous zero-weight recession directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_jC_j)\) is the projection of the displayed homogenized conic system.

notation.meaning: disaggregated continuous vector for disjunct j
closed convex cone defining disjunct j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: homogenization-based convex-hull formulation for conic disjunctions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and homogenized formulation fit the container, but the exact closed-hull conclusion depends on recession and closure hypotheses summarized only informally as absence of extraneous zero-weight directions. A source stating precise sufficient conditions is needed before the mathematical version can be trusted.

knowledge_statements.title: On–Off Quadratic Terms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective convexification of a positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph controlled by a binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) and consider the on-off epigraph \[S=\{(x,z,t):z\in\{0,1\},\ z=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ z=1\Rightarrow t\geq x^{\mathsf T}Qx,\ t\geq0\}.\] Its standard perspective relaxation is \[0\leq z\leq1,\qquad t\geq0,\qquad x^{\mathsf T}Qx\leq tz.\] The last inequality is convex and rotated-second-order-cone representable after factoring \(Q=L^{\mathsf T}L\), because it becomes \(\|Lx\|_2^2\leq tz\). With compatible perspective-scaled domain restrictions, this formulation gives the closed convex hull of the on-off quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The perspective inequality replaces an activated quadratic epigraph by a rotated-SOC constraint and, with compatible scaled domain restrictions, gives its closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: Any additional domain restrictions are perspective-scaled consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\leq tz\) is the perspective convexification and is representable by a rotated second-order cone.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical perspective formulation of an on-off convex quadratic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The perspective inequality and rotated-SOC representation are standard and fit the representation container. The closed-convex-hull qualification, especially with positive-semidefinite Q and possible additional domains, requires a specific source.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and contains \(0\).
The closed perspective convention is used at \(z=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(z,x,t):0\leq z\leq1,\ x\in zX,\ t\geq\|Bx\|\}\).

notation.meaning: scaled set containing points zx with x in X

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: perspective of a positively homogeneous norm over a scaled domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perspective hull formulation for an activated norm epigraph over a bounded convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, compact, and convex with \(0\in X\), and let \(f(x)=\|Bx\|\) for a norm \(\|\cdot\|\). For the on-off set consisting of \((z,x,t)=(0,0,t)\) with \(t\geq0\), or \(z=1\), \(x\in X\), and \(t\geq f(x)\), its convex hull is represented by \[0\leq z\leq1,\qquad x\in zX,\qquad t\geq zf(x/z)=\|Bx\|,\] using the closed perspective convention at \(z=0\). Thus homogeneity leaves the norm epigraph inequality unchanged; the scaled-domain constraint carries the essential on-off coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an activated norm epigraph, positive homogeneity leaves the norm inequality unchanged under perspective scaling; the scaled domain enforces the actual on-off coupling.
knowledge_statements.title: On–Off Norm Terms

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((t,z,\sqrt{2}Lx)\in\mathcal Q_r\) represents the closed perspective epigraph of \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z>0\), the perspective epigraph inequality \(t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx/z\) is equivalent to \((t,z,\sqrt{2}Lx)\in\mathcal Q_r\). At \(z=0\), the cone constraint implies \(Lx=0\); hence it gives the closure \[\operatorname{cl}\{(x,z,t):z>0,\ t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx/z\}.\] If \(Q\succ0\), the zero-activation slice forces \(x=0\). Restricting \(z\in\{0,1\}\) therefore yields an exact on-off quadratic epigraph, while allowing \(0\le z\le1\) gives its perspective relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic perspective epigraph is represented by one rotated second-order-cone constraint; with positive-definite curvature, zero activation forces the modeled vector to zero.

notation.meaning: Valid upper bound on the active variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete weakness of a valid big-M relaxation for an on-off quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the epigraph disjunction \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ t\ge0\) and \(z=1\Rightarrow t\ge x^2\), with \(0\le x\le U\). A valid big-M relaxation is \[t\ge x^2-U^2(1-z),\qquad 0\le x\le Uz,\qquad t\ge0.\] The fractional point \((x,z,t)=(U/2,1/2,0)\) satisfies these inequalities because its first right-hand side is \(-U^2/4\). The perspective relaxation requires \(t\ge x^2/z=U^2/2\), so it excludes that point. Thus validity of \(M=U^2\) does not prevent a strict continuous-relaxation gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid big-M quadratic epigraph formulation can admit fractional activation with zero epigraph cost, while the perspective formulation imposes a positive cost.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Big-M Formulations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness boundary for bound-based linearization of an unbounded on-off variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(X\) is not contained in any bounded interval. For any finite \(M\ge0\), the inequalities \[-Mz\le x\le Mz\] correctly force \(x=0\) when \(z=0\), but when \(z=1\) they restrict \(x\) to \([-M,M]\). Because \(X\nsubseteq[-M,M]\), some intended active feasible point is removed. Hence no finite symmetric big-M constant yields an exact formulation. An exact bound-based formulation requires finite valid lower and upper bounds for every controlled expression, or a different disjunctive or conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the active domain is unbounded, every finite big-M bound removes some intended active feasible point; exact bound-based linearization is therefore impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Missing Finite Bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity threshold and relaxation consequence for a scalar big-M indicator inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(z=1\), the big-M inequality reduces to \(g(x)\le0\). At \(z=0\), it permits all \(x\in X\) exactly only if \[M\ge M^\star:=\sup_{x\in X}g(x).\] If \(M<M^\star\), at least one intended inactive point is excluded, so the formulation is invalid. If \(M\ge M^\star\), the integer formulation is valid; however, increasing \(M\) enlarges the feasible set for fractional \(z\in(0,1)\). When \(M^\star\) is finite and attained, choosing \(M=M^\star\) is the tightest scalar constant for this inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A big-M indicator is valid exactly when its constant bounds the worst inactive violation; undersizing is invalid, while oversizing enlarges the fractional relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Bound Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The supremum threshold correctly characterizes validity of the scalar indicator inequality, and the fractional-relaxation monotonicity claim is appropriately scoped. No inspectable source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-activation closure of a proper closed convex perspective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed perspective of \(f\) is \[\widetilde f(x,z)=\begin{cases}z f(x/z),&z>0,\\ f^\infty(x),&z=0,\\ +\infty,&z<0.\end{cases}\] Therefore, imposing \(x=0\) whenever \(z=0\) reproduces the perspective closure only if every nonzero direction has infinite recession value. If some \(d\ne0\) satisfies \(f^\infty(d)<+\infty\), then \((d,0,f^\infty(d))\) belongs to the closed epigraph but is deleted by the imposed zero slice. Conversely, omitting all zero-slice restrictions can admit points for which \(f^\infty(x)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At zero activation, a closed perspective is governed by the recession function. Forcing the original variable to zero can therefore misrepresent the closure.
knowledge_statements.title: On–Off Domain-Closure Failures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recession-function zero slice and the stated boundary for imposing x=0 are mathematically consistent and fit a failure-boundary leaf. An authoritative source with a specific closed-perspective locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Template-level constraint counting for a fixed canonicalization and row-count convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a canonical expression graph with distinct instantiated atoms \(V_c\), define \(r_v\ge0\) as the number of generated affine equality or inequality rows and \(b_v\ge0\) as the number of scalar rows placed in cone blocks by the template for \(v\). Then \[R=R_0+\sum_{v\in V_c}r_v,\qquad B=B_0+\sum_{v\in V_c}b_v,\] where \(R_0\) and \(B_0\) count original model rows. If \(r_v+b_v\le q\) uniformly, total generated constraint rows grow by at most \(q|V_c|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed convention, generated constraint rows add across distinct atom templates and grow linearly when every template has uniformly bounded size.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_0\) be the number of original cone blocks and let every distinct canonicalized atom \(v\in V_c\) emit \(k_v\ge0\) additional blocks. Without block aggregation, \[K=K_0+\sum_{v\in V_c}k_v.\] Thus a family of \(m\) atom occurrences, each mapped to at least one separate block, produces \(K\ge K_0+m\) unless occurrences share a canonical node. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Process nodes of \(G=(V,E)\) in topological order, initialize \(H=\varnothing\), and compute \(\sigma(v)\) from the operator, immutable parameters, shape, and canonical child identifiers. The procedure stops after \(|V|\) node visits and emits at most one auxiliary lift for each structural equivalence class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relation between filled-graph edges and structural Cholesky entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symbolic Cholesky factorization of an \(n\times n\) positive-definite matrix under ordering \(\pi\), with numerical cancellation ignored, the structural off-diagonal nonzeros of the triangular factor are in bijection with \(E_\pi^+\). Hence \[\operatorname{nnz}(L)=n+|E_\pi^+|=n+|E|+|F_\pi|,\] so fill contributes exactly \(|F_\pi|\) additional structural entries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The filled graph is the symbolic Cholesky pattern, and each fill edge contributes one additional off-diagonal factor entry.
assumptions_latex: Each undirected edge is counted once in the triangular factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(L)-\bigl(n+|E|\bigr)=|F_\pi|.

knowledge_statements.title: Symbolic Factor Pattern and Fill Count

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp characterization of orderings that introduce no symbolic fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(\pi\) an elimination ordering. Then \(F_\pi=\varnothing\) if and only if the neighbors of each vertex occurring later in \(\pi\) form a clique. Thus \(G\) admits a zero-fill ordering if and only if \(G\) is chordal, and its zero-fill orderings are precisely its perfect elimination orderings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ordering produces no fill exactly when it is a perfect elimination ordering; such an ordering exists exactly for chordal graphs.
assumptions_latex: Elimination completes each eliminated vertex's remaining-neighbor set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_\pi=\varnothing\iff \pi\text{ is a perfect elimination ordering},\qquad \exists\pi:F_\pi=\varnothing\iff G\text{ is chordal}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Fill Characterization

Variables are eliminated according to an ordering \(\pi\).
Symbolic factorization is considered without numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fill-in consists exactly of edges added between later neighbors during elimination, and its amount depends on \(\pi\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graph elimination defines symbolic Cholesky fill by completing later-neighbor sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-theoretic definition of symbolic fill in sparse symmetric positive-definite Cholesky factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(A)=(V,E)\) contain edge \(\{i,j\}\) whenever \(i\ne j\) and \(A_{ij}\ne0\). Eliminate vertices in order \(\pi\). Immediately before eliminating vertex \(v\), connect every pair of its uneliminated neighbors, then remove \(v\). The resulting supergraph is \(G_\pi^+=(V,E_\pi^+)\), and its fill-in set is \[F_\pi=E_\pi^+\setminus E.\] In symbolic Cholesky factorization without numerical cancellation, edges in \(F_\pi\) correspond to factor entries absent from the original sparsity pattern. Different orderings can produce different fill sets and memory requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For sparse positive-definite Cholesky factorization, fill-in is the set of new graph edges created when later neighbors are connected during ordered elimination; it predicts additional symbolic factor entries.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity Fill-In

children.title: Memory-Footprint Growth
children.top_down_role: Storage growth attributable to expanded conic representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-precision storage of sparse canonical conic data before solver-specific factorization workspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider canonical data \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(k\) cone-block descriptors. Under fixed-precision compressed sparse storage with constant-size descriptors, storing these objects requires \[M_{\mathrm{rep}}=\Theta\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n+k\right).\] Here \(m\) and \(n\) include all generated rows and auxiliary variables. This bound concerns persistent canonical data and excludes factorization factors, iterates, symbolic analysis, and numerical workspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent storage of a sparse canonical conic representation is linear in its matrix nonzeros, row and variable counts, and cone-block metadata; solver factors and workspaces are additional.
assumptions_latex: Numeric entries, sparse indices, and cone-block descriptors occupy constant-size storage.
The affine operator is stored in a standard compressed sparse format.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_{\mathrm{rep}}=\Theta\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n+k\right).

notation.meaning: Persistent storage of the canonical representation

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Representation Storage Ledger

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of inferring peak factorization memory from stored input and factor nonzeros alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a specified sparse factorization implementation, partition simultaneous memory as \[M_{\mathrm{peak}}=M_H+M_L+M_{\mathrm{sym}}+M_{\mathrm{num}}+M_{\mathrm{pivot}}+M_{\mathrm{other}},\] representing input, factors, symbolic workspace, numerical workspace, pivoting data, and other live solver arrays. Thus \(\operatorname{nnz}(H)+\operatorname{nnz}(L)+n\) describes persistent input-and-factor storage under fixed precision, but does not by itself give a universal asymptotically tight peak-memory bound. Such a bound requires implementation-specific control of the workspace terms; dynamic pivoting may also change the factor pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Input and factor nonzeros describe persistent sparse storage, but peak memory additionally depends on symbolic, numerical, pivoting, and other simultaneously live workspaces.
assumptions_latex: All terms use a common fixed-precision storage model.
Peak memory means simultaneous live allocation in a specified implementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_{\mathrm{peak}}=\Theta\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(H)+\operatorname{nnz}(L)+n\right)\text{ requires corresponding bounds on every additional workspace term.}
knowledge_statements.title: Peak-Workspace Accounting Boundary
Memory-Footprint Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak storage for a sparse direct factorization of a canonical conic-system matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb{S}^n\) be a sparse KKT or normal-equations matrix, let \(P\) be a permutation matrix, and suppose \(PHP^{\mathsf T}=LDL^{\mathsf T}\) is computed without numerical pivoting. Under fixed-precision compressed sparse storage, the factorization memory satisfies \[M(P)=\Theta\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(H)+\operatorname{nnz}(L)+n\right).\] Consequently, a formulation sequence has linear sparse-memory growth precisely when the stored input and factor nonzero counts are both linear in the representation size; fill causing \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)\) to grow superlinearly produces corresponding superlinear memory growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse-factorization memory grows with the stored canonical matrix and its filled factor; superlinear factor fill therefore causes superlinear memory use.
assumptions_latex: \(H\in\mathbb{S}^n\) admits the stated factorization without numerical pivoting.
\(H\) and \(L\) use fixed-precision compressed sparse storage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(P)=\Theta\!\left(\operatorname{nnz}(H)+\operatorname{nnz}(L)+n\right)\).

notation.meaning: Number of stored nonzero entries of a matrix.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stored-matrix estimate is plausible, but the asserted peak-memory bound may omit symbolic and numerical workspaces. An authoritative sparse-factorization source specifying the storage and workspace model is required.

children.title: Ordering-Sensitive Fill
children.top_down_role: Fill behavior affected by variable, constraint, or block ordering.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit family producing asymptotically different symbolic fill under two orderings of the same sparse pattern.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=K_{1,n-1}\) be the star with center \(c\) and \(n-1\) leaves. Eliminating every leaf before \(c\) creates no fill, so the filled graph has \(n-1\) edges and the symbolic triangular factor has \(2n-1\) nonzeros. Eliminating \(c\) first connects every pair of leaves, producing the complete filled graph \(K_n\) and \(n(n+1)/2\) factor nonzeros. Thus two orderings of the same \(O(n)\)-edge graph yield respectively \(\Theta(n)\) and \(\Theta(n^2)\) factor storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leaves-first elimination of a star has linear factor storage, whereas center-first elimination fills the leaves into a clique and has quadratic storage.
assumptions_latex: Symbolic symmetric elimination is performed without numerical cancellation.
The triangular factor stores its diagonal and one entry for every filled-graph edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(L_{\mathrm{leaves\ first}})=2n-1,\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(L_{\mathrm{center\ first}})=\frac{n(n+1)}2.
knowledge_statements.title: Star-Graph Ordering Separation
Ordering-Sensitive Fill
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic fill under permutation-based sparse symmetric elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(H)=(V,E)\) be the undirected sparsity graph of a structurally symmetric matrix \(H\), and let \(\pi\) be an elimination ordering. Symbolic elimination successively connects every pair of uneliminated neighbors of the eliminated vertex, producing a filled graph \(G_\pi^+=(V,E_\pi^+)\). In the absence of numerical cancellation, the symbolic nonzero pattern of the triangular factor is determined by \(E_\pi^+\), with \[\operatorname{nnz}(L)=|V|+|E_\pi^+|.\] Since \(E_\pi^+\) depends on \(\pi\), different orderings of the same canonical conic system can require different factorization memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Elimination ordering changes which fill edges are created and can therefore change the triangular factor size and memory footprint.
assumptions_latex: Symbolic factorization is considered without numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)=|V|+|E_\pi^+|\), and this quantity may depend on \(\pi\).

notation.meaning: Undirected sparsity graph of the matrix.
Edges after symbolic fill under the ordering.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symbolic-fill statement is standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the filled-graph convention or the exact nonzero-count formula.

children.title: Exact Conic Representations
children.top_down_role: Conic formulations preserving the source feasible region exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Conic Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation of a feasible set by an affine conic slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(q\in\mathbb{N}_0\), let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) be a closed convex cone, and let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Define \[R_K:=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,\;Ax+By+b\in K\right\}.\] This lifted conic formulation is an exact conic representation of \(S\) when \(R_K=S\). Equivalently, every point of \(S\) has a conic lift, and projection introduces neither additional points nor loss of feasible points. When \(q=0\), the representation is an unlifted affine inverse image of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic formulation is exact when projecting its affine conic feasible set yields precisely the original feasible set.

notation.meaning: Projection of the affine conic feasible set.

source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_refs.locator: 6.4 Constructing Semidefinite Representations p. 271

source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry
source_witnesses.locator: 6.4 Constructing Semidefinite Representations p. 271

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties forced, and not forced, by finite lifted representations over closed convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every set with a finite affine representation over a convex cone is convex, but it need not be closed even when the representing cone is closed. For the rotated second-order cone \[K=\{(x,z,y):x\geq0,\ z\geq0,\ 2xz\geq y^2\},\] its projection onto \((x,y)\) is \[\{(x,y):x>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\},\] which is convex but not closed. Thus exact closed-cone representability does not authorize replacing the represented set by its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact affine-conic projections are convex, but projections of closed convex cones can be nonclosed.
assumptions_latex: Only finite affine constraints and coordinate projection are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is convex, while closedness of }K\text{ need not imply closedness of }S.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Nonclosed-Projection Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimization Fidelity of Exact Conic Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of objective values and original-variable minimizers under exact lifted reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_K=S\) be an exact conic representation and let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Then \[\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf\{f(x):Ax+By+b\in K\}.\] An original point \(x^\star\) is optimal exactly when it admits a lift \(y^\star\) for which \((x^\star,y^\star)\) is optimal. Exact representability alone does not imply attainment, strong duality, or numerical accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact conic lift preserves every objective on the original variables and their minimizers, but does not automatically provide attainment, strong duality, or numerical guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The lifted objective is \(f(x)\) and has no additional dependence on \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{Ax+By+b\in K}f(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Fidelity of Exact Conic Representations

children.title: Safe Outer Approximations
children.top_down_role: Conservative outer approximations used in conic modeling.

knowledge_statements.title: Safe Outer Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer conic relaxation and its valid lower bound for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the original feasible set, let \(O\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be conic representable, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The set \(O\) is a safe outer approximation of \(S\) when \(S\subseteq O\). Define \(p_S:=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\) and \(p_O:=\inf_{x\in O}f(x)\). Then \[p_O\le p_S.\] Thus an outer approximation cannot exclude an originally feasible point and supplies a valid lower bound for minimization, although an optimizer in \(O\setminus S\) need not be feasible for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer approximation contains the original feasible set and gives a valid lower bound for every extended-real-valued minimization objective on the ambient space.
assumptions_latex: The infima are interpreted in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_O\le p_S\).

notation.meaning: Infimum of the objective over a set \(T\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone bounds for a nested family of outer approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq O_{r+1}\subseteq O_r\) and define \(p_T:=\inf_{x\in T}f(x)\). Then \[p_{O_r}\le p_{O_{r+1}}\le p_S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tightening nested outer approximations weakly improves their minimization lower bounds.

children.title: Safe Inner Approximations
children.top_down_role: Feasibility-preserving inner approximations used in conic modeling.

knowledge_statements.title: Safe Inner Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inner conic restriction and its feasible upper bound for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the original feasible set, let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be conic representable, and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The set \(I\) is a safe inner approximation of \(S\) when \(I\subseteq S\). Define \(p_S:=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\) and \(p_I:=\inf_{x\in I}f(x)\). Then \[p_S\le p_I.\] Every point in \(I\) is feasible for the original problem, so any finite attained value over \(I\) is a valid upper bound on the original minimization optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner approximation lies inside the original feasible set, ensuring feasibility and a valid upper bound for every extended-real-valued minimization objective on the ambient space.
assumptions_latex: The infima are interpreted in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_S\le p_I\).

notation.meaning: Infimum of the objective over a set \(T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_r\subseteq I_{r+1}\subseteq S\) and define \(p_T:=\inf_{x\in T}f(x)\). Then \[p_S\le p_{I_{r+1}}\le p_{I_r}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding nested inner approximations weakly improves their minimization upper bounds.

children.title: Exactness-to-Conservatism Boundary
children.top_down_role: Transition from exact representation to controlled conservatism.

knowledge_statements.title: Exactness-to-Conservatism Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion and objective-value boundary separating exact formulations from conservative approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq S\subseteq O\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(I\) and \(O\) are respectively inner and outer conic approximations of \(S\), and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). For each \(T\in\{I,S,O\}\), define \(p_T:=\inf_{x\in T}f(x)\). Then \[p_O\le p_S\le p_I.\] The outer formulation is exact precisely when \(O=S\), and the inner formulation is exact precisely when \(I=S\). Their set-valued conservatism is measured by \(O\setminus S\) and \(S\setminus I\), respectively; both formulations are simultaneously exact precisely when \(I=S=O\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested inner, original, and outer feasible sets bracket every minimization value; each approximation is exact when its feasible set equals the original set.
assumptions_latex: The infima are interpreted in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_O\le p_S\le p_I\); outer exactness is equivalent to \(O=S\), inner exactness is equivalent to \(I=S\), and simultaneous exactness is equivalent to \(I=S=O\).

notation.meaning: Inner, original, and outer feasible sets.
Infimum of the objective over a set \(T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value Exactness Does Not Imply Set Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between formulation exactness and equality of optimal values for one objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=I=\{0\}\), \(O=[0,1]\), and \(f(x)=0\). Then \(I\subseteq S\subsetneq O\), but \[\inf_{x\in I}f(x)=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf_{x\in O}f(x)=0.\] Thus equality of optimal values for one objective does not imply equality of feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonexact outer approximation can have the exact value for a selected objective, so value exactness is weaker than formulation exactness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O\ne S\) although \(p_O=p_S=p_I\).

notation.meaning: Inner, original, and outer feasible sets.

children.title: Lift Size
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary dimensions introduced by lifted conic representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundant auxiliary variables can enlarge a lift without changing its projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(R=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in F\}\) is a lifted conic representation. For every integer \(k\ge1\), \[R=\{x:\exists y\,\exists z\in\mathbb R^k,\ (x,y)\in F,\ z=0\}.\] Hence a size measure counting auxiliary variables or affine equations can be increased arbitrarily without changing the represented set. Raw lift size is a property of a chosen formulation under a declared convention, not of the projected set alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant zero variables can make an equivalent lift arbitrarily larger, so raw lift size belongs to a formulation and convention rather than to the represented set alone.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) has a finite lifted conic representation.
The size convention counts auxiliary variables or affine equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) admits projection-equivalent formulations with arbitrarily inflated declared size.

notation.meaning: Redundant auxiliary vector constrained to zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Lift Size Is Representation Dependent
Lift Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A declared size measure for a product-cone extended formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a lifted formulation \[R=\left\{x:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,
\,A_jx+B_jy+b_j\in K_j,
\ j=1,
\ldots,
\ell\right\},\] where \(K_j\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_j}\). Under the aggregate-dimension convention, its lift size is \[\sigma(R):=q+\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}d_j.\] A complete size profile additionally records the number of cone blocks and affine scalar equations, namely \(\bigl(q,
\ell,
(d_j)_{j=1}^{\ell},
 m_{\mathrm{eq}}\bigr)\). Because distinct cones of equal dimension can have different computational costs, the convention used for \(\sigma\) must accompany any size comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift size counts auxiliary variables and cone dimensions under a declared convention; block structure and affine equations complete the profile.
assumptions_latex: All compared formulations use the same size convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(R)=q+\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}d_j\).

notation.meaning: Ambient dimension of cone block j.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record explicitly declares a coherent aggregate-dimension measure, but calling it lift size requires a source establishing or contextualizing this convention and its relation to other common size measures.

children.title: Relaxation Strength
children.top_down_role: Tightness of lifted conic relaxations relative to the source model.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-independent strength ordering for outer conic relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S,R_1,R_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfy \(S\subseteq R_1\cap R_2\). The outer relaxation \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\) when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\), and it is strictly stronger when \(R_1\subsetneq R_2\). If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), then \[\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)\le \inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)\le \inf_{x\in S}f(x).\] Hence the stronger relaxation gives a minimization lower bound no worse than that from the weaker relaxation, independently of the chosen objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among outer relaxations, the smaller feasible set is stronger and yields a minimization lower bound at least as tight for every extended-real-valued objective on the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)\le\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Strength Need Not Strictly Improve a Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict feasible-set containment does not force strict improvement for every objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{0\}\), \(R_1=[0,1]\), \(R_2=[0,2]\), and \(f(x)=x\). Then \(S\subseteq R_1\subsetneq R_2\), so \(R_1\) is strictly stronger, yet \[\inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)=\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly stronger relaxation can produce the same bound as a weaker relaxation for a selected objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\subsetneq R_2\) but \(p_{R_1}=p_{R_2}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Strength Need Not Strictly Improve a Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absence of containment prevents an objective-independent strength ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{0\}\), \(R_1=[-1,0]\), and \(R_2=[0,1]\). Neither outer relaxation contains the other. For \(f(x)=x\), \(\inf_{R_1}f=-1<0=\inf_{R_2}f\); for \(g(x)=-x\), \(\inf_{R_2}g=-1<0=\inf_{R_1}g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When outer relaxations are incomparable by inclusion, either can give the better minimization bound depending on the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\not\subseteq R_2\), \(R_2\not\subseteq R_1\), and their bound ranking reverses between \(f\) and \(g\).

notation.meaning: Objectives used to compare the relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomparable Relaxations Have Objective-Dependent Rankings

children.title: Size-Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representation choices balancing lift growth against relaxation tightness.

knowledge_statements.title: Size-Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone conic hierarchies in which tighter relaxations require no smaller declared lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((R_r)_{r\ge1}\) be outer conic relaxations of \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \[S\subseteq R_{r+1}\subseteq R_r\quad\text{and}\quad\sigma(R_{r+1})\ge\sigma(R_r)\] for every \(r\ge1\). Then increasing \(r\) weakly improves relaxation strength while weakly increasing lift size. For any \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\), define \(p_r:=\inf_{x\in R_r}f(x)\) and \(p_S:=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\). The bounds satisfy \[p_r\le p_{r+1}\le p_S.\] If additionally \(\bigcap_{r\ge1}R_r=S\), the hierarchy is setwise exact in the intersection limit, but finite exactness is not implied. Thus size and strength must be reported jointly for the hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a nested hierarchy, tighter outer relaxations give weakly better lower bounds while their declared lift sizes may increase; exactness of the limiting intersection does not ensure finite-level exactness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_r\le p_{r+1}\le p_S\).

notation.meaning: Minimization value over the level-\(r\) relaxation.
Minimization value over the original feasible set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint comparison of outer formulations under a fixed size convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_1,R_2\) be outer relaxations of the same set and let \(\sigma\) be a fixed formulation-size measure. Formulation \(R_1\) Pareto-dominates \(R_2\) when \[R_1\subseteq R_2,\qquad \sigma(R_1)\le\sigma(R_2),\] with at least one strict relation. A formulation is Pareto-efficient within a declared class if no formulation in that class dominates it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formulation dominates another when it is no larger and no weaker, with at least one strict improvement.
assumptions_latex: Both formulations relax the same original feasible set.
\(\sigma\) uses one fixed convention and formulation class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\) dominates \(R_2\) when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\), \(\sigma(R_1)\le\sigma(R_2)\), and at least one relation is strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Size–Strength Pareto Dominance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation size alone imposes no strength order without a structured family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For outer formulations \(R_1,R_2\), the inequality \(\sigma(R_1)\le\sigma(R_2)\) alone implies neither \(R_1\subseteq R_2\) nor \(R_2\subseteq R_1\). Redundant variables can increase size without changing the projected relaxation, and distinct larger formulations may be stronger, weaker, or incomparable. Monotone size–strength behavior must therefore be assumed or proved for the particular formulation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larger lifts are not automatically stronger, and smaller lifts are not automatically weaker.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) are outer formulations of the same source set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(R_1)\le\sigma(R_2)\not\Rightarrow R_1\subseteq R_2\text{ or }R_2\subseteq R_1\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Universal Size–Strength Monotonicity

children.title: SOC Representation Quality
children.top_down_role: Strength, size, and numerical quality of second-order cone representations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier Parameter of an SOC Product Lift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic barrier-complexity contribution of the SOC blocks in a lifted formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\prod_{j=1}^{\ell}Q_{d_j}\), where \(d_j\ge2\), and let \[F((t_j,u_j)_{j=1}^{\ell})=-\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}\log\!\left(t_j^2-\|u_j\|_2^2\right).\] Then \(F\) is a logarithmically homogeneous self-concordant barrier for \(K\) with parameter \(\nu=2\ell\). Thus generic short-step iteration bounds have a \(\sqrt{2\ell}\) barrier factor, while block dimensions, affine sparsity, and coupling determine per-iteration linear-algebra cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Cone Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a natural formulation relative to a specified primitive cone library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone designated as primitive by a modeling system. A conic representation of \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is natural relative to that library when there exist \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) such that
\[F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax+b\in K\},\]
and the membership condition is passed directly to the solver, without auxiliary variables or replacement of \(K\) by a projection of other cones. Naturalness is therefore relative to the declared primitive library, not an intrinsic property of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A model is natural when it expresses feasibility directly with a primitive cone, without lifting or decomposing that cone.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone.
\(K\) belongs to the specified primitive cone library.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\{x:Ax+b\in K\}\) is represented without auxiliary variables or cone decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposed Cone Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact lifted representation by a product of solver-supported cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). For integers \(p\geq 0\), \(q\geq 1\), and \(r_i\geq 1\), set \(r=\sum_{i=1}^q r_i\). An exact decomposed cone model of \(F\) consists of auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb R^p\), primitive cones \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{r_i}\), matrices \(G\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) and \(H\in\mathbb R^{r\times p}\), and \(h\in\mathbb R^r\) such that
\[F=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p,\;Gx+Hy+h\in K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\right\}.\]
Thus \(F\) is exactly the projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates of the lifted feasible set. Replacing equality by a strict inclusion produces a relaxation or restriction rather than an exact reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposed model introduces auxiliary variables and primitive product cones so that projecting the lifted feasible set exactly recovers the original feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(K_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{r_i}\) are closed convex cones supported by the solver.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{n+p}:Gx+Hy+h\in\prod_{i=1}^qK_i\}\).

children.title: Decomposition Quality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Size, strength, and numerical consequences of cone decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Quality Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact cone decompositions from relaxations, restrictions, and numerically fragile lifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an original feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and lifted set \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\), fidelity holds precisely when \(F=\operatorname{proj}_x L\). If \(F\subsetneq\operatorname{proj}_x L\), the decomposition is a relaxation; if \(\operatorname{proj}_x L\subsetneq F\), it is a restriction. Even under equality, numerical quality crosses a separate boundary when a sequence of equivalent lifts has constraint-map condition numbers tending to infinity. Hence exact projection is the fidelity boundary, while bounded conditioning distinguishes numerically stable exact decompositions from fragile ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection equality marks exact fidelity; strict inclusion creates a relaxation or restriction, while unbounded conditioning makes an exact lift numerically fragile.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+p}\) are nonempty feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact fidelity is equivalent to \(F=\operatorname{proj}_xL\); failure of either inclusion determines the direction of modeling error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient Spread Does Not Characterize Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary of entry-magnitude spread as a scaling diagnostic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\varepsilon\le1\), let \[A_\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1+\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}.\] Every nonzero entry lies in \([1,2]\), so the entry-magnitude spread is at most \(2\).
