children.title: Unit Imbalance
children.top_down_role: Numerical disparities arising from inconsistent physical or economic units.

knowledge_statements.title: Unit Imbalance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagnoses inconsistent characteristic units before numerical scaling is assessed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(Ax+b\in K\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\). Let \(x=D_u\hat x\), where \(D_u\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is positive diagonal and \(\hat x\) is dimensionless. If \(D_r\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is a positive diagonal matrix of compatible constraint-coordinate scales, define
\[\hat A=D_r^{-1}AD_u,\qquad \hat b=D_r^{-1}b,\qquad \hat K=D_r^{-1}K.\]
Then the equivalent dimensionless constraint is \(\hat A\hat x+\hat b\in\hat K\). Unit imbalance is present when terms combined in a constraint coordinate have incompatible physical dimensions, or when numerical spread is assessed by comparing raw coefficients carrying different units. Scaling diagnostics should instead use a dimensionally consistent transformed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit imbalance occurs when terms combined in a constraint have incompatible units or when raw coefficients with different units are compared; a consistent nondimensionalization must transform both the affine data and the cone.
assumptions_latex: \(D_u\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) and \(D_r\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) are positive diagonal characteristic-scale matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax+b\in K\) is equivalent under \(x=D_u\hat x\) to \(\hat A\hat x+\hat b\in\hat K\), with \(\hat K=D_r^{-1}K\).

children.title: Rescaling Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Representation behavior under changes of variable or constraint scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Rescaling Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent diagonal scalings can change numerical conditioning without changing exact solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(D_r\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) and \(D_x\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular positive diagonal matrices. Under \(x=D_xz\),
\[\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}=D_x\{z\in\mathbb R^n:D_rAD_xz=D_rb\}.\]
Thus exact feasibility is preserved by the variable correspondence, whereas spectral conditioning need not be preserved. For example, with \(A=I_2\), \(D_x=I_2\), and \(D_r=\operatorname{diag}(t,1)\) for \(t\geq1\), one has \(\kappa_2(D_rAD_x)=t\) although \(\kappa_2(A)=1\). Consequently, equivalent diagonal scalings can produce arbitrarily different condition numbers, and scaled residuals or stopping tests need not be uniformly comparable with their original-coordinate counterparts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal rescaling preserves exact feasibility, but an explicit two-dimensional family shows that it can make the matrix condition number arbitrarily large and alter residual interpretation.
assumptions_latex: \(D_r\) and \(D_x\) are nonsingular positive diagonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact feasible sets correspond under \(x=D_xz\), while \(\kappa_2(D_rAD_x)\) is not invariant and can be arbitrarily large in an equivalent scaled family.

notation.meaning: spectral condition number for the displayed nonsingular example

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative sensitivity of a nonsingular square linear system to row and variable scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,D_r,D_x\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, with \(D_r\) and \(D_x\) positive diagonal. Then \[\frac{\kappa_2(A)}{\kappa_2(D_r)\kappa_2(D_x)}\le\kappa_2(D_rAD_x)\le\kappa_2(D_r)\kappa_2(A)\kappa_2(D_x).\] If \(r=Ax-b\), \(x=D_xz\), and \(\widetilde r=D_rr\), then \[\sigma_{[4mmin[0m}(D_r)\|r\|_2\le\|\widetilde r\|_2\le\sigma_{\max}(D_r)\|r\|_2.\] Thus nonuniform scaling can amplify or suppress condition numbers and residual tests although exact feasibility is preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-sided diagonal scaling changes condition numbers by factors controlled by the scaling matrices and changes residual norms by the extreme row-scaling factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed two-sided condition-number and residual-norm bounds hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Number Bounds Under Two-Sided Rescaling
Nearly Singular Quadratic Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral condition for nearly singular factors of nonzero positive-semidefinite quadratic forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(0\neq Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and let \(R\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\) satisfy \(Q=R^\top R\). For \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), call the factor nearly singular at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) when
\[0<\sigma_{\min}^+(R)\leq\varepsilon\sigma_{\max}(R),\]
where \(\sigma_{\min}^+(R)\) is the smallest positive singular value. Defining \(\kappa_2^+(Q)=\lambda_{\max}(Q)/\lambda_{\min}^+(Q)\), this condition is equivalent to \(\kappa_2^+(Q)\geq\varepsilon^{-2}\). Directions associated with the smallest positive singular values have much smaller quadratic curvature than directions associated with the largest singular value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero quadratic factor is nearly singular at a declared tolerance when its smallest positive singular value is tiny relative to its largest; equivalently, the positive spectral condition number of the quadratic matrix is large.
assumptions_latex: \(0\neq Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(Q=R^\top R\) for \(R\in\mathbb R^{r\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\sigma_{\min}^+(R)\leq\varepsilon\sigma_{\max}(R)\) if and only if \(\kappa_2^+(Q)\geq\varepsilon^{-2}\).

notation.meaning: smallest positive singular value of the factor
ratio of largest to smallest positive eigenvalue of the nonzero positive-semidefinite matrix

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral Truncation of a Nearly Singular Quadratic Factor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Controlled low-rank approximation obtained by removing small factor singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_p)V^\top\), with \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_p\ge0\), and let \(R_\delta\) replace each \(\sigma_i\le\delta\) by zero. Set \(Q=R^\top R\), \(Q_\delta=R_\delta^\top R_\delta\), and \(\gamma_\delta=\max(\{\sigma_i:\sigma_i\le\delta\}\cup\{0\})\). Then \[\|Q-Q_\delta\|_2=\gamma_\delta^2\le\delta^2,\qquad 0\le x^\top(Q-Q_\delta)x\le[4m\delta[0m^2\|x\|_2^2.\] The truncation is an exact reformulation precisely when every discarded singular value is zero; otherwise it changes the quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncating small factor singular values perturbs the quadratic matrix by at most the squared threshold and is exact only when all discarded singular values are zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|R^\top R-R_\delta^\top R_\delta\|_2=\gamma_\delta^2\le\delta^2\), and exactness holds exactly when no positive singular value is discarded.

children.title: Redundant Constraint Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Constraint Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic redundancy for constraints in a conic feasible system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C_i\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the feasible set imposed by constraint \(i\), and let \(F=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\). Constraint \(j\) is redundant when
\[\bigcap_{i\ne j}C_i\subseteq C_j,\]
equivalently, when removing it leaves the feasible set unchanged. A collection \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is jointly redundant when \(\bigcap_{i\notin J}C_i=F\). This definition includes affine equalities, inequalities, and cone-membership constraints and concerns exact feasible sets; a mathematically redundant constraint may still affect numerical scaling or solver trajectories.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constraint is redundant when every point satisfying the remaining constraints already satisfies it, so its removal does not change feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constraint \(j\) is redundant exactly when \(\bigcap_{i\ne j}C_i=\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i\).

notation.meaning: feasible set of the ith constraint

Write the equality system as \(a_i^	op x=b_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Equality \(j\) may be deleted if coefficients \(\mu_i\), \(i
e j\), satisfy \[a_j=\sum_{i
e j}\mu_i a_i,\qquad b_j=\sum_{i
e j}\mu_i b_i.\] For a consistent system, repeated compatible deletions can produce an equivalent subsystem whose coefficient rows are linearly independent. If the coefficient identity holds but the right-hand-side identity fails, the original equality system is inconsistent rather than redundantly described.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete an equality only when its coefficient row and right-hand side are the same combination of retained equalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite constraint family contains an inclusion-minimal subfamily with the same feasible set, obtained by repeatedly deleting redundant constraints. Such a subfamily need not be unique: the equalities \(x=0\), \(2x=0\), and \(3x=0\) define \(\{0\}\), and any one alone is an inclusion-minimal equivalent subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated deletion yields an irredundant finite subsystem, but the result can depend on deletion choices.

children.title: Hidden Linear Dependencies
children.top_down_role: Implicit dependence among generated rows, columns, or affine expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Linear Dependencies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic dependence among affine equality constraints after canonicalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the equality subsystem \(Ax=b\), a hidden linear dependency exists when there is a nonzero vector \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[A^\top\lambda=0\quad\text{and}\quad b^\top\lambda=0.\]
Then the weighted sum of the equality rows is the identity \(0=0\), so at least one equality is implied by the others whenever the support of \(\lambda\) is inclusion-minimal. If instead \(A^\top\lambda=0\) but \(b^\top\lambda\ne0\), the equality subsystem is inconsistent rather than redundant. Dependencies may be hidden by auxiliary variables or separately generated canonical constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero combination of equality rows yielding zero coefficients and zero right-hand side reveals redundancy; a nonzero right-hand side reveals inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dependency is certified by \(0\ne\lambda\in\ker(A^\top)\cap b^\perp\).

notation.meaning: vectors orthogonal to the right-hand side

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Certified Detection of Hidden Equality Dependencies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact verification of dependencies suggested by numerical rank revelation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), form the augmented row-data matrix \(G=[A\; -b]\). A rank-revealing factorization may produce candidate vectors \(\widehat\lambda\), but a candidate is a certified compatible dependency only after verifying \[\widehat\lambda\ne0,\qquad A^\top\widehat\lambda=0,\qquad b^\top\widehat\lambda=0\] in exact arithmetic or with explicit residual bounds. If \(A^\top\widehat\lambda=0\) and \(b^\top\widehat\lambda\ne0\), the equality system is inconsistent. A verified row basis of \(G\) yields an equivalent retained equality subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reveal candidate left-null relations, verify their coefficient and right-hand-side residuals, and retain a verified row basis.
assumptions_latex: Numerical rank decisions are not treated as exact certificates without verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Verified vectors in \(\ker(A^\top)\cap b^\perp\) certify compatible dependencies; coefficient-null vectors with nonzero \(b\)-pairing certify inconsistency.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Detection of Hidden Equality Dependencies

children.title: Rank-Deficiency Consequences
children.top_down_role: Numerical and status effects attributable to structural rank loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficiency Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of deficient equality-row rank for linear systems and multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\). Then \(AA^\top\) is singular and there exists \(0\ne\lambda\in\ker(A^\top)\). If \(Ax=b\) is consistent, every such \(\lambda\) satisfies \(\lambda^\top b=0\), revealing a row dependency. Moreover, if a stationarity condition has the form \(c+A^\top y=0\), then \(y+\lambda\) satisfies the same stationarity equation whenever \(y\) does. Thus deficient row rank causes singular normal equations and permits nonunique equality multipliers, although primal solutions need not be nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deficient row rank makes normal equations singular and can make equality multipliers nonunique, but it does not by itself imply nonunique primal solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(AA^\top\) is singular, and equality multipliers are invariant under additions from \(\ker(A^\top)\).

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Singular value decomposition p. 123

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Singular value decomposition p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Row-Rank Deficiency Does Not Imply Primal Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp counterexample to an invalid inference from dependent equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=(1,2)^\top\in\mathbb R^{2\times1}\) and \(b=(1,2)^\top\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=1<2\) and \(AA^\top\) is singular, but \[\{x\in\mathbb R:Ax=b\}=\{1\}.\] Thus deficient equality-row rank can coexist with a unique primal feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependent equality rows can define a unique primal point, so deficient row rank alone does not imply primal nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<2\) while \(\{x:Ax=b\}=\{1\}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Row-Rank Deficiency Does Not Imply Primal Nonuniqueness
Ill-Conditioned Extended Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An exact lifted family whose equality matrix becomes arbitrarily ill-conditioned.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The feasible set \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R:x=0\}\) has, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the exact extended formulation
\[x-y=0,\qquad \varepsilon y=0.\]
Its projection onto the \(x\)-coordinate is exactly \(F\). The lifted equality matrix is
\[M_\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&\varepsilon\end{pmatrix}.\]
As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the largest singular value remains bounded away from zero while the smallest singular value tends to zero, so \(\kappa_2(M_\varepsilon)\to\infty\). This family shows that exact representational equivalence does not guarantee comparable numerical conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This exact lifted family preserves the projected feasible set while its equality-matrix condition number tends to infinity, demonstrating that exact and numerical equivalence differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:M_\varepsilon(x,y)^\top=0\}=\{0\}\), while \(\kappa_2(M_\varepsilon)\to\infty\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).

source_refs.locator: 5.1 Singular value decomposition p. 123

source_witnesses.locator: 5.1 Singular value decomposition p. 123

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditioning Diagnostic for an Extended Equality System
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-dependent spectral diagnosis of the lifted affine equations on the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an extended formulation contain \(M(x,y)=d\) with \(M\ne0\). Define \[\kappa_2^+(M)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}(M)}{\sigma_{\min}^+(M)},\] where \(\sigma_{\min}^+(M)\) is the smallest positive singular value. For a declared threshold \(\tau>1\), call the effective equality operator ill-conditioned when \(\kappa_2^+(M)>\tau\). If \(v\in\ker(M)^\perp\), \(\|v\|_2=1\), and \(\|Mv\|_2\le\eta\), then \(\sigma_{[4mmin[0m}^+(M)\le\eta\). Exact rank loss must be reported separately; without the restriction \(v\perp\ker(M)\), a null vector does not certify a small positive singular value. The diagnostic depends on the chosen lifted coordinates and does not by itself characterize the projected set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective lifted equality operator is ill-conditioned when its positive singular-value ratio exceeds a declared threshold; a nearly null direction certifies this only after structural nullspace directions are excluded.
assumptions_latex: \(M\ne0\) is expressed in fixed lifted coordinates.
A near-null certificate is restricted to \(\ker(M)^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_2^+(M)>\tau\) is the diagnostic, and \(v\in\ker(M)^\perp\), \(\|v\|_2=1\), \(\|Mv\|_2\le\eta\) implies \(\sigma_{[4mmin[0m}^+(M)\le\eta\).

notation.meaning: Ratio of the largest to the smallest positive singular value.
Nearly null direction in the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Diagnostic for an Extended Equality System

children.title: Strict Conic Models
children.top_down_role: Representability boundaries involving strict conic inequalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Conic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal strict feasibility relative to the interior of the modeling cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone with nonempty interior, and consider the affine conic system \(Ax+b\in K\). The model is strictly feasible when there exists \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) such that
\[A\bar x+b\in\operatorname{int}K.\]
Such a point is a strict feasible point. For a product cone \(K=K_1\times\cdots\times K_q\), strict feasibility requires every cone block to lie in its respective interior. This definition concerns primal strictness; dual strict feasibility is defined separately by requiring the dual slack to belong to the interior of the dual cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic model is strictly feasible when some point maps into the cone's interior, blockwise for product cones.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone with \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility holds exactly when \(\exists\bar x\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(A\bar x+b\in\operatorname{int}K\).

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Strict Feasibility for Lower-Dimensional Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic strictness when the modeling cone is not full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\) that may be lower-dimensional, intrinsic strict feasibility is
\[\exists\bar x\quad A\bar x+b\in\operatorname{ri}K.\]
When \(K\) is full-dimensional, \(\operatorname{ri}K=\operatorname{int}K\). Using ambient interior for a lower-dimensional cone would make strict feasibility impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility uses relative interior for a lower-dimensional cone and agrees with ordinary interior in the full-dimensional case.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar x:\ A\bar x+b\in\operatorname{ri}K\text{ is the intrinsic strict-feasibility condition.}

notation.meaning: Interior relative to the span of the cone

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Strict Feasibility for Lower-Dimensional Cones

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry of the Strict Feasible Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and relative openness of affine strict-cone feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be an affine decision domain and let \(s:D\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine. Then
\[F_{\mathrm{s}}:=\{x\in D:s(x)\in\operatorname{ri}K\}\]
is convex and relatively open in \(D\). For \(D=\mathbb R^n\) and full-dimensional \(K\), this is the inverse image of \(\operatorname{int}K\) and is open in \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict feasible set is convex and relatively open in its affine decision domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is an affine set and \(s:D\to\mathbb R^m\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{\mathrm{s}}=s^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}K)\text{ is convex and relatively open in }D.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry of the Strict Feasible Set

children.title: Nonstrict Conic Models
children.top_down_role: Closed-inequality conic formulations used by standard canonical forms.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{ns}}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:b-Ax\in K\}\), and slacks in \(\partial K\) are admissible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine conic feasibility with closed cones.

source_refs.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The nonstrict conic model associated with \(A\), \(b\), and \(K\) has feasible set \[F_{\mathrm{ns}}:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:b-Ax\in K\}.\] Unlike the strict model, it permits \(b-Ax\in\partial K\). Thus feasibility is expressed by membership in the closed cone itself, not membership in its interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstrict conic model permits feasible slacks anywhere in the closed cone, including its boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonstrict Conic Models

source_witnesses.locator: 11.1 From linear to conic models p. 381

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity of Nonstrict Feasible Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology and convexity of an affine preimage of a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a closed convex cone and \(s(x)=b-Ax\). Then
\[F_{\mathrm{ns}}=\{x:s(x)\in K\}=s^{-1}(K)\]
is closed and convex. It may nevertheless be empty, unbounded, or lower-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstrict affine conic feasible set is closed and convex, but need not be nonempty, bounded, or full-dimensional.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{\mathrm{ns}}=s^{-1}(K)\text{ is closed and convex.}
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Convexity of Nonstrict Feasible Sets

children.title: Strictness Closure Gap
children.top_down_role: Topological mismatch between strict source sets and closed conic representations.

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone with nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(F_{\mathrm{s}}\neq\varnothing\), then \(\overline{F_{\mathrm{s}}}=F_{\mathrm{ns}}\); if \(F_{\mathrm{s}}=\varnothing\) and \(F_{\mathrm{ns}}\neq\varnothing\), then the equality fails.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure identity and its failure when strict feasibility is absent.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict feasibility makes strict feasible points dense in the nonstrict set. If the strict set is empty while boundary-feasible points remain, their closures differ.
knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Closure Gap

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-Only Feasibility Produces a Closure Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal system whose feasible slacks remain in a proper cone face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\mathbb R_+^2\) and \(s(x)=(x,0)\). Then
\[F_{\mathrm{ns}}=[0,\infty),\qquad F_{\mathrm{s}}=\varnothing,\]
so \(\overline{F_{\mathrm{s}}}=\varnothing\ne F_{\mathrm{ns}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all feasible slacks remain on a proper cone face, nonstrict feasibility may be nonempty while strict feasibility is empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline{F_{\mathrm{s}}}=\varnothing\ne[0,\infty)=F_{\mathrm{ns}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Only Feasibility Produces a Closure Gap

children.title: Nonclosed Linear Images
children.top_down_role: Nonclosure arising under linear images of conic sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Closedness Boundaries for Linear Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties automatically preserved by linear imaging and elementary sufficient conditions for closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:E\to F\) be linear between finite-dimensional real vector spaces and let \(C\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone. Then \(T(C)\) is a convex cone but need not be closed. It is closed if \(C\) is polyhedral. It is also closed if \(T|_{\operatorname{span}C}\) is injective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a closed convex cone remains a convex cone but may be nonclosed; polyhedrality or injectivity on the cone span guarantees closedness.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(F\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(C\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(C)\text{ is a convex cone and is closed under either stated sufficient condition.}
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Closedness Boundaries for Linear Images

assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb{S}_+^2\) denotes the cone of positive semidefinite real symmetric \(2\times2\) matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The linear image \(T(\mathbb{S}_+^2)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete nonclosed image of a closed semidefinite cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T:\mathbb{S}^2\to\mathbb{R}^2\) by \[T\!\left(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\right)=(a,b).\] Positive semidefiniteness implies either \(a>0\), with arbitrary \(b\) attainable by choosing \(c\geq b^2/a\), or \(a=b=0\). Consequently \[T(\mathbb{S}_+^2)=\{(a,b):a>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.\] The sequence \((1/k,1)\) lies in this image and converges to \((0,1)\), which does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinate image of the closed semidefinite cone can omit a finite limit point and therefore be nonclosed.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Linear Images

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically coherent and the counterexample kind fits the leaf, but no citation or inspectable locator is supplied for this nontrivial construction.

children.title: Nonclosed Projections
children.top_down_role: Nonclosure arising after elimination or projection of lifted variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard sufficient conditions under which coordinate elimination preserves closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+m}\) and \(\pi(x,y)=x\). If \(C\) is compact, then \(\pi(C)\) is compact and closed. If \(C\) is a polyhedron, then \(\pi(C)\) is a polyhedron and closed. Closed convexity alone is insufficient: a closed spectrahedron may have a nonclosed coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coordinate projections of compact sets and polyhedra are closed, but a closed convex spectrahedron can have a nonclosed projection.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to\mathbb R^n\) is the coordinate projection \(\pi(x,y)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ compact or polyhedral}\Longrightarrow\pi(C)\text{ closed; closed convexity alone does not suffice.}
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Projection Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2\) is defined by one positive semidefinite constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The closed convex set \(C\) has the nonclosed projection \(\pi_x(C)=(0,\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A spectrahedral projection exhibiting nonclosedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[C:=\left\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\begin{pmatrix}x&1\\1&y\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\] This spectrahedron is closed and convex. Its defining condition is equivalent to \(x>0\) and \(y\geq1/x\). Hence its first-coordinate projection satisfies \[\pi_x(C)=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in C\}=(0,\infty),\] which is not closed although \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection can destroy closedness: a closed spectrahedron may project exactly onto the open positive half-line.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The spectrahedral projection calculation is precise and the counterexample kind fits the terminal container, but the record has no authoritative source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Attainment Consequences
children.top_down_role: Primal attainment and status issues associated with nonclosed represented sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Preserves Linear Infima but May Create Minimizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment effect of closing a nonclosed feasible image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Then
\[\inf_{x\in S}\langle c,x\rangle=\inf_{x\in\overline S}\langle c,x\rangle.\]
If the common value is finite and every minimizer over \(\overline S\) lies in \(\overline S\setminus S\), the problem over \(S\) does not attain its infimum although the closure-regularized problem does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a feasible set preserves every linear-objective infimum but can introduce minimizers absent from the original problem.
assumptions_latex: The objective is the finite-dimensional linear functional \(x\mapsto\langle c,x\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in S}\langle c,x\rangle=\inf_{x\in\overline S}\langle c,x\rangle,\text{ while attainment may differ.}

notation.meaning: Topological closure of the feasible image

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Preserves Linear Infima but May Create Minimizers

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem \(\inf\{x:(x,y)\in C\}\) has value \(0\) but no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of primal attainment caused by a nonclosed projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(\pi_x(C)=(0,\infty)\), the conic problem \[p^\star:=\inf\{x:(x,y)\in C\}\] has \(p^\star=0\). Every feasible pair has \(x>0\), so no feasible pair attains this value. Thus replacing a projected feasible image by its closure preserves the infimum here but creates the spurious minimizer \(x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonclosed projected feasible set can have a finite infimum that no feasible lifted point attains.
knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Consequences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonattainment claim is consistent with the stated projection and the failure-boundary kind is appropriate, but the record supplies no source. Its statement also contains derivational proof text that should be removed after sourcing.

children.title: Weak-Feasibility Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Modeling interfaces where feasibility lies near conic closure boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric classification of a closed affine set relative to a closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed affine set \(L\) and a nonempty closed convex cone \(K\), exactly one of the following holds: \[\begin{aligned}\text{feasible}&:\ L\cap K\neq\varnothing,\\\text{strongly infeasible}&:\ L\cap K=\varnothing,\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0,\\\text{weakly infeasible}&:\ L\cap K=\varnothing,\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0,\end{aligned}\] where \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=\inf\{\|u-v\|:u\in L,v\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine conic system is feasible, disjoint with positive distance, or disjoint with zero distance; the last case is weak infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a nonempty closed affine set.
\(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
A fixed finite-dimensional norm defines the set distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exactly one of feasibility, strong infeasibility, and weak infeasibility holds.}

notation.meaning: Distance between the affine set and cone

knowledge_statements.title: Metric Conic-Feasibility Trichotomy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximating-sequence form of disjoint zero-distance affine conic feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system is weakly infeasible if and only if \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and there exist \(u_j\in L\), \(v_j\in K\) with \(\|u_j-v_j\|\to0\). When \(L\) and \(K\) are closed and disjoint, every such approximating pair is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility is equivalent to disjoint affine and conic points approaching one another; closed disjoint approximating sequences must escape to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(K\) are nonempty closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\iff\exists u_j\in L,\ v_j\in K:\ \|u_j-v_j\|\to0,\text{ and such pairs are unbounded.}

notation.meaning: Approximating points in the affine set and cone

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Characterization of Weak Infeasibility

assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed affine set and \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface distinguishes feasible, strongly infeasible, and weakly infeasible systems by intersection and distance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric classification of affine conic feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasibility interface for \(L\cap K\) assigns: \[\begin{aligned}\text{feasible}&\iff L\cap K\neq\varnothing,\\ \text{strongly infeasible}&\iff L\cap K=\varnothing\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)>0,\\ \text{weakly infeasible}&\iff L\cap K=\varnothing\ \text{and}\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0,\end{aligned}\] where \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K):=\inf\{\|u-v\|:u\in L,\ v\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine conic systems are feasible, positively separated, or disjoint at zero distance; the last case is weak infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Feasibility Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The metric trichotomy is standard and locally relevant, but terminology such as strong and weak infeasibility requires an authoritative source with a specific locator before acceptance.

children.title: Status Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Indeterminate or unstable solver statuses associated with weak feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frobenius-norm example showing tolerance-induced ambiguity at weak infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathbb S_+^2\) and \(X(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&t\end{pmatrix}\). No \(X(t)\) is positive semidefinite, while \[\lambda_{\min}(X(t))=\frac{t-\sqrt{t^2+4}}2\uparrow0\quad(t\to\infty),\qquad \operatorname{dist}_F(X(t),K)=\left|\lambda_{\min}(X(t))\right|\to0.\] Hence every positive cone-residual tolerance accepts some infeasible member as approximately cone-feasible; residual acceptance alone cannot determine exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This infeasible two-by-two SDP family approaches the PSD cone arbitrarily closely, so any fixed positive residual tolerance is compatible with both approximate acceptance and exact infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: Distance is measured with the Frobenius norm on \(\mathbb S^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X(t)\notin K\ \forall t,\qquad \operatorname{dist}_F(X(t),K)\to0.

notation.meaning: Distance induced by the Frobenius norm

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing-Residual Infeasible SDP Family

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), some infeasible \(X(t)\) lies within \(\varepsilon\) of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based ambiguity near a weakly infeasible semidefinite system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: No \(X(t)\) is positive semidefinite, because a positive semidefinite matrix with zero first diagonal entry must have zero first row. Nevertheless, \[\lambda_{\min}(X(t))=\frac{t-\sqrt{t^2+4}}{2}\uparrow0\quad\text{as }t\to\infty.\] Hence \(\operatorname{dist}(X(t),K)\to0\). Any status rule based only on a fixed cone-residual tolerance can therefore report approximate feasibility for members of this infeasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility produces arbitrarily small cone residuals, so a fixed numerical tolerance cannot reliably distinguish infeasibility from approximate feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Status Ambiguity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The eigenvalue formula supports vanishing residual under standard unitarily invariant matrix norms, but the distance norm is not identified and no authoritative source is cited. The counterexample kind otherwise fits the status-ambiguity leaf.

children.title: Certificate Interpretation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on translating solver certificates into source-model conclusions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Separation Certificate and Its Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretation of an exact multiplier certificate for affine conic infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), any \(y\) satisfying \[A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0\] certifies infeasibility. It also gives a positive separation margin between \(K\) and \(\{x:Ax=b\}\), so no such multiplier exists for a weakly infeasible system. Approximate satisfaction of these relations or a small primal residual alone does not certify exact infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact strict dual separator certifies strong infeasibility, but weakly infeasible systems have no such certificate and numerical residuals alone settle no exact status.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^*y\in K^*,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\ \Longrightarrow\ \{x\in K:Ax=b\}=\varnothing.

notation.meaning: Dual cone under the nonnegative-inner-product convention

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Certificate and Its Limit

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear, and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vector \(y\) with \(A^*y\in K^*\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\) certifies infeasibility, but cannot exist for a weakly infeasible system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between strict separation certificates and weak infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), any \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \[A^*y\in K^*,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0\] is a directly verifiable infeasibility certificate, since feasibility would imply \(\langle b,y\rangle=\langle x,A^*y\rangle\geq0\). Such a strict separator implies positive separation and therefore cannot exist when the system is weakly infeasible. A small residual alone is consequently not an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict dual separation certifies strong infeasibility. Weakly infeasible systems admit no such strict certificate, and small residuals certify neither status.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Interpretation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed dual vector is a valid infeasibility certificate under the stated dual-cone convention, and certificate is the correct content kind. The asserted boundary between strict certificates, positive separation, and weak infeasibility needs an authoritative cited locator.

children.title: Regularization Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Model transformations intended to improve stability near degenerate boundaries.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive cone enlargement for affine conic feasibility near zero set distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty closed affine set, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, and let \(B=\{u:\|u\|\leq1\}\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), \[L\cap(K+\varepsilon B)\neq\varnothing\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)\leq\varepsilon,\] while \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)<\varepsilon\) implies that intersection. Consequently, if \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\), every positive enlargement is feasible although the original system is infeasible. A point feasible only for the enlargement certifies a distance bound for the original system, not exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive additive tolerance makes a weakly infeasible system perturbed-feasible, but this certifies only proximity to the original cone, not exact source-model feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is a nonempty closed affine set.
\(K\) is a nonempty closed convex cone.
\(B\) is the closed unit ball for the norm defining set distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L\cap K=\varnothing,\ \operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\ \Longrightarrow\ L\cap(K+\varepsilon B)\neq\varnothing\quad(\varepsilon>0).
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Regularization and Exact-Status Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(L\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is closed affine, \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) is a closed convex cone, and \(B:=\{u:\|u\|\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L\cap K=\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(L,K)=0\), then \(L\cap(K+\varepsilon B)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive feasibility regularization at zero set distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon>0\), define the regularized feasibility condition \[L\cap(K+\varepsilon B)\neq\varnothing.\] If the original system is weakly infeasible, then this condition holds for every \(\varepsilon>0\), although \(L\cap K=\varnothing\). Thus additive regularization converts weak infeasibility into perturbed feasibility; it approximates the distance relation but is not an exact equivalence transformation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive additive tolerance makes a weakly infeasible system feasible, so regularization changes exact status even while approximating zero distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularization Interfaces

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive regularization property follows the zero-distance definition and fits the interface leaf, but no source or inspectable locator is provided for the claimed regularization interpretation.

children.title: Facial-Reduction Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Modeling handoffs to reduced-face representations of degenerate conic systems.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a closed convex cone and the feasible slack set \(S:=K\cap(b-A\mathbb{R}^n)\) is nonempty.
The required faces are exposed within their current ambient faces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Facial reduction replaces \(K\) by the minimal face \(F_{\min}\) containing \(S\), with \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_{\min}\neq\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the cone containing all feasible slacks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact facial reduction for a feasible finite-dimensional conic system.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37
4.4 Symmetries, Dual Cones, and Facial Structure p. 167
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F_0:=K\). While \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i=\varnothing\), choose an exposing vector \(y_i\in F_i^*\) satisfying \(\langle y_i,s\rangle=0\) for every \(s\in S\), and update \[F_{i+1}:=F_i\cap y_i^\perp.\] Stop when \(S\cap\operatorname{ri}F_i\neq\varnothing\), and output that face. With complete exposing steps, the output is \(F_{\min}\), and replacing \(K\) by \(F_{\min}\) preserves the feasible slack set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facial reduction repeatedly exposes smaller faces containing all feasible slacks until relative strict feasibility holds in the minimal face.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Interfaces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case length of a proper-face facial-reduction sequence in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F_0\supsetneq F_1\supsetneq\cdots\supsetneq F_r=F_{\min}\) and every \(F_{i+1}\) is a proper face of \(F_i\), then \[r\leq \dim(\operatorname{span}F_0)-\dim(\operatorname{span}F_{\min}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper reduction lowers the span dimension, so facial reduction terminates after at most the dimension lost between the initial and minimal faces.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\) is a finite-dimensional closed convex cone.
Each update produces a proper face of the current face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r\leq \dim(\operatorname{span}F_0)-\dim(\operatorname{span}F_{\min}).

notation.meaning: Minimal face containing the feasible slacks

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Facial-Reduction Length

children.title: Preprocessing-to-Solution Boundary
children.top_down_role: Division of responsibility between canonicalization, structural preprocessing, and downstream solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient contract for transferring solutions, values, and certificates between an original problem and a preprocessed problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F,\widehat F\) be the original and preprocessed feasible sets with objectives \(f,\widehat f\). If maps \(P_0:F\to\widehat F\) and \(R:\widehat F\to F\) satisfy \[\widehat f(P_0x)=f(x)\quad(x\in F),\qquad f(R\widehat x)=\widehat f(\widehat x)\quad(\widehat x\in\widehat F),\] then the two problems have the same attainable objective values and optimizers transfer through these maps. A reduced-model certificate supports a conclusion about the original problem only when retained transformation data map it to quantities satisfying the original certificate predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bidirectional feasibility and value-preserving maps give an exact solution handoff; certificates transfer only when they can be reconstructed and checked against the original data.
assumptions_latex: The original and preprocessed problems have feasible sets \(F\) and \(\widehat F\) and objectives \(f\) and \(\widehat f\).
The displayed maps are defined on their full feasible sets and preserve feasibility and objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{f(x):x\in F\}=\{\widehat f(\widehat x):\widehat x\in\widehat F\},\text{ with optimizer transfer through }P_0\text{ and }R.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Preprocessing Handoff Contract

assumptions_latex: An original conic problem \(P\) and a preprocessed problem \(\widehat P\) have feasible sets \(F\) and \(\widehat F\).
Their objective functions are \(f\) and \(\widehat f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Preprocessing is solution-equivalent only when feasible solutions, objective values, and claimed certificates admit valid transfer maps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness requirements at the preprocessing and solver boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A preprocessing interface is solution-equivalent only if maps \(P_0:F\to\widehat F\) and \(R:\widehat F\to F\) are specified so that \[\widehat f(P_0x)=f(x)\quad(x\in F),\qquad f(R\widehat x)=\widehat f(\widehat x)\quad(\widehat x\in\widehat F),\] and every reported optimality or infeasibility certificate has a verifiable pullback for the original data. Facial reduction can satisfy this boundary by retaining reconstruction data; a feasibility regularization without exact pullback does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preprocessing supports original-model conclusions only when solutions, values, and certificates can be reconstructed and verified against the unmodified problem.
knowledge_statements.title: Preprocessing-to-Solution Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed transfer maps give a useful sufficient interface, but the statement presents them as necessary for solution equivalence and adds a certificate-pullback requirement without a source or formal definition of equivalence. The exact mathematical version is therefore not reliable enough to accept.

assumptions_latex: Only affine equations, affine maps, projections, and membership in convex cones are permitted in the selected conic library.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonconvex quadratic region has no exact representation using only those convex conic operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex-conic representability boundary for quadratic sublevel regions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine preimages and projections of convex conic feasible sets are convex. Accordingly, a nonconvex quadratic region \[Q:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x^\top Hx+2h^\top x+r\leq0\}\] has no exact formulation using only convex cones and affine constraints. One such region is \[Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}:1-x^2\leq0\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine convex-conic formulations produce convex sets, so a genuinely nonconvex quadratic region has no exact representation using only those operations.

children.title: Finite Unions of Conic Sets
children.top_down_role: Representability limits for finite disjunctions of conic regions.

assumptions_latex: A conic formulation uses a closed convex cone \(K\) and continuous auxiliary variables only.
Each set \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is representable as a projection of an affine slice of a cone from the selected library.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite union is not, in general, representable by one continuous convex conic formulation; exact modeling generally requires a disjunctive or integer-valued selector unless the union itself admits a separate convex conic representation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous convex conic representability, excluding integer or explicit disjunctive extensions.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\geq 2\), let each \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be the projection of an affine slice of a closed convex cone. Every such \(S_i\) is convex, whereas \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m S_i\) need not be convex. For example, \(S_1=\{-1\}\) and \(S_2=\{1\}\) are polyhedrally representable, but \(S_1\cup S_2\) is nonconvex. Because projections of convex feasible sets are convex, this union has no exact formulation using only affine constraints, continuous auxiliary variables, and one convex cone. Exact representation requires additional disjunctive structure unless the particular union is convex and independently conic representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite unions of conic-representable sets may be nonconvex, so continuous convex conic formulations are not closed under finite union without extra disjunctive structure.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Unions of Conic Sets

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Conic-Set Complements
children.top_down_role: Representability limits for complements of conic-representable sets.

assumptions_latex: The formulation class consists of projections of affine slices of closed convex cones with continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The class is not closed under set complementation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementation relative to the full Euclidean ambient space.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be conic representable by continuous variables over a convex cone. Although \(S\) is convex, its complement \(S^c=\mathbb{R}^n\setminus S\) generally is not. For instance, the interval \(S=[-1,1]\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) is polyhedrally representable, while \(S^c=(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty)\) is nonconvex. Hence \(S^c\) cannot be the projection of an affine slice of any convex cone. Complementation therefore leaves the continuous convex conic modeling class in general, even when the original set has a simple linear-conic description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conic-representable set can have a nonconvex complement, so continuous convex conic representability is not closed under complementation.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Set Complements

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Disjunctive Representation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary between continuous conic models and formulations requiring discrete structure.

assumptions_latex: Each branch \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has an exact continuous convex conic formulation.
The desired feasible set is the logical disjunction \(x\in S_1\lor\cdots\lor x\in S_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An exact continuous conic formulation exists only when the union has an independent convex conic representation; otherwise discrete or explicit disjunctive structure is necessary.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between continuous conic modeling and mixed-integer conic disjunctions.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be continuously conic representable and let \(S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m S_i\). If \(S\) is nonconvex, no exact formulation of \(S\) can consist solely of affine constraints, continuous auxiliary variables, and membership in convex cones, because projection preserves convexity. An exact branch-selection formulation must therefore introduce nonconvex structure, commonly variables \(z_i\in\{0,1\}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i=1}^m z_i=1\), together with constraints activating the selected branch. The boundary disappears only when \(S\) itself possesses an independent convex conic representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A genuinely nonconvex disjunction cannot be encoded exactly by continuous convex cones; it needs discrete selectors or another nonconvex mechanism.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Representation Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251

assumptions_latex: A fixed cone library \(\mathcal{L}\) and allowed affine-lift operations are specified.
Representability means exact equality after projecting finitely many auxiliary variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of \(\mathcal{L}\)-representability is library-relative and does not imply nonconvexity or failure of representation over a richer cone library.

notation.meaning: Selected collection of admissible convex cones

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability is relative to a fixed finite-lift modeling language.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a cone library \(\mathcal{L}\). A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) lies outside \(\mathcal{L}\) when there do not exist a finite-dimensional auxiliary variable \(u\), affine maps \(F_j\), and cones \(K_j\in\mathcal{L}\) such that \[S=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists u,\ F_j(x,u)\in K_j\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,r\}.\] This classification is relative to the selected library and permitted lift operations. A set outside a polyhedral library may be representable using second-order or semidefinite cones, while a set outside every considered convex-cone library may fail because it is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is outside a selected cone library when no allowed finite affine lift over that library projects exactly to the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Sets Outside Selected Cone Libraries

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Obstruction for Continuous Convex-Cone Libraries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal necessary condition under finite affine operations over convex cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every cone in \(\mathcal L\) is convex and the permitted operations are finite affine inverse images, intersections or products, and coordinate projections, then every exactly \(\mathcal L\)-representable set is convex. Hence every nonconvex target lies outside this continuous convex-conic language, although convexity alone is not sufficient for representability over a fixed library.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite continuous affine formulations over convex cones can represent only convex sets, while convexity alone need not ensure representation over a restricted library.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive cone in \(\mathcal L\) is convex.
Only finite affine-conic constraints and coordinate projection are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\in\operatorname{Rep}(\mathcal L)\Longrightarrow S\text{ is convex}.

notation.meaning: Class of sets exactly representable over the selected library

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Obstruction for Continuous Convex-Cone Libraries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representability ordering induced by enlarging the primitive cone library.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal L_1\subseteq\mathcal L_2\), with the same permitted finite affine-lift operations. Then every exactly \(\mathcal L_1\)-representable set is exactly \(\mathcal L_2\)-representable. Equivalently, a set outside \(\mathcal L_2\) is also outside \(\mathcal L_1\). The converse implications need not hold when the enrichment is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enlarging a cone library can only enlarge the class of exactly representable sets.
assumptions_latex: Both libraries use the same finite affine-lift syntax.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Rep}(\mathcal L_1)\subseteq\operatorname{Rep}(\mathcal L_2).

notation.meaning: Class of sets exactly representable over library \(\mathcal L\)

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Under Cone-Library Enrichment

children.title: Exact Representability Regime
children.top_down_role: Problem classes admitting exact models over the selected cone library.

assumptions_latex: A cone library \(\mathcal{L}\) and finite affine-lift syntax are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact representability means equality, not merely containment or asymptotic convergence, between \(S\) and the projected conic feasible set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact lifted conic representation relative to \(\mathcal{L}\).

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is exactly \(\mathcal{L}\)-representable if there exist a finite-dimensional auxiliary space, cones \(K_j\in\mathcal{L}\), and affine maps \(F_j\) for which \[Q=\{(x,u):F_j(x,u)\in K_j,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\quad\text{and}\quad S=\pi_x(Q).\] Exactness requires both implications: every \(x\in S\) has a feasible lift \(u\), and every feasible lifted point projects into \(S\). No approximation tolerance, limiting hierarchy, closure operation, or unmodeled integrality condition is included in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact conic representability requires the projected lifted conic set to equal the target set in both directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Representability Regime

source_witnesses.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

children.title: Inner-Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of feasibility-preserving conic inner approximations.

assumptions_latex: Each approximation \(S_k^{\mathrm{in}}\) is representable over the selected cone library.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inner approximation preserves feasibility for retained points but may exclude feasible points and raise a minimization optimum.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set containment and objective effects for minimization models.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic set \(S_k^{\mathrm{in}}\) is an inner approximation of \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) when \(S_k^{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq S\). Thus every point feasible for the approximate model is feasible for the original model, but points in \(S\setminus S_k^{\mathrm{in}}\) are lost. For any real-valued objective \(f\), whenever both infima are defined, \[\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\leq \inf_{x\in S_k^{\mathrm{in}}}f(x).\] Exact representability occurs at level \(k\) precisely when \(S_k^{\mathrm{in}}=S\); convergence of a hierarchy without equality at any finite level remains approximation rather than exact representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner conic approximation lies inside the target, guarantees original feasibility, and can worsen a minimization value by discarding feasible points.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Approximation Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nesting Does Not Ensure Target-Value Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone bounds and the exact value-convergence boundary for nested inner approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_1^{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq S_2^{\mathrm{in}}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S\), and set \(v_k=\inf_{x\in S_k^{\mathrm{in}}}f(x)\) and \(v=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\). Then \(v\leq v_{k+1}\leq v_k\) and \[\lim_{k\to\infty}v_k=\inf_{x\in\bigcup_k S_k^{\mathrm{in}}}f(x).\] Therefore nesting alone does not imply convergence to \(v\); convergence occurs exactly when \(\inf_{ igcup_kS_k^{\mathrm{in}}}f=\inf_S f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding inner approximations give decreasing valid upper bounds, but their limit is the infimum over their union and need not equal the target optimum.
assumptions_latex: The extended-real infima are defined without an indeterminate comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\leq v_{k+1}\leq v_k,\qquad \inf_k v_k=\inf_{x\in\bigcup_kS_k^{\mathrm{in}}}f(x).
knowledge_statements.title: Nesting Does Not Ensure Target-Value Convergence

children.title: Outer-Approximation Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of containment-preserving conic outer approximations.

assumptions_latex: Each approximation \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\) is representable over the selected cone library.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outer approximation supplies a minimization lower bound but may return points infeasible for the target set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set containment and objective effects for minimization models.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4
source_refs.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conic set \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\) is an outer approximation of \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) when \(S\subseteq S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\). It retains every original feasible point but may admit spurious points in \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\setminus S\). For any real-valued objective \(f\), whenever both infima are defined, \[\inf_{x\in S_k^{\mathrm{out}}}f(x)\leq \inf_{x\in S}f(x).\] Consequently the approximate minimization value is a lower bound, while an approximate optimizer need not be feasible for \(S\). Equality \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}=S\) marks entry into the exact-representability regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer conic approximation contains the target and yields a minimization lower bound, but its optimizer may violate the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer-Approximation Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4
source_witnesses.source_title: Advances in Linear Matrix Inequality Methods in Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient regularity for convergence of nested outer-approximation lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq S_{k+1}^{\mathrm{out}}\subseteq S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\), let \(S=\bigcap_kS_k^{\mathrm{out}}\), and set \(v_k=\inf_{x\in S_k^{\mathrm{out}}}f(x)\) and \(v=\inf_{x\in S}f(x)\). Then \(v_k\leq v_{k+1}\leq v\). If the sets \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\) are closed, \(f\) is lower semicontinuous, \(v\) is finite, and for some \(\alpha>v\) the set \(\{x\in S_1^{\mathrm{out}}:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact, then \(v_k\uparrow v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tightening outer approximations raises valid lower bounds, and closedness, lower semicontinuity, and a common compact sublevel set ensure convergence to the target value.
assumptions_latex: Every \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\) is closed and \(f\) is lower semicontinuous.
\(v=\inf_Sf\in\mathbb R\), and \(\{x\in S_1^{\mathrm{out}}:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact for some \(\alpha>v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v_k\leq v_{k+1}\leq v,\qquad v_k\uparrow v.
knowledge_statements.title: Value Convergence Under Compactness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer Set Convergence Without Value Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of objective-value convergence without lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{0\}\), \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}=[0,1/k]\), and define \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(x>0\). Then \(S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\downarrow S\), but \[\inf_{x\in S_k^{\mathrm{out}}}f(x)=0\quad\text{for every }k,\qquad \inf_{x\in S}f(x)=1.\] Thus exact decreasing set convergence alone does not force convergence of the lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decreasing outer sets can converge exactly to the target while their lower bounds fail to converge when the objective is discontinuous at the limit set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_k^{\mathrm{out}}\downarrow S,\qquad \lim_k\inf_{S_k^{\mathrm{out}}}f=0<1=\inf_Sf.
knowledge_statements.title: Outer Set Convergence Without Value Convergence

children.title: Duality Boundary
children.top_down_role: Division between conic modeling choices and downstream duality analysis.

assumptions_latex:
The canonical primal problem is \(\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,
 x\in K\}\) with \(K\) a closed convex cone.
The dual cone is formed using the same inner product and sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonicalization determines the formal dual and weak duality, but zero gap and attainment require additional regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic duality under a fixed primal sign convention.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Duality, optimality conditions, and perturbation analysis p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal conic program \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,
 x\in K\}\), canonicalization determines the formal dual \[d^*=\sup\{\langle b,y\rangle:c-A^*y=s,
 s\in K^*\}.\] Every primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \((y,s)
 satisfy \(\langle b,y\rangle\leq\langle c,x\rangle\), so \(d^*\leq p^*\). The modeling layer alone does not imply \(d^*=p^*\), primal or dual attainment, or existence of optimal certificates. Those conclusions cross the duality boundary and require constraint qualifications or other closedness and regularity hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical form determines a formal dual and weak duality, but strong duality and attainment require separate regularity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Duality Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Duality, optimality conditions, and perturbation analysis p. 67

children.title: Certificate Boundary
children.top_down_role: Division between model canonicalization and certificate interpretation.

assumptions_latex: The canonical primal problem is \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a closed convex cone.
The tuple \((x,y,s)\) satisfies the primal and dual feasibility conditions exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple certifies upper and lower objective bounds; zero gap proves optimality, and a gap at most \(\varepsilon\) proves an absolute objective gap at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasible primal-dual certificates for canonical conic programs; tolerance-based residual certificates require separate error bounds.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Duality, optimality conditions, and perturbation analysis p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\) and its dual, a tuple \((x,y,s)\) satisfying \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), \(A^*y+s=c\), and \(s\in K^*\) is an exact primal-dual certificate. It verifies \[\langle b,y\rangle\leq p^*\leq\langle c,x\rangle,\qquad g=\langle c,x\rangle-\langle b,y\rangle=\langle s,x\rangle\geq0.\] If \(g=0\), both feasible points are optimal. If \(g\leq\varepsilon\) for \(\varepsilon\geq0\), their objective values are each within an absolute primal-dual gap of at most \(\varepsilon\). Certificates based on nonzero feasibility or cone-membership residuals require additional residual-to-objective error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly feasible primal-dual tuple certifies objective bounds; zero gap proves optimality, and a gap at most epsilon bounds the absolute primal-dual objective gap. Nonzero feasibility residuals require separate error analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Boundary

children.title: Modeling-to-Duality Handoff
children.top_down_role: Representation data passed from canonical models to dual analysis.

assumptions_latex: An original model is transformed into an equivalent canonical conic program.
The transformation records the objective offset and maps between original and canonical variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Only canonical dual variables together with the recorded transformation maps can be interpreted as certificates for the original model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic preservation across canonicalization and dual interpretation.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Duality, optimality conditions, and perturbation analysis p. 67

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose canonicalization maps an original minimization model in \(z\) to \(p^*=\inf\{\langle c,x\rangle+\alpha:Ax=b,
 x\in K\}\). A valid modeling-to-duality handoff records: an embedding that gives a canonical feasible \(x\) from each original feasible \(z\); a recovery map from canonical solutions to original solutions; the objective offset \(\alpha\); and the correspondence between generated conic rows and original constraints. The formal dual is then constructed from \((A,b,c,K)
. Without the recorded correspondence, dual feasibility remains meaningful for the canonical problem but multipliers and certificates cannot reliably be attributed to the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical duals become meaningful for the original model only when canonicalization preserves variable, objective, and constraint provenance maps.
knowledge_statements.title: Modeling-to-Duality Handoff

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Duality, optimality conditions, and perturbation analysis p. 67

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The handoff principle is plausible and fits the terminal container, but the cited duality section does not specifically establish canonicalization provenance maps, recovery maps, objective offsets, or attribution of generated dual multipliers to original constraints. A source on conic canonicalization or disciplined-convex-program transformations with dual-variable recovery is required.

children.title: Solver Algorithm Boundary
children.top_down_role: Division between canonical model construction and numerical solution procedures.

assumptions_latex: The model has been reduced to finite-dimensional affine constraints and memberships in supported closed convex cones.
A solver declares its supported cone blocks, numerical precision convention, and admissible problem regularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Canonical representability supplies solver input, not a guarantee of convergence, accuracy, or a particular algorithmic trajectory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface from canonical representation to numerical conic algorithms.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A canonical conic representation consisting of \(Ax=b\) and \(x\in K_1\times\cdots\times K_r\) crosses into the solver layer only after each cone block has a supported computational interface, such as a barrier, projection, or separation oracle. Exact representability alone does not select an algorithm or imply that a solver returns an \(\varepsilon\)-accurate solution. Convergence and termination additionally depend on the chosen method, scaling, initialization, regularity, arithmetic model, and stopping residuals. Thus the modeling layer is responsible for producing canonical data and recovery maps, while algorithm selection and numerical behavior lie beyond its boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A canonical conic model is solver input, but algorithm choice, convergence, and numerical accuracy require additional computational assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Solver Algorithm Boundary

children.top_down_role: Division between representation-size discussion and formal solver complexity.

assumptions_latex: A canonical conic formulation and an accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed.
The computational model specifies arithmetic costs and the cone operations or oracles counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A complexity claim requires representation-size and cone-geometry parameters beyond mere exact conic representability.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.2 Approximation and complexity p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The statement that a feasible region has an exact conic representation does not by itself yield an iteration or bit-complexity bound. Such a bound must specify the canonical encoding length \(L\), the accuracy criterion \(\varepsilon\), the algorithm, the arithmetic or oracle model, and geometric parameters of the cones. For example, an interior-point analysis additionally depends on existence and parameter \(\nu\) of a suitable self-concordant barrier and on assumptions ensuring an appropriate starting point or embedding. Lifted formulations representing the same set may have different dimensions, barrier parameters, sparsity, and conditioning, and therefore different computational complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic representability alone gives no complexity bound; analysis also needs encoding size, accuracy, algorithm, oracle costs, and cone geometry.
