children.title: Representation-to-Solver Handoff
children.top_down_role: Structural model information exposed to downstream conic solvers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic conditions under which canonical primal data and recovery information preserve the original optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_o\) be the original feasible set with objective \(f\), and let \(F_c:=\{z:Az=b,\ z\in K\}\) have objective \(\langle c,z\rangle+\delta\). A recovery map \(T:F_c\to F_o\) defines an exact handoff when
\[T(F_c)=F_o,\qquad f(Tz)=\langle c,z\rangle+\delta\quad(z\in F_c).\]
The handoff data must also specify dimensions, pairings, cone-block ordering, and an adjoint satisfying \(\langle Az,y\rangle=\langle z,A^*y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver handoff is exact when recovered canonical feasible points exhaust the original feasible set and preserve every objective value, with dimensions, pairings, cone blocks, and adjoints declared consistently.
assumptions_latex: \(F_o\) and \(F_c\) are the original and canonical feasible sets.
\(T\) is a declared recovery map and \(\delta\) is the canonical objective offset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(F_c)=F_o\ \text{and}\ f\circ T=\langle c,\cdot\rangle+\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ \inf_{x\in F_o}f(x)=\inf_{z\in F_c}(\langle c,z\rangle+\delta).

notation.meaning: Recovery map from canonical variables to original variables

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Representation-to-Solver Handoff Contract

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Which solver conclusions transfer through an exact primal handoff and which require additional certificate maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under an exact handoff, canonical feasibility, infeasibility, attained optima, and objective unboundedness transfer to the original problem through the feasible-set and objective identities. A canonical dual multiplier, residual, or infeasibility certificate is not automatically an original-model certificate: such transfer additionally requires an explicitly declared map whose sign, pairing, and pullback identities verify the corresponding original bound or alternative condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact primal equivalence transfers primal status and values, but dual or infeasibility certificates require separately verified certificate-recovery maps.
assumptions_latex: The exact handoff identities \(T(F_c)=F_o\) and \(f(Tz)=\langle c,z\rangle+\delta\) hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Primal statuses transfer by exactness; certificate semantics transfer only through verified certificate maps.}
knowledge_statements.title: Status and Certificate Transfer Boundary

assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(E\).
\(A:E\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is linear, with declared adjoint \(A^*\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \(c\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal H=(A,b,c,K,T,\delta)\) is a complete representation-to-solver handoff precisely when the conic data, dual convention, and recovery map satisfy the stated compatibility conditions.

notation.meaning: Dual cone \(\{s\in E:\langle s,x\rangle\geq0\text{ for all }x\in K\}\).
Recovery map from canonical solver variables to original model variables.
Constant objective offset introduced by canonicalization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness conditions for passing a finite-dimensional conic representation to a primal-dual solver.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The canonical problem and its declared dual are
\[\inf_{x\in E}\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\},\qquad \sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\,s\in K^*}\{\langle b,y\rangle:A^*y+s=c\}.\]
A handoff \(\mathcal H=(A,b,c,K,T,\delta)\) is complete when all dimensions and inner products are declared, the implemented adjoint satisfies \(\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,A^*y\rangle\), and every canonical feasible \(x\) is recovered as an original feasible point \(T(x)\) whose original objective equals \(\langle c,x\rangle+\delta\). Cone ordering, sign conventions, and block structure must be supplied without changing these equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver handoff is complete when conic data, adjoint and dual conventions, cone blocks, recovery mapping, and objective offset are explicit and mutually consistent.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation-to-Solver Handoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited semidefinite-optimization section does not specifically support the proposed general conic handoff contract, recovery map, objective offset, or asserted completeness criterion. Mathematically, mapping every canonical feasible point to an original feasible point with the same objective is only one-directional and does not ensure that the canonical representation preserves all relevant original feasible points or the optimal value. A source and precise equivalence conditions are required before the claim can be reviewed reliably.

children.title: Semidefinite Modeling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Division between general conic canonicalization and specialized semidefinite modeling.

assumptions_latex: All matrix pencils and auxiliary-variable spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) lies within the semidefinite modeling boundary if and only if it has a finite spectrahedral lift of the displayed form.

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive semidefinite matrices of order \(q\).
Affine symmetric-matrix pencil in visible and auxiliary variables.
Projection of the feasible spectrahedron onto the visible variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lifted semidefinite representability, including spectrahedra as the zero-lift special case.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) lies within the semidefinite modeling boundary if there exist integers \(r\geq 0\) and \(q\geq 1\), matrices \(F_0,F_1,\ldots,F_n,G_1,\ldots,G_r\in\mathbb{S}^q\), and auxiliary variables \(w\in\mathbb{R}^r\) such that
\[S=\left\{u\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists w\in\mathbb{R}^r,\ F(u,w):=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n u_iF_i+\sum_{j=1}^r w_jG_j\succeq0\right\}.\]
Thus spectrahedra and their finite-dimensional linear projections are admitted; the case \(r=0\) gives a direct affine linear matrix inequality. Whether a set belongs to this boundary is determined by the existence of such a representation, independently of how the set was originally described.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The semidefinite modeling boundary consists exactly of sets that are finite-dimensional linear projections of affine positive-semidefinite matrix inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Modeling Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3

children.title: Algebraic Modeling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Division between conic representations and polynomial or algebraic formulations.

assumptions_latex: All variables are real and all polynomial coefficients are explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A model lies within the algebraic boundary when its objective and feasible set admit the displayed finite polynomial description.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite polynomial optimization models over basic closed semialgebraic sets; convexity is not assumed.

source_refs.locator: Part II Polynomial and Semi-Algebraic Optimization p. 79

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite optimization model lies within the algebraic modeling boundary when it can be written as
\[\inf_{x\in X}p(x),\qquad X:=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:g_i(x)\geq0\ \text{for }i=1,\ldots,m,\ h_j(x)=0\ \text{for }j=1,\ldots,\ell\right\},\]
where \(p,g_i,h_j\in\mathbb{R}[x]\). The boundary permits nonconvex objectives and feasible sets, but excludes transcendental, discontinuous, or implicitly defined relations unless they are replaced by an equivalent finite polynomial system, possibly using additional real variables whose projection recovers the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algebraic optimization model has a polynomial objective and finitely many polynomial equality and inequality constraints, possibly after an exact finite-variable lift.
knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Modeling Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transcendental Graph Outside the Algebraic Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard nonsemialgebraic relation excluded from exact finite polynomial-lift modeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph \(G=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y=e^x\}\) is not semialgebraic. Therefore there are no finitely many auxiliary real variables and finitely many polynomial equalities and inequalities whose projection onto \((x,y)\) equals \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full graph of the exponential function has no exact finite real-polynomial lift because it is not semialgebraic.
assumptions_latex: Only finitely many real auxiliary variables and finitely many polynomial equality or inequality constraints are allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) does not admit an exact finite polynomial lift.

notation.meaning: Graph of the real exponential function

knowledge_statements.title: Transcendental Graph Outside the Algebraic Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary representability property of finite polynomial equality-and-inequality models with auxiliary real variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+r}\) be semialgebraic and let \(\pi:\mathbb{R}^{n+r}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be a coordinate projection. Then \(\pi(T)\) is semialgebraic. Consequently, every visible feasible set represented by finitely many polynomial equalities and inequalities with finitely many real auxiliary variables is semialgebraic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tarski–Seidenberg projection preserves semialgebraicity, so every feasible set represented by a finite polynomial lift is semialgebraic.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is a coordinate projection onto the visible variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(T)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is semialgebraic.

notation.meaning: Visible feasible set obtained by projection

children.title: Cone-to-Polynomial Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between conic models and algebraic representations.

assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) has degree at most \(2d\), where \(d\) is a nonnegative integer.
\(v_d(x)\in\mathbb{R}^N\), with \(N=\binom{n+d}{d}\), is the vector of all monomials in \(x\) of total degree at most \(d\), listed in a fixed order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polynomial \(p\) is a sum of squares of polynomials of degree at most \(d\) if and only if the coefficient-matching system admits a matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^N\).

notation.meaning: Monomial basis vector through total degree \(d\), of length \(N=\binom{n+d}{d}\).
Coefficient of the monomial \(x^\alpha\) in a polynomial.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram-matrix interface from bounded-degree sum-of-squares membership to semidefinite feasibility.

source_refs.locator: 3 Polynomial Optimization, Sums of Squares, and Applications p. 47
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite relaxations for polynomial optimization p. 87
source_refs.source_title: An Introduction to Polynomial and Semi-Algebraic Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The polynomial \(p\) is a sum of squares of polynomials of degree at most \(d\) if and only if there exists a matrix \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^N\) such that
\[p(x)=v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x).\]
For the fixed monomial vector \(v_d\), this identity is equivalent to the affine coefficient equations
\[[x^\alpha]p=[x^\alpha]\bigl(v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x)\bigr)\quad\text{for every multi-index }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n\text{ with }|\alpha|\leq2d.\]
Consequently, bounded-degree sum-of-squares membership is represented as affine equations in the entries of \(Q\) together with the semidefinite constraint \(Q\in\mathbb{S}_+^N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial of degree at most twice the degree bound is a sum of squares within that bound exactly when it has a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix of the declared monomial-basis dimension satisfying linear coefficient-matching equations.
knowledge_statements.title: Cone-to-Polynomial Interface

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegativity Does Not Imply an SOS Gram Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp limitation of the SOS-to-PSD interface: it represents the SOS cone, not the full polynomial-nonnegativity cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Motzkin polynomial \[M(x,y)=x^4y^2+x^2y^4+1-3x^2y^2\] is globally nonnegative on \(\mathbb R^2\) but is not a sum of squares of real polynomials. Consequently, it has no positive-semidefinite polynomial Gram representation, despite being nonnegative everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Motzkin polynomial is globally nonnegative but not SOS, so the PSD Gram interface does not characterize general polynomial nonnegativity.
assumptions_latex: Polynomials and sums of squares are over \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\geq0\text{ on }\mathbb R^2\quad\text{and}\quad M\notin\Sigma[x,y].\)

notation.meaning: Cone of sums of squares of real polynomials

knowledge_statements.title: Nonnegativity Does Not Imply an SOS Gram Matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure, nonuniqueness, factor recovery, and rank interpretation of PSD Gram representations in a fixed monomial basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(p\) and \(v_d\), the Gram set \(\mathcal G(p)=\{Q\in\mathbb S_+^N:v_d(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv_d(x)=p(x)\}\) is a spectrahedron and need not be a singleton. If \(Q\in\mathcal G(p)\) has rank \(r\), a factorization \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\) gives \(p=\sum_{i=1}^r(R_{i:}v_d)^2\). Conversely, a representation of \(p\) as \(r\) squares of polynomials in the span of \(v_d\) gives a member of \(\mathcal G(p)\) of rank at most \(r\). Thus the minimum number of squares equals the minimum rank over \(\mathcal G(p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible Gram matrices form a possibly non-singleton spectrahedron, and their minimum rank equals the minimum number of squares in an SOS decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(v_d\) spans the polynomials of degree at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{r:p=\sum_{i=1}^r q_i^2,\ \deg q_i\le d\}=\min\{\operatorname{rank}Q:Q\in\mathcal G(p)\}.\)

notation.meaning: PSD Gram spectrahedron of the polynomial

knowledge_statements.title: Gram Spectrahedron and Square-Length Rank
